Preface 
This volume contains the proceedings (Par t II) of the 4th KES Symposium on Agent 
and Multi-Agent Systems – Technologies and Applications (KES-AMSTA 2010) held 
at Gdynia Maritime University in Pola nd during June 23–25, 2010. The symposium 
was organized by Gdynia Maritime University, KES International and its Focus Group 
on Agent and Multi-Agent Systems. The KES-AMSTA Symposium series is a sub-
series of the KES Conference series. 
Following the successes of the First KES Symposium on Agent and Multi-Agent 
Systems – Technologies and Applications (KES-AMSTA 2007) held in Wrocław, 
Poland, the Second KES Symposium on Agent and Multi-Agent Systems  
(KES-AMSTA 2008) held in Incheon, Korea, and the Third KES Symposium on 
Agent and Multi-Agent Systems (KES-AMSTA  2009) held in Uppsala, Sweden,  
KES-AMSTA 2010 featured keynote talks, oral presentations, and a number of invited 
sessions, closely aligned to the theme of the conference. 
 The aim of the symposium was to provide an internationally respected forum for 
scientific research in the technologies and applications of agent and multi-agent sys-
tems. The discussed field is concerned with the development and analysis of sophisti-
cated, AI-based problem-solving and contro l architectures for both single-agent and 
multiple-agent systems. Current topics of research in multi-agent systems include, 
among others, agent-oriented software engineering, beliefs, desires, and intentions, 
agent cooperation, coordination, negotiation, organization and communication,  
distributed problem solving, specification of agent communication languages and 
formalization of ontologies.  
The symposium attracted a substantial number of researchers and practitioners from 
all over the world who submitted their papers for nine main tracks covering the meth-
odology and applications of agent and multi-agent systems and five special sessions 
on specific topics within the field. Subm issions came from over 35 countries. Each 
paper was peer reviewed by at least two members of the International Program Com-
mittee and International Reviewer Board. Only 83 papers were selected for oral pres-
entation and publication in the two volumes of the KES-AMSTA 2010 proceedings.  
The Program Committee defined the following main tracks: Multi-Agent Systems 
Design and Implementation, Negotiations and Social Issues, Web Services and  
Semantic Web, Cooperation, Coordination and Teamwork, Agent-Based Modeling,

Preface

Simulation and Decision Making, Multi-Agent Applications, Management and  
e-Business, Mobile Agents and Robots, and Machine Learning. In addition to the 
main tracks of the symposium there were the following five special sessions: Agent-
Based Optimization (ABO2010), Agent-Enabled Social Computing (AESC2010), 
Digital Economy (DE2010), Using Intelligent Systems for Information Technology 
Assessment (ISITA2010) and a Doctoral Track. 
Accepted and presented papers highlight new trends and challenges in agent and 
multi-agent research. We hope these results will be of value to the research commu-
nity working in the fields of artificial intelligence, collective computational intelli-
gence, robotics, machine learning and, in particular, agent and multi-agent systems 
technologies and applications.

Agent-Based Decision Making in the Electronic 
Marketplace: Interactive Negotiation 
Sung Ho Ha 
School of Business Administration, Kyungpook National University, Daegu, Korea 
hsh@mail.knu.ac.kr 
Abstract. Negotiation is a process of reaching an agreement on the transaction 
terms (e.g., price, quantity) for two or more parties. Negotiation tries to maxi-
mize the benefits for all parties concerned. Instead of human-based negotiation, 
the e-commerce environment provides such an environment as adopting auto-
mated negotiation. Under these circumstances, choosing agent technology is 
appropriate for an automatic electronic negotiation platform, since autonomous 
software agents try to perform the best deal on behalf of the human participants. 
Negotiation agents need a clear-cut definition of negotiation models or strate-
gies. In reality, most bargaining systems embody almost one negotiation model. 
In this article, a multi-agent negotiation system with selectable negotiation 
strategies is introduced. It allows agents to select a user’s favorite negotiation 
strategy, which can be preinstalled as a component in the system. A prototype 
system is implemented in compliance with FIPA specifications.  
Keywords: Multi agent, mobile agent, negotiation agent, negotiation strategy. 
1   Introduction 
Negotiation is a process of reaching an agreement on the terms of a transaction, in-
cluding price and quantity, for two or more parties [1]. It tries to reach a deal to 
maximize the benefits for all parties concerned. Human-based negotiation, however, 
could be an expensive and non-optimal method, even though beneficial to the partici-
pants. Traditional human-based negotiation has several shortcomings. More time may 
be needed to reach a consensus, if some of the human parties involved do not concede 
in order to maximize their own benefits or goals. It could be difficult for novice nego-
tiators to mimic experts who have skillful negotiation tactics. Therefore, automated 
negotiation is particularly useful in an e-commerce environment. 
A negotiation process is competitive and is entirely dependent of negotiation coun-
terparts. Thus, choosing agent technology is appropriate for an automatic electronic 
negotiation platform, since autonomous software agents strive for the best deal on 
behalf of the human participants [2][3]. In order to achieve the best results, a negotia-
tion agent needs a clear-cut definition of what capabilities it can provide––negotiation 
models or strategies. There are currently several types of negotiation models for 
automated bargaining and many researchers have designed systems using the models. 
Nevertheless, most bargaining systems embody only one negotiation model [4].

2 S.H. Ha 
In this article, the MANS/SNS (multi-agent negotiation system with selectable ne-
gotiation strategies) is presented, which allows agents to dynamically embody a user’s 
favorite negotiation strategy which can be preinstalled as a component within the 
system. The system allows multiple agents to travel from one server to another on the 
network to negotiate autonomously and automatically with counterpart agents regard-
ing offers. The system has a mechanism, called SNS, to enable the negotiating agents 
to combine pluggable strategy components that integrate negotiation capabilities to 
implement negotiation strategies.  
2   Negotiation in the Electronic Commerce 
Electronic commerce systems allow buyers to purchase goods through the Internet. 
However, it becomes much difficult to trace all available sellers through the Internet. 
Hence, the buyer may be interested in delegating their purchase tasks (including nego-
tiations) to a software agent. With the increasing importance of electronic commerce 
across the Internet, the need for agents to support both buyers and sellers in purchas-
ing and selling goods is growing rapidly. 
According to several reference models [5 ], the electronic commerce is comprised 
of three phases: information, negotiation, and settlement. In the first phase, prospec-
tive buyers identify and evaluate their needs as well as alternative sources to fulfill 
them, while sellers arrange to provide their goods and identify potential buyers.  
Subsequently, prospective buyers and sellers negotiate the terms of a deal, which is 
finalized by a contract. Eventually, the cont ract is executed and the objects of the 
transaction are exchanged according to the conditions previously stipulated. There 
have been several approaches dealing with the first and third phase, and a few systems 
exist for automatic negotiation concerning the second phase. This includes Market-
Maker from MIT Media Labs [6]. Until now, a few commercial systems exist, which 
equip mobile agents with automatic negotiation mechanisms. 
There are some requirements for negotiation within electronic commerce. One is to 
formulate the negotiation. Ontology must cover all important attributes of a product, 
such as price, quantity, or quality. Each of essential variables must be specific to the 
agent for a valid comparison. The second requirement is a negotiation process. The 
negotiation process of software agents typically goes through four major steps: Dele-
gation of a negotiating authority to agents; the initialization of a negotiation task and 
the proposal of an offer by one of the parties; the evaluation of proposals by others; 
and suggestions of a new counter-proposal if other parties do not accept the offer. 
This process may be repeated several times until both parties reach an agreement.  
The last requirement is to determine appropriate system architecture. Such a sys-
tem must have the capability to use the Internet as a backbone for transmitting data to 
different negotiating parties. In addition, the architecture must have the ability to 
support both synchronous and asynchronous negotiations. The widespread acceptance 
of Java provides the essential groundwork upon which an agent-based framework can 
be built. There have been several agent models, which have embedded multi-agent 
system architecture into their designs: Aglet, Agent Tcl [7], ARA [8], Concordia [9], 
Mole [10], Odyssey, TACOMA [11], Voyager, SHIPMAI [12], and Nomad [13]. 
Each framework promotes a different concept in the agent programming. The use of

Agent-Based Decision Making in the Electronic Marketplace: Interactive Negotiation 3 
abstractions varies, as well as the actual capabilities provided by each class library, as 
do the benefits they bring [13][14][15]. 
3   Architecture of Multi-agent Negotiation System 
A multi-agent-based negotiation system with the adaptive negotiation strategies has 
been developed. Fig. 1 illustrates the detailed architecture of the MANS/SNS at the 
component level, including agents, objects, and databases.  
 
 
Fig. 1. Component-level architecture of the MANS/SNS for the electronic negotiations 
This e-marketplace system consists of an interface agent (IA), a catalog manager 
(CM), a brokering manager (BM), and an electronic marketplace shared repository 
(EMSR). The IA assists users in interacting with the e-marketplace system, tracking 
users’ behavior, and providing users with interesting items in a user-adaptive form. 
The CM and BM are ordinary business logic components that are parts of the  
e-marketplace. Market participants (buyer s and sellers) post and notify products or 
services, which they want to trade through the CM. The BM makes decisions  
that help determine what to buy and from whom to buy. The EMSR stores an  
e-marketplace’s activity history, which results from the CM and BM.  
The negotiation manager (NM) is one of the major concerns outlined in this article. 
The MANS/SNS has nine major components that have close relationships with the 
NM, and each component is tightly integrated to meet the goals of achieving multiple-
issue negotiations:

4 S.H. Ha 
• There are a negotiation manager agent (N MA), a negotiation shared repository 
(NSR), a mobile-agent creation agent (MCA), and an agent-dock management 
agent (AMA) in a negotiation control server (NCS) which takes charge of the 
whole process of negotiation; 
• There are a negotiation strategy agent (NSA), a negotiation strategy ontology 
(NSO), and a negotiation strategy library (NSL) in a negotiation strategy shared 
server (NSSS) which enables negotiation agents to reuse adaptive negotiation 
strategies; 
• There are a negotiation control agent (N CA) and a negotiation transaction reposi-
tory (NTR) in negotiation agent execution servers (NAES) which provide a run-
time environment for negotiation agent execution. 
 
While a user sends a request to create a negotiation agent to the NMA, he or she details 
highly-tailored negotiation parameters and issues. The NMA stores the user’s request 
on the NSR and it is forwarded to the MCA. The MCA locates a suitable NAES, cre-
ates agents, and launches them onto the selected NAES where the computational load 
is low or the connection to the NCS is less congested in the network. An agent is clas-
sified as either a negotiation provider agent (NPA) or a negotiation decider agent 
(NDA). A buyer or a seller can be an owner of either the NPA or the NDA. 
An agent management system (AMS) agent––a required component of the Java 
agent development (JADE) environment––helps the MCA to do load balancing and it 
enables mobile agents to locate a NAES in which they reside. A traveling agent con-
sists of a code, data, and state. The transmission of these things is handled through 
Java’s object serialization methods and the agent system’s class-loading mechanism. 
The NMA registers new agents at the NSR, monitors the progress of agents, and 
maintains the state of agents and system statistics. A user can see and manage mobile 
agents after they are registered at the repository. When an authenticated user asks 
about agent status, the NMA displays all of the user’s registered agents. In an agent 
execution environment on a NAES, the agents communicate directly with each other 
and actively negotiate on the owner’s behalf, even when the user is disconnected from 
the network. This eventually reduces network traffic and the agents continue to  
operate while network connections are down. In addition, since agents are executed 
on the separate servers, an e-marketplace site can relieve the burden of executing the 
computationally-intensive negotiation strategies. 
Once a negotiation agent travels to a NAES, the NCA manages the life cycle of an 
agent and it provides the mechanism to destroy agents. If a user requests to terminate 
an agent, the NMA receives the message from the user and sends it to the NCA. The 
NCA terminates the agent in question and the NMA makes the killed agent unregis-
tered from the NSR. Before executing negotiations, the NCA refers to the negotiation 
specifications of the agents and asks the NSA to choose appropriate negotiation 
strategies. The NSA refers to the NSO, and then, generates a negotiation strategy 
object from the template strategy classes that have been installed in advance in the 
NSL. Negotiation strategies are the formal descriptions of negotiation rules. They 
include complex computations, and are implemented by using game-theory or  
machine-learning techniques. When executing negotiations, the NAs use the NTR as a 
safe workplace, which can store intensive calculation history. When a NA puts forth a 
request, the NCA records what a NPA negotiates with a NDA into the NTR. The

Agent-Based Decision Making in the Electronic Marketplace: Interactive Negotiation 5 
NCA reports the final results to the NSR. A user does not need to be continuously 
connected to the e-marketplace site, because the NMA can send an e-mail to the user 
when a negotiation ends or the user can see the results through the NMA whenever he 
or she wants to. 
3.1   Negotiation Strategy 
A negotiation can be seen as a sequence of negotiation messages that are generated by 
the participating agents. An agent constantly receives and produces such messages. 
These messages are the results of intentional computations taken by the individual 
agents in order to achieve their goals. These intentional computations are modeled as 
negotiation strategies [16].  
To provide a variety of negotiation strategies currently available, the MANS/SNS 
maintains a library of preinstalled negotiation strategies and it allows a user to choose 
a particular type of strategies from the library. In order to set up the library, a negotia-
tion strategy literature has been examined and it was found that there were primarily 
two types of techniques which implement negotiation strategies: machine learning 
and game-theoretic techniques. The MANS/SNS is designed to allow agents to nego-
tiate using these techniques: 
 
• Machine learning techniques.  Several research papers use a genetic algorithm 
(GA) or evolutionary algorithm as a negotiation strategy. The GA models negotia-
tion strategies as sequential rules with a utility threshold. The GA often employs 
game theory, Q-learning, or finite state machines either separately or in conjunc-
tion. Fuzzy constraint-based reasoning, fuzzy relational analysis, and fuzzy rule  
inference with simple-weighting are also widely used. Bayesian learning and rule-
based knowledge are other choices as a negotiation strategy [17][18][19]. 
• Game-theoretic techniques.  Game-theoretic techniques encompass the adjusted-
winner (AW) procedure, multi-attribute utility function (MAUT), Pareto optimal 
solutions, the Kasbah model, and other scoring functions [20][21]. 
 
Fig. 2 illustrates how to define classes that encapsulate different types of strategies in 
Unified Modeling Language (UML) to construct a negotiation strategy library. A 
negotiation agent (NPA and NDA) includes negotiation behaviors which implement 
the Iterated Contract Net Interaction Protocol of the Foundations of Intelligent Physi-
cal Agents. This standard protocol allows multi-round iterative bidding. It enables 
negotiation agents to communicate with each other via a common interface, even 
though they have a variety of negotiation strategies. The owner of the negotiation 
agent can specify which type of negotiation strategy should be used. A negotiation 
agent maintains a connection with a negotiation strategy object to implement the 
chosen strategy. When an agent generates a negotiation message, the responsibility is 
forwarded to its strategy object. 
An abstract class, NS in Fig. 2 declar es an interface which is common to all sup-
ported strategies [22]. A subclass, ML specifies an interface that is unique to the 
strategies using machine learning techniques. A subclass GT clarifies an interface  
for the game-theoretic strategies. A negotiation agent uses these interfaces to call

6 S.H. Ha 
 
Fig. 2. The negotiation strategy library and its patterns expressed in the UML notation diagram 
concrete algorithms, including GA, fuzzy logic, or MAUT. When algorithms are 
called, an agent passes all required data and parameters to the algorithm objects. The 
hierarchy of negotiation strategy classes helps define a family of algorithms that ne-
gotiation agents can choose and reuse. Encapsulating an algorithm into a separate 
class, it is easier to adaptively modify the algorithm independent of the negotiation 
agents. The MANS/SNS implements a negotiation strategy ontology component that 
is responsible for managing the negotiation strategies in a modular fashion. The on-
tology is used to handle the registration of negotiation strategies and the notification 
of them to the users. It is also used to control versions of the strategies. 
3.2   Collaboration and Messaging between Agents 
Collaboration among member agents is comprised of the dynamic interaction of agents 
in the negotiation system. In this article, collaboration can occur in accordance with the 
seven negotiation stages: Negotiation agent creation (step 1); negotiation agent migra-
tion (step 2); negotiation strategy loading (step 3); negotiation process initiation (step 
4); negotiation progress (step 5); negotiation completion (step 6); and negotiation proc-
ess termination (step 7). Fig. 3 shows a collaboration diagram which is expressed in the 
agent unified modeling language, which explores associations among agents and the 
sequence of messages that are exchanged among agents during negotiation.  
The arrows represent messages and they are labeled with a dot-separated list of 
step numbers and sequence numbers. Messaging within the NCS occurs ten times, 
including two times with the AMS agent. Messaging within the NAES occurs 13 
times, including iterative proposals between the NPA and NDA. Messaging takes 
place five times between the NCA and NAES. Messaging between the NSA and 
NAES happens four times. Table 1 describes messaging details among agents in steps 
1 and 2, for example. The Agent Communication Language (ACL) of the FIPA is 
used as the communicative protocol [23].

4   Implementation of the MANS/SNS  
The MANS/SNS was developed under JADE 3.0, which has been fully implemented 
in Java language and has been a framework for the development of multi-agent sys-
tems in compliance with FIPA specifications [24]. The main container, Remote Man-
agement Agent (RMA), was used internally by JADE. The other agent containers, 
such as NSSS, NAES1, NAES2, and NCS, were connected to the main container via 
the remote method invocation registry, and provided a run-time environment for the 
execution of a set of negotiation agents. The MCA was in charge of generating nego-
tiation agents in the NCS, and generated NPA1 and NDA1 on NAES1 and NPA2 and 
NDA2 on NAES2. The followings were the input parameters to generate mobile ne-
gotiation agents for this system: agent information, such as user identifier and agent 
identifier; negotiable issues which both parties agree on and desirable values for the 
desirable item; negotiation constraints such as the number of maximum trials or other 
termination conditions; and a type of negotiation strategy, such as GA, fuzzy logic, or 
MAUT. When called upon to find an appropriate negotiation strategy, the NSA re-
ferred to the NSO component with the nego tiation specifications as specified. Given

8 S.H. Ha 
the information of a strategy class, the NSA located the class file from the NSL. The 
NSA created an instance of this negotiation strategy for a negotiation agent and sent it 
back to the NCA.  
Fig. 4(a) shows a GUI that allows the NCA in NAES to provide functions to submit 
requests for negotiation strategies. This GUI screen can be used to monitor all FIPA 
ACL messages issued from/to the NCA in order to request negotiation strategies.  
Fig. 4(b) illustrates a GUI screen that was developed to facilitate the management of 
negotiation strategies. The NSO contains information about negotiation strategy 
classes, such as strategy name, authors, version, algorithm, negotiable issues, descrip-
tion, and storage location. An e-marketplace provider or third parties could supply 
negotiation strategies in the form of Java’s JAR file in advance. Each JAR file contains 
a Java class, which implements a negotiation strategy.

5   Conclusion  
In this article, a multi-agent negotiation system in an electronic commerce was pre-
sented. The system offered several characteristics over a typical mobile agent system: 
(1) the MANS/SNS supported bilateral, multi-issue negotiations; (2) the system  
allowed the NAs to migrate from the NCS to NAESs to reduce the workload of a 
server running an e-marketplace; (3) users could choose template strategies from the 
NSL to generate their own strategies. Therefore third parties could build templates for 
the e-marketplace intermediary; (4) the pattern of negotiation strategy classes made it 
easy for negotiation agents to reuse a family of algorithms. Encapsulating the algo-
rithms in the separate classes made it easier to modify the algorithms independent of 
its negotiation agent; (5) By keeping an agent database at the NCS, this enabled users 
to keep track of agents’ states, even if communication between the NCS and NAES 
was down; (6) To achieve the division of labor, the NTR stores the intermediate out-
comes and the NSR stores the final negotiation results. Table 2 summarizes the dif-
ferences between Nomad [13] and MANS/SNS.

Modeling and Verifying Business Interactions
via Commitments and Dialogue Actions
Mohamed El-Menshawy1,J amalB entahar2, andR a c hida Dssouli2
1 Concordia University, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Canada
2 Concordia University, Concordia Institute for Information Systems Eng., Canada
m_elme@encs.concordia.ca,
{bentahar,dssouli}@ciise.concordia.ca
Abstract. A variety of business interactions in open environments can
be captured in terms of creation and manipulation of social commitments
among the agents. Such interactions include B2B and B2C processes and
contracts as realized via web services and other technologies. Also, the
interaction protocols are formulated in terms of commitments to regulate
agents’ behaviors. However, such protocols can beneﬁt from a stronger
treatment of ﬂexible interactions via dialogue actions to capture a rich va-
riety of real-life business scenarios. This paper addresses the challenges of
modeling and verifying business interactions using commitments and ac-
tions on such commitments augmented with dialogue actions to reconcile
conﬂicts and reason about the validity of such commitments. We intro-
duce the NetBill protocol taken from e-business domain to demonstrate
the speciﬁcation of a new class of formal protocols for agent negotiation.
Finally, we use the MCMAS symbolic model checker to automatically
verify this protocol against some given properties. We present the imple-
mentation and experimental results of this protocol and its veriﬁcation.

3 Modeling Social Negotiation Protocol
In this section, wep r e s enta new formal protocol for agent negotiation based on
our conceptual framework (see Sect.2). In particular,o ur protocol supports two
types ofc ommitments: social andd ialectical commitments.T he former one is
about what ist o be done [13] whilet h elatter one, as in argumentation theory
[14], isc oncerned with arguinga bout the agreement.F ore xample,i n the NetBill
protocol, as longa st h egoods are in as tock, then the customer cann egotiate
the price oft h e s egoods with the merchantu singad ialectical commitment but
when the customer andm e r c h ant reach a mutua l agreementa bout thisp rice,
then the commitment that the cust omer created t o pay the speciﬁed price is
called a social commitment.
3.1 Protocol Speciﬁcation
Our socialn egotiation protocol (SNP) merges a set ofd ialogue games, commit-
menta c tionsa ndd ialogue actions.I n particular, the protocol uses four dialogues
games: the main game (MG), the defense game (DFG), the challenge game (CHG)
and the attack game (ATG). Thisp rotocol begins with the entry-dialogue action
followed by the dialectical commitment (DC), which iss imilar to as ocial com-
mitment but with the possibility ton egotiate the condition and/orc ontent of
the commitmentf ollowed by the main dialogue game (MG) and the protocol ends
with doingt h eexit-dialogue action.
The main dialogue game beg ins with accepting, refusing orc h allengingt h e
content oft h edialectical commitment.A ccepting MG meansc r e a tingt h esocial
commitment (CR-sc), which itc oulde ither fulﬁlled (FUL), violated (VIO), as-
signed (ASS)o rd elegated (DEL). The delegated (resp. the assigned) commitment

can be accepted or refused.W hen MG is refused, then the interacting agentc an
open the negotiation dialogue either by the defense game, attack game orb y
challenge game to reach a mutual agreement.T he defense game (DFG) consists
of the defense-action that the debtoru s e sto persuade the creditorf ollowed ei-
ther by callingt h em ain dialogue game that openst h eﬂexibility to the creditor

attack game (ATG) enables agents to attack the commitmentc ontent of other

of SNP protocol can be deﬁned usinga BNF-like grammar with meta-symbols:
“::=” and “|” fort h ec hoice and “;” fora c tion sequence (see Table2 ).

SNP ::= Entry-dialogue; DC; MG; Exit-dialogue
MG ::= ACC | REF |CHG
ACC ::= CR-sc; FUL | VIO | (ASS | DEL; ACC | REF-ad)

ATG ::= attack-action; (MG | refusal-action)

Personalized Support for Management of Financial 
Instruments by Means of Software Agents 
Jarogniew Rykowski 
Department of Information Technology, the Poznan University of Economics 
Mansfelda 4, 60-854 Poznan, Poland 
Tel./Fax: +48 61 848-0549

Abstract. In the paper a new approach is proposed to support personal man-
agement of financial instruments such as e-bank accounts and investment funds. 
The approach is based on using personalized software agents. A set of user 
agents implements an idea of a personal financial advisor, starting from the root 
– the main agent-interface to a transactional system of a financial institution, via 
marketing agents responsible for the generation of personal financial advices 
based on current user activities, and finishing on specialized agents-interfaces to 
contact the personal access devices of the users. An “intelligence” of the agents 
makes it possible to send the requests and gather the answers to/from the agents 
in different forms, and using different communication channels, natural-
language-based communication included. 
Keywords: Software agents, personalization, e-banking, e-finances. 
1   Introduction 
Recently we observe a boom of offers of diverse financial instruments: bank savings, 
investment funds, credits and credit lines, bonds and shares, etc. Many financial insti-
tutions, not only traditional banks, are providing different financial instruments  
for mass clients. Despite the business model used, the main goal of introducing  
consulting services is to provide the best advice how to invest client’s money – the 
consulting companies try to help clients in optimizing their ways of money invest-
ment and savings. Traditionally, these institutions are focused on clients with surplus 
of money, looking for an advice how to invest. For the clients with high surplus, thus 
potentially high profits for the institution, a support is provided in by a human finan-
cial advisor. The advisor is in turn supported by sophisticated software to foresee 
possible future trends on the financial market, and to react in advance for the market 
changes. A typical role of such human advisor is to continuously monitor the financial 
market, detect some important changes and trends, and inform the clients about such 
facts, showing possible consequences on their investments and savings. 
There are several differences between the level and quality of support offered by a 
human financial advisor, and automated financial system. First, human support is 
often initiated by the institution staff, once a change occurs that may be of a potential

Personalized Support for Management of Financial Instruments 23 
interest to the client. Automated support requires manual interaction of the client in 
order to detect the change – one must access the financial information and assess the 
real meaning of detected change, if any. There is a limited notification about changes; 
however, this support is related with a fact of processing a transaction on a user-
owned bank account or a share, with no real assessment of this fact. For example, a 
client is informed about the fact of an ATM transaction last night, and he/she starts to 
remember if there was his/her own operation, or a theft. Second, once notified by a 
human advisor about a change, a client is able to get more information about this 
change, by an interaction with the advisor. For the automated support, no such inter-
action is possible unless it is provided in a pre-defined system functionality. Third, an 
interaction with the human advisor is pers onalized and adjusted to the individual 
expectations, and possibilities of the client. There is limited personalization support 
for the automated financial support system, usually aimed at registering private user’s 
phone number/e-mail address and the preferred way of notifications (SMS, e-mail, a 
voice message, etc.). 
In this paper, we propose a new solution for mass, personalized financial support, 
aimed in applying the technology of software agents. As a technical basis, we propose 
Agent Computing Environment (ACE) [1]. The main idea of our approach is to use 
distributed, mobile, user-defined software agents for continuous monitoring of se-
lected information sources and informing users about detected information changes 
[2]. Once developed, an agent performs autonomously given tasks, pre-programmed 
according to its owner’s needs. The agent ma y adjust its behavior to the environment 
where it is executed at a moment [3], as well  as to some user-independent restrictions 
[4], e.g., communication costs, limitations of end-user hardware, etc. Several agents 
may be logically combined to create a complex agent able to fulfill more sophisticated 
tasks. Complex agents may be settled both statically, as a result of a user request, and 
dynamically, as a result of environmental changes. 
A set of ACE agents plays a role of a human-like personal financial advisor,  
asynchronously providing crucial information about changes related with personally-
owned, different financial instruments, and assessing the real impact of such changes 
to private investments and savings of the agent owner. On one hand, a client is 
equipped with a tool for continuous monitoring of a summary of all his/her finances 
regardless number, types, and access methods of the financial institutions to be ad-
dressed. On the other hand, these institutions  are able to advertis e their offers accord-
ing to the current financial state of the client, to convince this client to use some new 
financial instruments. As these offers are targeted on particular clients, probably  
such advertisement will be effective and not perceived by the clients as yet another 
irritating spam. Moreover, individual treatment of each client makes it possible to 
introduce individual bank offers, adjusted to particular clients, e.g., bank deposits 
with individual provisions. 
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. First, a brief introduction to the 
technology of software agents is given, followed by a short description of the Agent 
Computing Environment ACE framework. Based on this description, generic system 
architecture is presented. Following architecture description, some examples are given 
of using ACE agents for personal brokerage and advertisement related with the finan-
cial services. Finally, a short comparison is given of the functionality of the proposed 
framework and the support offered by main Polish e-banks.

24 J. Rykowski 
2   Software Agents Technology 
To solve the problem of mass personalized assistance, we propose to use imperative, 
distributed software agents and the Agent Computing Environment ACE, already 
developed and implemented by us for unrestricted personalization of network data 
sources and systems. In our approach, we define software agents in classical way [5, 
6, 7]. A software agent is a program, executed at a given place, characterized by: (1) 
autonomy – agents process their work independently without the need for human 
management, (2) communication – agents are able to communicate with one another, 
as well as with humans, and (3) learning – agents are able to learn as they react with 
the environment. Agents may be programmed by their owners, thus allowing behavior 
personalization [8]. Agents may be executed in different places, according to owners’ 
needs. We propose to use Agent Computing Environment (ACE) framework as a 
basic agent-based environment. This framework is based on a set of distributed Agent 
Servers, each of them capable of storing and executing software agents. The agents 
may be moved among several Agent Servers. There are “light” Agent Servers with 
limited functionality to be executed in a “thin” hardware/software environment (like 
for example mobile phones, PDAs, etc.), and “thick”, massively used Agent Servers 
located in stationary network hosts. The “t hin” servers are mainly used for executing 
individual agents of device owners, while the latter are used by many users in parallel 
to access certain services, external systems, and public communication channels.  
There are two basic classes of ACE agents: public System Agents, and Private 
Agents. System Agents SAs are created by trusted users (usually system designers), to 
be used in a mass manner by many users. SAs are treated as trustful system elements. 
Their efficiency is of primary concern. Thus, SAs are programmed in Java. A way of 
usage of a given SA cannot be changed by an ordinary user; however, it may be pa-
rameterized during the invocation. SAs are us ed when there is a need for mass access 
by many users to given information, providing this information in a standardized form 
and with optimum effort (from the system point of view). The most frequently used 
SAs are the following: communication wrappers, cache utilities, synchronizers,  
brokers, etc. Private Agents  PAs are created and controlled by their owners. Unless 
directly ordered by its owner, the agent cannot be accessed by any other agent and 
service. For a trade-off between overall system efficiency and user privacy, a special-
ized language is proposed to program agent behavior, based on XML and imperative 
programming, and equipped with several non-standard mechanisms to improve effi-
ciency and security. An agent is controlled by its owner, i.e., the code is defined by 
the owner or by a programmer on behalf of the agent owner, and the internal agent 
variables (agent’s state) are defined and accessible for the owner only. Agent’s behav-
ior, programmed in its code and variables, is determined by the owner and used for 
his/her/its individual purposes. Although theoretically owners have full control over 
the behavior of their agents, in the reality they are not obliged to set up all their agents 
individually. 
3   Overall System Architecture  
In order to efficiently support personalized management of financial resources by the 
use of ACE agents, we propose to develop some specialized system agents SAs – 
gateways to financial institutions included, and some prototypes (patterns, skeletons)

Personalized Support for Management of Financial Instruments 25 
for private agents PAs, to be further personalized by the end-users. The telecommuni-
cation gateways are responsible for assuring communication with the users 
(WAP/WWW, e-mail, SMS/MMS, and voice gateways) and the financial institutions, 
standardization of input/output messages, basic brokerage with the services offered by 
the financial institutions, caching and synchronizing access to these services, etc. 
There are as well some specialized SAs being system-defined utilities, as for example 
chatterbot support with national-language detector [9]. 
There are three basic system layers (Fig. 1) : (1) connections with external software 
systems of financial institutions, and telecommunication channels, (2) system agents, 
including gateways and predefined agents for specific tasks related with interaction 
with the financial institutions, and (3) private, user-defined agents. The presented 
architecture comprises only logical connections among agents and external software 
systems. The agents may be distributed in the network, in particular, some (private) 
agents may be executed in end-user device (a notebook, a stationary host), while some 
agents (both system and private) – in the local area network of a given financial insti-
tution, i.e., an e-bank. Physical connections among distributed agents are realized via 
specialized agent-agent gateways of distributed Agent Servers, with a possibility of 
safety increase by encryption, tunneling, firewalling, etc.

Beside typical gateways for basic communication channels (e-mail, WAP/WWW, 
SMS/MMS, PTT/voice gateway) and standard public utilities such as a calculator-
agent, there are three basic classes of pr edefined agents: (1) communication-agents 
capable of contacting local area networks of financial institutions in a secured way, 
(2) marketing-agents responsible for generating marketing information for the clients 
(i.e., agent owners), and (3) personal financial assistants. Below we describe a strat-
egy of providing and using agents belonging to all these classes. Note that fixing

26 J. Rykowski 
agent classes and thus (somehow) agent functionality does not restrict introducing 
new agents and their classes, in particular monitoring agents, directory-agents, agent-
brokers to/from additional financial services, etc. 
3.1   Communication Agents 
For obvious security reasons, user agents should not access directly services from a 
local area network of a financial institution such as an e-bank. Instead, specialized 
gateways should be provided to act as a firewall/proxy between ACE agents (both 
system and private) and internal resources and applications of the local area network 
of the financial institution. Basic functionality of such gateway(s) is the following: 
─ Multiplexing and synchronizing requests generated asynchronously by the popu-
lation of ACE agents (a proxy for all the traffic to/from financial systems). 
─ Access standardization – providing one single standardized way of accessing all 
the resources related with all the financial institutions involved. To this  
goal, XML should be used as a basic communication and data storage tool. A 
gateway may be specialized for communication with different data sources ac-
cessible by different communication standards and with different data format. 
─ Continuous control over connections to/from the resources of the financial insti-
tution, including billing for using the services/information, storing logs of user 
and system activities, verifying access rights, generating security alerts, etc. 
─ Caching frequently accessed information  – for slowly-changed information (as 
most of the administrative information provided by the financial institutions  
except for brokerage companies) for mass users, an information-cache may  
substantially reduce network traffic to and from massively accessed resources. 
For example, actual interest rate of an account may be distributed efficiently on 
the mass scale.  
─ Generating user- and source-specific alerts  the ACE agents are waiting for. Im-
portant changes in the information provided by bank data sources may be 
quickly reported to the agents. To this goal, user-defined subscriptions may  
be used, to free agents from continuous monitoring and comparison of informa-
tion changes. 
The details about an implementation of a safe connection between communication-
agents and external data sources are usually hidden for the ordinary users. So, the 
communication-agent may be able to filter (inspect) the whole information flow, 
including blocking given users (i.e., their private agents), addresses, specific requests, 
messages containing specific words, etc. 
3.2   Marketing Agent 
The main task of the marketing-agent is related with a distribution of marketing in-
formation (advertisement) based on: (1) a global strategy defined by a local marketing 
staff, (2) some global values obtained from the services and servers belonging to the 
financial institutions involved, and (3) detailed state of private user financial re-
sources, including not only current financial balance, but also individual history of 
transactions. The agent may be invoked by the communication-agent (as mentioned

Personalized Support for Management of Financial Instruments 27 
above), by human staff (to manually set the above-mentioned global strategy), and by 
user private agents, to generate at-the-moment targeted advertisement. Global strategy 
of generating marketing information is usually controlled by a specialized application, 
in turn prepared and controlled by the human staff of the financial institution. The 
application makes it possible to manage mark eting templates. Each template relates a 
parameterized text of an advertisement with some activation conditions. In general, 
once any change is detected in a financial resource of a given user, a set of templates 
is examined towards accordance with the current and past balance of this financial 
resource. For each template found, an adve rtisement message is generated according 
to the marketing pattern and current state of the user financial resource(s). It is up to 
the user to accept a delivery of the message, via private agents, to one of the end-user 
devices (e.g., a mobile phone).  
To facilitate management of all the templates, a dedicated application is provided 
being a GUI interface to the marketing-templates agent. Both the marketing agent and 
the above-mentioned application for managing marketing templates are not fixed and 
may be adjusted to current needs of the bank. To preserve simplicity of the descrip-
tion of our system, we provide here a quite simple example of such agent/application. 
However, this simplified functionality of the marketing agent, in particular the algo-
rithm for alert generation and propagation, may be extended. 
A typical marketing template consists of a condition under which the template is 
activated, related with account name/number, account balance, etc., change-detection 
period and repetition period – when to activate the same template for the same user 
for the next time, a priority – a level of importance for the alert eventually generated 
by the template (priorities may be used by personal agents to filter/classify marketing 
alerts according to individual user  preferences), and parameterized marketing mes-
sage, being any string of characters; parts of  the message marked with “%” character 
are replaced at run-time (i.e., at the moment  of the alert generation) by real values 
related with user’s accounts. For example, the above template: 
Don’t you know what to do with your debit $%s on ‘%n’ account 
for last %m days? Ask for a credit line! 
will be used to eventually generate the following SMS alert: 
Don’t you know what to do with your debit $412 on ‘a-vista’ 
account for last 5 days? Ask for a credit line! 
As it may be seen, the above marketing information is so personalized that this  
information is not perceived as yet-another irritating spam. Moreover, the above-
mentioned priorities make it possible to easily adjust number and importance of the 
incoming alerts to individual user preferences and skills. One may expect that this 
form of an advertisement will be more effective than the classical advertisement sent 
to everybody in unique form, with no user-targeted parameterization. This way of 
marketing seems to be promising and profitable, both for the bank, and its clients. 
3.3   Personal Financial Assistants 
Personal agent-assistant is a main entry point for a particular user, synchronizing all 
the incoming and outcoming messages, storing user preferences (with reference  
to preferred communication links, data formats, presentation interfaces, etc.). The

28 J. Rykowski 
assistant is used as a main broker/synchronizer for all the traffic between a user (agent 
owner) and all the other agents working for this user (both system and private agents). 
Usually, the main task if this agent is to collect user request via a certain communica-
tion channel (i.e., from a certain agent-gateway), standardize this request (usually to 
the form of an XML message), choose the most adequate private/system agent to 
serve this request, and finally collect the response to send it back to the user.  
The personal assistant is also used for sending alerts generated by the user-defined 
subscriptions. According to current user pref erences, an alert is formatted and sent via 
a certain communication channel – an SMS/MMS, e-mail, IM or a similar chat-based 
system, a notification waiting in a WWW server, etc. The best (at the moment) com-
munication channel may be chosen automatically, taking into account current position 
of a user (reported by a specialized agent), user’s last login (place and time), and 
independent restrictions (e.g., user’s availability, scheduled meetings, etc.). 
A special interest is taken to assure efficient communication with the use of hard-
ware/software-restricted devices as for example mobile phones. To this goal, a natural-
language interface is provided, aiming in a personalized chatterbot conversation. Such 
simplified natural-language interface may be personalized for given user(s), which 
limits a necessity of learning different, fixed, complicated interfaces for accessing 
different financial institutions. This also greatly improves an effectiveness of commu-
nicating via limited mobile channels, as for example popular SMS messaging, by  
incorporating user-defined abbreviations and vocabularies. Personal assistant is  
responsible for: (1) permanent storage of parameters of bank account(s) and other 
financial resources, including transaction history, (2) permanent storage of alerts and 
advertisements, (3) filtering marketing information, (4) computing some statistical 
information, and (5) registering and computing payments related with access to the 
financial resources, etc. 
3.4   Personalization of Private Agents 
Below, a strategy is proposed of personalization of user agents according to the 
(growing) user level. At the beginning, the system offers a set of predefined agents, 
with a functionality common for all the users. As time goes by, user expectations 
grow, and the system is ready to satisfy the user with new/extended functionality. TO 
this goal, a client provides some personal preferences: mobile and stationary devices 
used, identifiers (e.g., a phone number, IMEI number, PKI signature, IP/DNS address, 
etc.), preferable communication channels, etc. The institution proposes a set of prede-
fined SAs and PAs to be installed for the supplicant in the Agent Servers belonging to 
this institution. This set of agents is capable of serving client’s requests in a prede-
fined way, according to a common strategy. The institution proposes a set of PAs to 
be installed at client-side, to facilitate contacts with this institution in the future. It is 
up to the user to accept this set of agents or not. In the latter case, only the PAs  
executed in the institution network are used. However, once a client accepts PAs 
agents in his/her private hardware/software environment, he/she may profit in faster 
notifications (e.g., SMS messages sent to mobile phones), better adjustment to end-
user devices, more personalized presentation methods, and more functionality related 
with client-side data processing. As the supplicant may provide some information

Personalized Support for Management of Financial Instruments 29 
about own devices and preferable communication channels, the generated client-side 
PAs may be customized, even if the server-side PAs remain standardized. 
The SAs and PAs installed are equipped with a set of predefined variables and sub-
scriptions, to deal with the private financial resources of the client, i.e., e-bank  
accounts. The subscriptions are parameterized by user-dependent information, e.g., 
resource identification and type, predicted incomes and outcomes, etc. The set of ac-
cepted agents is installed and activated each time the change of information is detected 
related with any active subscription. The detected changes are filtered and potentially 
sent to the client (usually, to the personal assistant, and further via given communica-
tion channel directly to the end-user device, e.g., a mobile phone). Once the client is 
not satisfied with a subscription or PA behavior, he/she has some rights to redefine 
both data and code of his/her agents. For advanced users it is possible to fully personal-
ize the behavior of the system, both at server-, and at the client-side. For non-advanced 
users, it is still possible to define preferable communication channel, ways and timings 
of sending alerts, formats and contents of messages generated by the bank agents (e.g., 
small SMS alerting vs. formatted HTML e-mails). Such changes are easily introduced 
by the bank staff (at supplicant’s request) or by the users. In this way, system function-
ality grows as user requirements and expectations grow. 
4   Comparison with Commercial e-Banking Support Systems 
In this section we present a comparison of functionality of our proposal based on 
ACE agents and three Polish e-banks: Bank Zachodni BZ WBK owned by the Allied 
Irish Bank, mBank (the first virtual bank in Poland), and PKO B.P. / Inteligo (the 
biggest Polish bank). The comparison covers asynchronous bank alerts, SMS messag-
ing to/from the bank about current state of bank account, and basic account/fund 
management. Note that we do not take into consideration other e-offers of these 
banks, such as Internet- and phone-banking, as such functionality is not the main goal 
of our agent-based system. 
Clients of Bank Zachodni BZ WBK ar e entitled to use WA P/WWW standard ac-
cess as well as preformatted SMS messages in order to get some information about 
current state of user bank account [10]. While accessing the system, a user is given 
the following information: account balance, last transactions on each account (for past 
3 months), current deposits and investment fund units owned by the client, and cur-
rency-exchange information. By sending an SMS message, the client is given account 
balance, last few transactions, and currency-exchange rates. The format of all the 
accepted messages is fixed and common for all the users, according to the schema: 
<NIK> <PIN> service-code parameters 
where: NIK is a unique client identifier, PIN is personal client’s password, service-
code is a single letter describing a requested service (“S” for account balance, “H” for 
list of transactions, “K” for currency-exchange rates, etc.), and parameters provide 
some additional information, such as detailed account or currency number. For exam-
ple, in order to know current account balance, one has to send “12345678 0000 S” 
message, where 12345678 stands for client identifier, and 0000 for PIN.  
There are several disadvantages of the above presented way of contacting the bank. 
First, the authorization information – both NIK and PIN – are sent via non-secured

30 J. Rykowski 
SMS channel. Second, it is not possible to personalize system usage, neither by  
adjusting a format of a request, not by adding some additional services. The fixed 
format of incoming and outcoming SMS messages makes it difficult to efficiently use 
the system by non-advanced users one hand, and demanding users on the other hand. 
It looks like our proposal, with personalized functionality, information format, com-
munication channels etc. is much more user-friendly and secured. 
The first Polish virtual bank, mBank (a branch of the BRE bank) [11] offers a pos-
sibility to send request via SMS messages. System functionality and accepted mes-
sage formats (<REQUEST># <NIK>#<PIN>#<PARAMETERS>) are quite similar, 
except the SMS messages are much less user-friendly. For example, SMS request 
“3#01234567#999999#00345678#01122009#31122009” stands for asking for a com-
plete list of bank transactions during December 2009. 
The biggest Polish bank, PKO B.P., incorporated Inteligo virtual bank [12] in order 
to provide e-bank functionality. In addition to the above presented functionality, an 
owner of a PKO account is able to receive SMS and e-mail messages pointing out 
changes of the account balance. It is also possible to ask for the nearest ATM ma-
chine, providing (a part of) geographical address. However, it is not possible to filter 
incoming alerts and personalize information format and contents. In particular, one is 
not able to filter out transactions below certain limit – each account change is reported 
that may be quite irritating. Comparing such alerts with our approach, one may note 
that personalized ACE agents are much more flexible and efficient. 
None of the above mentioned e-banks provides any functionality similar with our 
personal bank marketing. Even if PKO B.P./Inteligo includes some marketing infor-
mation at the end of the e-mails with balance alerts, such information is not personal-
ized and concerns global bank activities, such as information about new credit cards, 
new saving methods, etc. In any case such information is addressed to particular bank 
clients, and, as any generic marketing information, is usually treated as an unwanted 
or even irritating spam. Our approach makes it possible to generate marketing  
information as it is an advice coming from a human staff of the bank, thus a level of 
acceptance is probably greater [13]. Moreover, the marketing information is generated 
only to those clients who are interested in obtaining such information [14]. 
5   Conclusions  
To summarize the paper, the advantages of using ACE agents to support personal 
management of financial resources are listed are the following. 
From the client point of view, all the financial resources involved are uniformly 
accessed and managed. Thus, a client is provided with a total overview of all his/her 
financial resources with a single service. 
Personalized asynchronous alerts improve reaction time for unexpected situations, 
e.g., incidental debit, extra income/outco me, etc. System-generated alerts may be 
adjusted to personal preferences of bank clients, thus the alerting is not irritating. 
It is possible to use any modern telecommunication technology in order to get ac-
cess to the information, including for example popular SMS/MMS gateways, e-mails, 
PTT (Push-To-Talk), etc. The choice for the best communication channel is up to the 
particular client and may be automatically adjusted to current situation.

Personalized Support for Management of Financial Instruments 31 
Access to the information may be personalized at several levels, starting from auto-
adjustment to the communication channel and end-user device, and finishing on de-
fining a specific dictionary for the chatterbot, natural-language conversation. 
The system is open and flexible and may be easily extended both from the points 
of view of users (new individualized functionality) and the financial institution (new 
communication channels, new financial services, new accounts/deposits/funds etc.). 
An implementation of the system is not expensive and may be realized with lim-
ited, standard hardware and software. At the same time, individual client’s devices 
(PDAs, mobile phones, portables and notebooks) may be incorporated in order to 
facilitate data transfer and treatment. The system was tested in two Polish e-banks, 
with both real and simulated (i.e., cloned) clients [4]. Although the results of these 
tests were quite promising, the system has not been yet incorporated into practice.

MAS Approach to Business Models Simulations:  
Supply Chain Management Case Study 
Jacek Jakieła, Paweł Litwin, and Marcin Olech 
Rzeszow University of Technology, Faculty of Mechanical Engineering and Aeronautics, 
Department of Computer Science,  
Powstancow Warszawy Avenue 8, 35-959 Rzeszow, Poland 
{jjakiela,plitwin,molech}@prz.edu.pl 
Abstract. The main aim of the paper is to show that an agent paradigm may be 
considered as a powerful conceptual framework for organization modeling and 
testbed for business simulations. The sections of the paper gradually prove 
these theses. Firstly the agent orientation has been presented as a source of 
natural and very intuitive modeling constructs and complexity management 
tools. Then the classical model of supply chain simulation was altered to its 
agent version. Finally the case study concerning the agent based simulation ex-
periment of supply chain has been elaborated and results of the simulation runs 
carefully analyzed as well as interpreted. 
Keywords: agent-oriented modeling, agent-oriented simulation, business  
modeling, supply chain modeling, extended enterprise simulation. 
1   Introduction 
Rapid development of electronic marketspaces forced companies to search for new 
sources of effectiveness and efficiency, both intra- and inter-organizational. As 
a consequence the complexity of business models has been growing constantly. This 
complexity concerns not only structural characteristics, but also behavioral ones.  
What is more, completely new business structures have emerged. In order to  
respond quickly to changing customer preferences, companies decide on which activi-
ties they can perform best and integrate their value chains with business models of 
their partners. As a result the value net is created where each of its components should 
act in the optimal way, and therefore the whole net is able to maximize efficiency and 
provide the end customer with the high level of value added. 
The key element of such extended enterprises is their supply chain. It determines 
how effective the company can be. The main problem is that even the simplest supply 
chains can behave in an unpredictable way and it is very hard to make accurate deci-
sions. Sometimes demand for single merchandise or level of stock starts to change 
randomly and the behavior of whole supply chain becomes extremely complex. Only 
way to be prepared for risky situations and make informed decisions is to use the simu-
lation model, which becomes the workbench for extended enterprise. In that case simu-
lation model is used in the process of analyzing the characteristics of the real system.

MAS Approach to Business Models Simulations: Supply Chain Management Case Study 33 
The purpose of this paper is to show how an agent paradigm may be used as busi-
ness modeling and simulation approach to describing and analyzing extended enter-
prises. The problem domain taken into consideration has been cut down to supply 
chain management area. In [15] conceptual basis for simulation experiment has been 
described in detail. It presents the model of supply chain for traditional simulations. 
Case study elaborated and analyzed in this paper concerns agent-oriented version of 
the model mentioned above and has been developed and implemented from scratch. 
2   Multi-agent System as a Simulation Workbench 
2.1   Using Agents in Simulations 
Multiagent-based simulation (MABS) can be defined as the modeling and simulating 
real world system or phenomena where the model consists of agents cooperating with 
one another in carrying out tasks and achieving goals. The advent of multi-agent 
based modeling has introduced an important innovation: behavior of complex systems 
with many active entities can be simulated by modeling individual entities and their 
interactions. Importantly, the operation of the system need not be defined a priori as 
set of equations, terms or logical statements, but the whole behavior emerges from 
individual objects behaviors, their interactions and impact of the environment. 
The MABS approach has been becoming more and more popular and its models 
and their advantages have been widely described in [12][16]. Contributions to the 
MABS domain are periodically published among others in Springer’s LNAI series. 
According to AgentLink Roadmap [9] "agent -based simulation is characterized by 
the intersection of three scientific fields, namely, Agent-Based Computing, the Social 
Sciences and Computer Simulation" (Figure 1).   
 
Fig. 1. Map of the agent oriented research areas [3] 
Location of MABS at the intersection of agent-based computing and computer 
simulation can be accepted if we consider the application of MABS in simulation of 
manufacturing systems and business processes. Due to the fact that vast majority of 
cases requires the inclusion of human factor in simulation of real world system or 
phenomena (for example manufacturing systems, supply chain management), it is 
assumed that social science also affects the MABS.

34 J. Jakieła, P. Litwin, and M. Olech 
When using simulation, the experiment creation process is of great significance. The 
case study presented in the next sections has been build according to steps listed below. 
 
1. Identify and formulate a problem that is to be solved with simulation  
experiment. It is important to have the list of questions articulated, which are 
supposed to be answered with the use of simulation runs. 
2. Create the model. Definition of the real system model, which should provide 
a compromise between the detailed mapping of real system (impeding its im-
plementation and validation), and simplification that suppresses the similarity 
between the model and real system, but making model easier to build. 
3. Choose the metrics.  After the problem is formulated it is important to have 
set of indicators to monitor the state of the modeled system and to draw  
conclusions as well as to find hidden rules or laws. 
4. Set the initial values for simulation parameters.  The sample parameter is 
duration of simulation or number of simulation cycles. During every cycle all 
necessary tasks will be done, of course, only if their preconditions are met. 
The example of other parameters may be demand distribution (Normal, Pois-
son or Exponential distribution), parts and products prices or stock levels. 
5. Run the simulation. After model is fully elaborated, and all variables are set 
up, the simulation may start and operate the predefined number of cycles  
during which values of variables are captured and saved.  
6. Calculate the metrics. Metrics enable to better understand modeled object or 
process. Based on this data the simulation analysis is done. 
7. Interpret simulation results. The last phase is related to the careful analysis 
of simulations results and calculated values of variables. It may lead to  
discovering new rules or dependencies that may be used in the real system 
management process. 
8. Validate the model.  It is based on a comparison of real system results and 
results of simulation, carried out with parameters corresponding to the actual 
operation of the system. The model can be considered valid (verified posi-
tive) if it (repetitively) reflects the behavior of real system. 
The complexity of simulation experiment building process as well as semantic gap 
related to simulation model may be significantly reduced when agent orientation is 
used as modeling paradigm. Next section refers to work that explains why agent is 
intuitive modeling metaphor as well as why agent paradigm is especially well suited 
for managing complexity of problem domain.  
2.2   Using Agent as a Modeling Metaphor and Complexity Management Tool 
One of the fundamental assumptions for this paper is that organization modeling 
process is based on multi-agent system metaphor that leads to perceiving and under-
standing of firm in the way typical for multi-agent systems software engineering,  
but also takes under consideration business aspects along with basic organization 
characteristics. 
The use of a metaphor during the process of organizational analysis and under-
standing is of great significance. Morgan says that metaphor is frequently understood 
as a way to make an argument more appealing, however its meaning is much more

MAS Approach to Business Models Simulations: Supply Chain Management Case Study 35 
important. The use of a metaphor is a consequence of a way one thinks and perceives 
which penetrate our understanding of the world that surrounds us [11]. 
The appearance of obvious similarities between multi-agent systems and business 
organizations is particularly visible in the case of extended enterprises which adopted 
such strategies as decentralization of operations and process orientation. These simi-
larities have been carefully analyzed and described in [7]. Author put together and 
compare structural and behavioral characteristics of multi-agent systems, and features 
of modern organizations extracted from key titles which deal with organization design 
and process orientation [4][5][6][13]. What is more, the process of reducing the se-
mantic gap between the problem domain and the model built for business simulation 
purposes has been presented. Thank to this, the whole modeling process may be very 
intuitive and natural.  
Agent paradigm has also more inherent features that can be used in complexity 
management process which is a serious problem in case of contemporary organiza-
tions modeling. Taking under consideration basic characteristics of complex systems 
defined by Herbert Simon [14] as well as analysis related to agent oriented software 
engineering provided by Jennings and Wooldridge [8], it’s possible to easily prove 
advantages of agent approach in the context of complexity management in the organi-
zation modeling process. 
Additional benefits connected with agent oriented approach during computational 
models development have been analyzed in detail in monograph written by Professor 
Cetnarowicz [1]. As it is claimed, agent oriented approach should lead to improvement 
and enrichment such characteristics of computational representation as flexibility, 
reliability, ability to combine functions of various systems flexibly, as well as ability to 
create new properties such as self-organization or self-adaptation.  
Next section shows the application of MABS to Supply Chain Management. 
3   An Example of Agent Oriented Approach to Business 
Simulations – Supply Chain Case Study 
The following sections present short case study, which illustrates how the multi-
agent-based simulation can be used as a support tool in supply chain management 
process. 
3.1   The Concept of Supply Chain Management 
According to McCormack et al. [10] a Supply Chain is the global network used to 
deliver products and services from raw materials to end customers through an engi-
neered flow of information, physical distribution, and cash. 
Common knowledge is that even small fluctuation of one supply chain parameter 
(for example demand) may lead to the unpredictable behavior of the whole supply 
chain system. It is also worth to mention that executing experiments on the real  
system is usually impossible. These are the reasons why simulation approach has been 
adopted. The process of building the simulation experiment has been based on multi-
agent approach according to the scenario described in the section 2.1.

36 J. Jakieła, P. Litwin, and M. Olech 
3.2   The Scenario of Simulation Experiment 
The simulation experiment has been elaborated in the steps presented below. Descrip-
tion of each step reveals the design decisions which have been made with regard to 
Supply Chain modeling and simulation processes. 
1. Identify and formulate a problem that is to be solved with simulation  
experiment. The main goal of the multi-agent simulation is to check how the 
bullwhip effect may influence the retailer’s delivery time.  
2. Create the model. The application of multi-agent approach to supply chain struc-
ture based on [15] has led to the following model elements: 
• consumer market agent – this element is responsible for buying and consum-
ing products, 
• retailer agent – its mission is to buy products from manufacturer and to sell 
them to consumers, 
• manufacturer agent – it is obliged to purchase materials from supplier,  
process them to final products and sell final products to retailer, 
• supplier agent – this element produces materials and sells them to  
manufacturer. 
Very important part of the model is the logic of agents’ operation which is usually 
formalized with behavioral rules. The sample behavioral rule of manufacturer agent is 
presented on Figure 2 in the form of activity diagram. In order to show the entire 
business logic on one diagram, the level of abstraction is rather high. In fact every 
activity has been split into smaller ones, and therefore the complexity of implementa-
tion realized in NetLogo 4.04 environment is slightly higher. 
During runtime agents communicate using the following flows : 
• goods flow – in the direction from the supplier through manufacturer and  
retailer to consumers, 
• orders (information) flow – from consumers through retailer and manufac-
turer to supplier. 
• money flow – shows how the money circulates in supply chain. 
As a rule the modeling process has several simplifications. They are presented below.  
• time flow when demand occurs and order is placed is skipped, 
• minimal order lot is skipped, 
• minimal production size is skipped, 
• some inner operations are skipped e.g.: production task planning, capacity 
requirements planning, demand planning and forecasting and so on. 
The conceptual model of the supply chain is depicted on the figure 3. 
3. Choose the metrics. The equation (1) describes total delivery time measured 
from the moment when the retailer has ordered products up to the moment when 
products have arrived to retailer.

MAS Approach to Business Models Simulations: Supply Chain Management Case Study 37 
 
Fig. 2. Manufacturer conceptual model 
PCDCPDT TTTTT +++=  (1) 
where: 
TT – total delivery time, T D – delivery time between manufacturer and retailer,  
TP– production time at manufacturer’s floor (it’s skipped if manufacturer has prod-
ucts’ stock greater than the order lot), T DC – delivery time between supplier and 
manufacturer (included only if manufacturer product’s stock is smaller than order lot, 
what is more, supplier has enough part’s stock to meet manufacturer’s order), T PC – 
part’s production time at supplier (included only if supplier part’s stock is not suffi-
cient to meet manufacturer’s order) 
The algorithm realizing this function is implemented in main part of the simulation 
process. Metrics’ values are calculated automatically at a runtime. 
4. Set the initial values for simulation parameters. Because the goal of the simu-
lation experiment is to compare, how the bullwhip effect may influence total  
delivery time of retailer, minimum two simulation runs have to be executed. The 
first run is without inclusion of the bullwhip effect. Second run takes into consid-
eration the bullwhip effect. The case study contains two simulation experiments 
and two runs in each of them. Initial conditions of simulation runs are in table 1. 
5. Run the simulation.  The simulation has been run four times, with parameters 
values as presented in table 1. The results have been saved in text files and used 
in the process of metrics calculations. 
6. Calculate the metrics. The calculated metrics have been presented in table 2. 
Deliveries have been split into three categories A, B and C. The logic of each 
category is explained as follows. Category A denotes direct delivery between 
manufacturer and retailer (products). Category B delivery consists of three 
phases: 1. delivery between supplier and manufacturer (parts), 2. production at

38 J. Jakieła, P. Litwin, and M. Olech 
manufacturer’s plant (parts Æ products), 3. delivery between manufacturer and 
retailer (products). Delivery of category C has four phases: 1. production at  
supplier’s (parts), 2. Delivery between supplier and manufacturer (parts), 3. pro-
duction at manufacturer’s (parts Æ products) 4. delivery between manufacturer 
and retailer (products). 
7. Interpret simulation results.  The interpretation of simulation results has been 
divided into two sections, each related to specific experiment.

not simulated and 6.99 h in the second case. Difference equals 0.72 %, so it is very 
small change. Average time of direct deliveries has changed from 4.00 h to 4.18 so

MAS Approach to Business Models Simulations: Supply Chain Management Case Study 39 
difference is 4.50%. It is clear that bullwh ip effect caused longer direct deliveries 
time, because of temporary lack of goods needed to fulfill the higher demand. The 
time of deliveries in category B was shorter in second run (about 2.74%) than in first 
one. It was mainly caused by different values of demand, which was randomly gener-
ated according to chosen demand distribution. As it can be seen the C type deliveries 
have been affected the most by bullwhip effect. The difference in delivery time was 
more than 3.67%. Bullwhip effect is clearly shown in the longest delivery time. In the 
first run, we had 25.8 h, in second run we had 36 h. Difference equals 39.53% and it 
could be the serious problem in real circumstances.
