An Agent-Based Simulated Annealing Algorithm  
for Data Reduction 
Ireneusz Czarnowski and Piotr Jędrzejowicz 
Department of Information Systems, Gdynia Maritime University  
Morska 83, 81-225 Gdynia, Poland 
{irek,pj}@am.gdynia.pl 
Abstract. Data reduction in the supervised machine learning aims at deciding 
which features and instances from the training set should be retained for further 
use during the learning process. Data reduction can result in increased capabili-
ties and generalization properties of the learning model and shorter learning 
process time. It can also help in scalin g up to a large data sources. This paper 
proposes an approach based on a combination of the simulated annealing tech-
nique and the multi-agent architecture designed for solving the data reduction 
problem. The paper includes the overview of the proposed approach and shows 
the computational experiment results. Experiment has shown that the proposed 
agent-based simulated annealing outperforms the traditional simulated anneal-
ing approach when solving the data reduction problem.  
1   Introduction 
Learning from examples remains the most important paradigm of the machine learn-
ing. Learning from examples is understood as the process of finding a model (or  
function) that describes and distinguishes data classes or concepts, for the purpose of 
being able to use the model to predict the class of objects whose class labels are un-
known [ 8]. The process of finding a classification model is also called learning process 
or learning classifier and the final model is, in short, called the classifier. Learning 
classifiers is also considered as a basic task in many application areas, including, for 
example, data mining, pattern recognition and computer vision. 
Research in the field of machine learning resulted in development of numerous 
approaches and algorithms for classificatio n problems. One of the recent focuses of 
such research includes methods of selecting relevant information, by data reduction, 
and presenting the reduced dataset to a machine learning algorithm [  12]. It is obvious 
that removing some instances from the training set reduces time and memory  
complexity of the learning process [ 18].  
Data reduction can be achieved by selection of instances, by selection of attrib-
utes/features or by simultaneous reduction in both dimensions [  16]. Since the instance 
selection and feature selection are known to belong to the NP-hard problem class 
[ 9, 11], none of the approaches proposed so far can not be considered as a superior nor 
guaranteeing satisfactory results in terms of the learning error reduction or increased 
efficiency of the learning process. Hence, searching for robust and efficient ap-
proaches to data reduction is still an open field of research.

An Agent-Based Simulated Annealing Algorithm for Data Reduction 131 
This paper focuses on data reduction through simultaneous instance and feature 
selection. The main contribution of the paper is proposing and evaluating through 
computational experiment a combination of the simulated annealing algorithm with 
the agent-based population algorithm. The proposed approach assumes that optimi-
zation procedures of the population-based algorithm are implemented as agents 
within an asynchronous team of agents. The proposed approach is compared with an 
implementation of the traditional simulated annealing algorithm to data reduction. 
To validate the approach, a number of computational experiment runs have been 
carried out. 
The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 contains the formulation of the data 
reduction problem. Section 3 gives some details on simulated annealing algorithm and 
agent-based population algorithm. Section 4 explains main features of the proposed 
implementation of the agent-based simulated annealing algorithm. Section 5 provides 
details on the computational experiment setup and discusses its results. Finally, the 
last section contains conclusions and suggestions for future research. 
2   Data Reduction Problem 
The problem of learning from data can be formulated as follows: Given a data set D, a 
set of hypothesis H, a performance criterion P, the learning algorithm L outputs a 
hypothesis h∈H that optimizes P. The data D consists of N training examples, also 
called instances. Each example is described by a set A of n features. The goal of learn-
ing is to produce a hypothesis that optimizes the performance criterion. In the pattern 
classification application, h is a classifier that has been induced based on the training 
set D.  
The learning process can be reinforced by data preprocessing of which data reduc-
tion is an important element. The data reduction process aims at finding patterns or 
regularities within certain features, allowing to induce the so called prototypes or 
reference vectors. The ultimate goal of the data reduction is to reduce the size of train-
ing dataset without losing extractable information. A lot of research work confirms 
that data reduction through instance or feature or instance and feature selection can 
play a pivotal role in building robust learning models [ 5,  12,  13,  14,  16,  18]. 
It can be stipulated that the data reductio n should be considered as the problem of 
finding an optimal subset of prototypes. In the formal manner the problem of data 
reduction can be formulated as follows: Given a learning algorithm L, and dataset D 
with features described by feature set A, an optimal prototype dataset, Sopt, is a subset 
of the dataset D, where each example is described by set of A’⊂A, such that the per-
formance criterion of the learning algorithm L is maximized. Commonly used per-
formance criteria include: accuracy of classification, complexity of the hypothesis, 
classification cost or classification error. 
With respect to learning from data, when data reduction process is carried out, the 
task of learner L is to output the hypothesis h∈H that optimizes performance criterion 
P using data set S which is a subset of the set D, such that S<D (ideally S=Sopt), where 
each example x∈S is described by a set A’ of m features, where m<n.

132 I. Czarnowski and P. J ędrzejowicz 
3   Simulated Annealing and Agent-Based Population Learning 
Algorithm for Data Reduction 
Since data reduction belongs to the class of computationally difficult combinatorial 
optimization problems, one may try to apply a selected metaheuristic like, for exam-
ple, simulated annealing or agent-based population learning algorithm.  
3.1   Simulated Annealing 
The idea of using simulated annealing (SA) has been proposed by Kirkpatrick et al. 
[ 10]. SA is a local search technique simulating the physical process of “annealing”. 
Different from other metaheuristics as for example population based techniques, in 
the SA a single solution is maintained. SA starts with a random solution and next, at 
each step during the neighbourhood search, a move is made. Moves are controlled by 
some probability function. The acceptance of a downhill move depends on the magni-
tude of the decrease in the objective function value and the search time. SA has been 
successfully applied to a variety of difficult optimization problems. The pseudocode 
of the basic SA algorithm is shown as Algorithm 1. More details of this algorithm and 
its applications can be found in [ 1]. 
 
Algorithm 1: Simulated annealing algorithm 
1. Set the initial temperature T0 and the low temperature TL; 
2. Set the number of iteration I; 
3. Set the control temperature Ti:=T0; 
4. Set i=0; 
5. Create initial solution s;  
6. Calculate fitness of s: f(s); 
7. While (i < I) 
8.  Apply neighborhood search procedure producing a new  
solution s’; 
9.    Calculate fitness of s’: f(s’); 
10.   If (s' is better then s) then s:=s'; 
11.   Else  
12.     Generate random number d in the interval (0,1); 
13.     If (d<exp(mod(f(s)-f(s’))/Ti)) then s:=s'; 
14.   End if 
15.   Update the control temperature Ti=f(T0,TL,i); 
16.   i:=i+1; 
17. End while. 
3.2   Agent-Based Population Learning Algorithm  
The A-Team architecture has served as a problem-solving paradigm that has been 
used to design the proposed population learning algorithm. The A-Team concept was 
originally introduced in [  17]. The concept of the A-Team was motivated by several 
approaches like blackboard systems and evolutionary algorithms, which have proven 
to be able to successfully solve some difficult combinatorial optimization problems. 
Within an A-Team agents achieve an implicit cooperation by sharing a population of

An Agent-Based Simulated Annealing Algorithm for Data Reduction 133 
solutions, to the problem to be solved. Following the evolutionary algorithms, such 
solutions form a population consisting of individuals.  
An A-Team can be also defined as a set of agents and a set of memories, forming 
a network in which every agent remains in a closed loop. Each agent possesses some 
problem-solving skills and each memory contains a population of temporary solutions 
to the problem at hand. All agents can work asynchronously and in parallel. During 
their work agents cooperate to construct, find and improve solutions which are read 
from the shared, common memory.  
Main functionality of the agent-based population learning approach includes orga-
nizing and conducting the process of search for the best solution. It involves a  
sequence of the following steps: 
- Generation of the initial population of solutions to be stored in the common  
memory. 
- Activation of optimizing agents which apply solution improvement algorithms to 
solutions drawn from the common memory and store them back after the at-
tempted improvement applying some user defined replacement strategy. 
- Continuation of the reading-improving-replacing cycle until a stopping criterion is 
met. Such a criterion can be defined either or both as a predefined number of itera-
tions  or a limiting time period during which optimizing agents do not manage to 
improve the current best solution. After computation has been stopped  the best 
solution achieved so far is accepted as final. 
More information on the population learning algorithm with optimization procedures 
implemented as agents within an asynchronous team of agents (A-Team) can be 
found in [ 4]. In [ 4] also several its implementations are described.  
4   An Agent-Based Simulated Annealing Algorithm  
This paper proposes an A-Team in which agents execute the simulated annealing 
algorithm based and cooperate in a manner describe in the preceding section with a 
view to solve instances of the reduction problem. The approach is called ABSA 
(Agent-Based Simulated Annealing). To implement the ABSA one has to set and de-
fine the following:  
- solution representation format,  
- initial population of individuals,  
- fitness function, 
- neighborhood search procedure or procedures, 
- replacement strategy implemented for managing the population of individuals. 
4.1   The Solution Representation Format 
A potential solution is represented by a string consisting of two parts. Its first part 
represents numbers of the selected reference instances. The second part includes 
numbers of the selected features.

134 I. Czarnowski and P. J ędrzejowicz 
4.2   The Initial Population 
The initial population is generated randomly. When the initial population is generated, 
the instances are grouped into clusters using the procedure proposed in [  6]. Then 
instances with identical values of this coefficient are grouped into clusters.  
Random selections of instances from initialized clusters constitute the main step of 
the first stage of generating the initial population of individuals. The number of se-
lected instances is equal to the number of initialized clusters, which means that in a 
feasible solution each cluster is represented by a single instance from the training set. 
The second part of a string representing th e solution to the data reduction problem 
and containing numbers of the selected featur es is, at this stage, generated randomly. 
To assure the required diversity the initial solutions are drawn in such a way that 
random individuals represent different numbers of features. The discussed part of the 
string has a length of minimum 1 and maximum n. 
4.3   The Fitness Function 
Each solution from the population is evaluated and the value of its fitness is calcu-
lated. The evaluation is carried out by estimating classification accuracy of the classi-
fier, which is constructed taking into account the instances and features as indicated 
by the solution. 
4.4   The Optimizing Agents  
In the proposed approach optimizing agents, which operate on individuals, are im-
plementations of the simulated annealing algorithm. Each optimizing agent tries to 
improve quality of the received solutions by applying the simulated annealing algo-
rithm. An agent, after being supplied with an individual to be improved, explores its 
neighborhood with the aim of finding a new, better solution in the neighborhood. 
To explore the neighborhood, it has been decided to implement three different  
local search moves:  
- instance replacement procedure (IRP) – the move is defined as replacing a  
randomly selected instance from a randomly chosen cluster with some other ran-
domly chosen instance thus far not included within the solution. The pseudocode 
of IRP is shown as Algorithm 2. 
 
Algorithm 2: Instance replacement procedure 
Input: s - individual representing a solution; L - list of 
numbers of instances not in s; t - number of clusters in s. 
Output: s’ - the modified solution. 
1. Set k by drawing it at random from  {1,2,…,t}; 
2. Identify r which is an instance number representing the k-
th cluster of s; 
3. Set r by drawing it at random from L; 
4. Replace the instance numbered r by the instance numbered 
r’ within the k-th cluster of s thus producing  
individual s’;

An Agent-Based Simulated Annealing Algorithm for Data Reduction 135 
- feature replacement procedure (FRP) – the move is defined as replacing a ran-
domly selected feature with some other random feature thus far not included 
within the solution. The pseudocode of FRP is shown as Algorithm 3. 
 
Algorithm 3: Feature replacement procedure 
Input: s - individual representing a solution; M - list of 
numbers of features in s; M’ - list of numbers of features 
not in s. 
Output: s’ - the modified solution. 
1. Set f by drawing it at random from M; 
2. Set f’ by drawing it at random from M’; 
3. Replace f in s by f’ thus producing s’; 
 
- feature adding/removing procedure (FARP) – the move is defined as adding a new 
feature so far not included within the solution or removing a randomly selected 
feature from the solution. Operations of adding or removing a feature are equally 
probable. The pseudocode of FARP is shown as Algorithm 4. 
 
Algorithm 4: Feature adding/removing procedure 
Input: s - individual representing a solution; M - list of 
the numbers of features in s; M’ - list of the numbers of 
features not in s. 
Output: s’ - the modified solution. 
1. Set h by drawing it at random from the set {0,1}; 
2. If (h==0) then 
3.   Set f’  by drawing it at random from M’; 
4.   Add f’  to s producing s’; 
5. Else  
6.   Set f by drawing it at random from M; 
7.   Remove f from s producing s’; 
8. End if. 
 
The proposed A-Team is constructed from a number of the optimizing agents execut-
ing the simulated annealing algorithm using different local search moves or different 
combinations of such moves.  
4.5   The Replacement Strategy 
The proposed A-Team uses a simple replacement strategy. Each optimizing agent 
receives a solution drawn at random from the population of solutions (individuals). 
The solution returned by optimizing agent is merged with the current population re-
placing the current worst solution.

136 I. Czarnowski and P. J ędrzejowicz 
5   Computational Experiment 
5.1   Computational Experiment Settings 
To validate the proposed approach it has b een decided to carry out the computational 
experiment. The experiment aimed at answering the following two questions:  
- Does the ABSA perform better then the classic simulated annealing approach?  
- Does the choice of the local search moves influence the performance of the classi-
fication model?  
In the reported research the following A-Team architectures have been considered: 
- ABSA #1 – each optimizing agent runs the simulated annealing algorithm using 
one of the neighborhood search moves randomly drawn from the three imple-
mented, that is IRP, FRP or FARP.  The drawing takes place at each iteration, that 
is each time a solution to be improved has been forwarded to an agent  
- ABSA #2 – there are two kinds of optimizing agents – one with the IRP neighbor-
hood search procedure and another running the simulated annealing algorithm  
using one of the neighborhood search moves randomly drawn from the two im-
plemented, that is FRP or FARP. The drawing takes place at each iteration, that is 
each time a solution to be improved has been forwarded to an agent  
- ABSA #3 – three kinds of optimizing agents, each running an implementation of a 
different neighborhood search procedure. 
5.2   Dataset Choice and the Experiment Plan 
Datasets used in the experiment have been obtained from the UCI Machine Learning 
Repository [ 2]. They include:  Cleveland heart disease (303 instances, 13 attributes, 2 
classes, the best reported classification accuracy 90% [  7]), credit approval (690, 15, 2, 
86.9% [ 7]), Wisconsin breast cancer (699, 15, 2, 97.5% [  2]), sonar problem (208, 60, 
2, 87.1% [ 7]).  
Each benchmarking problem has been solved 30 times, and the experiment plan 
involved 3 repetitions of the 10-cross-validation scheme. The reported values of the 
quality measure have been averaged over all runs. The quality measure in all cases 
was the correct classification ratio. In th e 10-cross-validation scheme, for each fold, 
the training dataset was reduced using the proposed approach.  
During the experiment population size for each investigated A-Team architecture 
was set to 20. The process of searching for the best solution has been stopped either 
after 100 iterations or earlier in case there has been no improvement of the current 
best solution for one minute of computation. Values of these parameters were set 
arbitrarily. The initial temperature T0 and the low temperature TL within simulated

reduced dataset, 
- results obtained using the reduced dataset produced using the standard simulated 
annealing algorithm (SA).

6   Conclusions 
The main contribution of the paper is proposing and validating a novel approach to 
solving data reduction problem. The proposed approach uses the multi-agent para-
digm and enables solving difficult data reduction optimization problem using a set of 
optimizing agents based on the simulated annealing algorithm.  
The proposed approach extends the available range of algorithms for solving data 
reduction problem. Computational experiment results have confirmed that the agent-
based simulated annealing is an effective da ta reduction tool contributing to achieving 
higher quality of machine learning classification in comparison to a standard simu-
lated annealing implementation.  It has been also shown that the parallel reduction of 
both – instances and features assures better overall results as compared with other 
considered schemes.  
Properties of the proposed approach in the term of its efficiency and computation 
time will be further studied. The future research will also focus on examination of the 
influence of the number of copies of optimizing agents on the quality of the selected 
prototypes and computation speed-up factor. It is also planned to consider hybrid 
solutions where the simulated annealing algorithm will be integrated with other local 
search procedures.

Katarzyna Drozdz and Halina Kwasnicka
Institute of Informatics, Wroclaw University of Technology, Wroclaw, Poland
halina.kwasnicka@pwr.wroc.pl, katarzyna.drozdz@gmail.com

Abstract. Together with increasing sizes of collected data, the prob-
lem of feature set reduction becomes more important. Machine learning
methods, including classiﬁers, are sensitive to the training data. One of
the known problems is called ’curse of dimensionality’. Some features (at-
tributes) in the collection of data may not be informative so they obstruct
the learning process. Removing them is very desirable from the classiﬁ-
cation quality point of view. In the paper we focus on wrapper approach
to feature set reduction. We propose an evolutionary method to feature
reduction by means of selection and construction. Genetic Algorithm is
used as a tool for feature selection and Gene Expression Programming
as a tool of dimensionality reduction by features construction. The paper
presents the approach and the results of conducted experiments. Conclu-
sions and future plans end the paper.

Iterative Method for Improving Consistency
of Multi-attribute Object Judgments
Performed by Teams of Decision Makers
Henryk Piech and Urszula Bednarska
Institute of Comp. & Information Sci., Czestochowa University of Technology,
Dabrowskiego 73, 42-200 Czestochowa, Poland
h.piech@adm.pcz.czest.pl
Abstract. Groups of decision makers form judgments of given objects,
using sets of inconsistent data. This issue was described in many papers
and the practical usage was presented by Saaty in his method of relative
judgments. Typically only some attributes are chosen for judging. Judg-
ments are relative, usually scaled or normalized. In this paper we try to
aggregate the given judgments and make them consistent. We allocate a
single elements of the Saaty’s matrix (vectors or rows) for each decision
maker. We need to remember that consistency of group decision making
can be achieved in many ways and that it concerns diﬀerent structural
level of judgments.

Experimental Investigation of the Synergetic Effect 
Produced by Agents Solving Together Instances of the 
Euclidean Planar Travelling Salesman Problem 
Piotr Jędrzejowicz and Izabela Wierzbowska 
Department of Information Systems, Gdynia Maritime Academy, 
Morska 81-87, 81-225 Gdynia, Poland 
{pj,iza}@am.gdynia.pl 
Abstract. The goal of the paper is to identify and confirm the existence of the 
synergetic effect produced by agents solving together instances of the Euclidean 
planar travelling salesman problem. The research included the computational 
experiment in which computation results produced by six implemented A-
Teams are analyzed. The reported A-Teams have been built using the JABAT 
environment. Combinations of five local search procedures, each encoded as an 
optimizing agent, have been used. The experiment involved instances of the 
Euclidean planar travelling salesman problem of different sizes. Problem  
instances have been solved by different A-Teams  with different numbers of in-
dividuals in the population of solutions stored in the common memory. The  
research has confirmed that constructing an A-Team from heterogeneous opti-
mizing agents might result in achieving a synergetic effect and thus increasing a 
quality of the computation results. 
Keywords: agents, optimization problem, asynchronous team. 
1   Introduction 
The techniques used to solve difficult combinatorial optimization problems have 
evolved from constructive algorithms to local search techniques, and finally to popu-
lation-based algorithms. In recent years, technological advances have enabled devel-
opment development of various parallel and distributed versions of the population 
based methods. At the same time, as a result of convergence of many technologies 
within computer science such as object-o riented programming, distributed computing 
and artificial life, the agent technology has emerged. An agent is understood here as 
any piece of software that is designed to use intelligence to automatically carry out an 
assigned task, mainly retrieving and delivering information.  
Paradigms of the population-based methods and multiple agent systems have been 
during mid nineties integrated within the concept of the asynchronous team of agents 
(A-Team). A-Team is a multi agent architecture, which has been proposed in several 
papers of S.N. Talukdar and co-authors [1], [2], [3], [4].  
The middleware platforms supporting implementation of A-Teams, is represented 
by the JADE-Based A-Team environment (JABAT). Its different versions were

Experimental Investigation of the Synergetic Effect Produced by Agents 161 
proposed in [5], [6] and [7]. The JABAT middleware was built with the use of JADE 
(Java Agent Development Framework), a software framework proposed by TILAB 
[8]. JABAT complies with the requirements of the next generation A-Teams which 
are portable, scalable and in conformity with the FIPA standards. JABAT produces 
solutions to optimization problems using a set of optimizing agents, each representing 
an improvement algorithm. The process of solving a single task (i.e. the problem 
instance) consists of several steps. At first the initial population of solutions is gener-
ated. Individuals forming the initial population are, at the following computation 
stages, improved by independently acting agents, thus increasing chances for reaching 
the global optimum. Finally, when the stopping criterion is met, the best solution in 
the population is taken as the result.  
In this paper we investigate experimentally the synergetic effect produced by 
agents solving together instances of the Euclidean planar travelling salesman problem. 
It is assumed that agents work together within a JABAT-implemented A-Team. The 
goal of the paper is to establish the existence of such synergetic effect and, if possible, 
to discover some rules for selecting and composing an A-Team with a view to support 
the design of A-Teams with a synergetic effect feature present. The research is  
motivated by an absence of such rules in the literature-reported cases on the A-Team 
engineering. 
The paper is constructed as follows: Section 2 describes the implementation of the 
A-Team designed to solve instances of the Euclidean planar travelling salesman prob-
lem, Section 3 gives details of the experiment settings and experiment plan and  
Section 4 contains a discussion of the experiment results. Finally some conclusions 
and suggestions for future research are drawn. 
2   A-Team Implementation 
2.1   Problem Formulation 
The Euclidean planar travelling salesman pr oblem (EPTSP) is a particular case of the 
general TSP.  EPTSP can be formulated as follows: given n cities (points) in the plane 
and their Euclidean distances, the problem is to find the shortest TSP-tour, i.e. a 
closed path visiting each of the n cities exactly once.  
2.2   A-Team Working Strategy 
The process of solving a single task in JABAT is defined by a working strategy un-
derstood as a set of rules responsible for the process of maintaining the common 
memory. The common memory contains a population of solutions called individuals. 
All individuals are feasible solutions of the instance to be solved.  
The considered A-Teams implemented using the JABAT environment follow the 
working strategy in which: 
− All individuals in the initial population of solutions are generated randomly.   
− Selection of individuals for improvement is a random move.

162 P. J ędrzejowicz and I. Wierzbowska 
− Returning individual replaces the first found worse individual. If a worse individ-
ual can not be found within a certain number of reviews (review is understood as 
a search for the worse individual after an improved solution is returned) then the 
worst individual in the common memory is replaced by the randomly generated 
one representing a feasible solution.  
− Computation time is arbitrarily set in advance.  
2.3   Optimizing Agents 
Among several types of agents performing administration, maintenance, communica-
tion and optimization tasks which are standardized in JABAT, only optimizing agents 
directly influence the quality of individuals (i.e. solutions) stored in the common 
memory. Individuals from the common memory are selected in accordance with the 
current working strategy and forwarded for improvement to the independently run-
ning optimizing agents. Such an agent attempts to improve the received solution and, 
subsequently, resends it to the common memory.   
In the reported research there are five types of optimizing agents, each of them at-
tempts to improve the initial solution or solutions executing utmost 100 random 
moves. The first encountered improvement stops this process. The random moves 
employed by the agents are as follows: 
− Simple exchange (Ex2) – deletes two random edges from the input solution thus 
breaking the tour under improvement into two disconnected paths and reconnects 
them in the other possible way, reversing one path.  
− Triple exchange (Ex3) – deletes three random edges from the input solution thus 
breaking the tour under improvement into three disconnected paths. These paths 
can be reconnected in two other possible ways. Algorithm chooses the best of the 
resulting tours. 
− Recombination1 (R1) – there are two input solutions. A subpath from one of 
them is randomly selected. In the next step it is supplemented with edges from 
the second solution. If this happens to be  impossible the procedure constructs an 
edge connecting endpoint of the sub path with the closest point in the second in-
put solution not yet in the resulting tour.  
− Recombination2 (R2) – there are two input solutions. A sub path from one of 
them is randomly selected. In the next step it is supplemented by the remaining 
points in a sequence taken from the second solution.  
− Mutation (M) – two randomly selected points from the input solution are directly 
connected. This subpath is supplemented with edges as in R1.  If this happens to 
be impossible the procedure constructs an edge connecting endpoint of the sub-
path with the closest remaining point from the initial solution.   
3   Computational Experiment Settings 
Instances used in the reported experiment come from TSPLIB – a library of sample 
instances for the TSP [9]. The following instances have been used: pr76 (76 cities), 
pr152 (152), pr226 (226), pr299 (299) and pr439 (439).

Experimental Investigation of the Synergetic Effect Produced by Agents 163 
In each experiment run 10 optimizing agents have been employed. To identify and 
evaluate synergetic effect of different agents working together six A-Team architec-
tures with different combinations of optimizing agents have been tested. Five  
A-Teams have been constructed from the homogenous agents of each kind and one 
Team included all implemented optimization agents. The resulting A-Teams are  
further on referred to using the following notation:  
− Ex2 consisting of 10 Ex2 type agents 
− Ex3 consisting of 10 Ex3 type agents 
− M consisting of 10 M type agents  
− R1 consisting of 10 R1 type agents  
− R2 consisting of 10 R2 type agents  
− All consisting of 2 Ex2 type agents plus 2  Ex3,  2 M, 2 R1 and 2 R2 type (in total 
10 agents) 
For each problem instance and for each of the six considered A-Teams calculations 
have been carried-out for several variants of the common memory size from the inter-
val of (2 – 15) individuals.  The remaining settings included:  
− Maximum number of the allowed reviews on returning of individuals  – 5 
− Termination condition - 10 minutes calculation time  
Experiment has been carried out on the cluster Holk of the Tricity Academic  
Computer Network built of 256 Intel Itanium 2 Dual Core with 12 MB L3 cache 
processors with Mellanox InfiniBand interconnections with 10Gb/s bandwidth.  
4   Computational Experiment Results 
For each instance, each A-Team kind (i.e. th e considered combination of agent types) 
and each considered population size, the results  - in terms of computation error - have 
been averaged over not less than six runs. Computation errors have been calculated in 
relation to the optimum results known from the TSPLIB. 
On average, the computation error produced by the All A-Team is smaller than av-
erage errors generated by A-Teams composed of the homogenous agents, as it can be 
seen in Fig. 1. All A-Team remains a winner for all the investigated common memory 
sizes as shown in Fig. 2. The worst performer remains R2 team which results do not 
even fit to the scale used to draw Fig. 2. 
Tab. 1 shows for which instances the considered A-Teams achieved the smallest 
average computation error averaged over  all considered common memory size. 
Again, the A-Team constructed from heterogeneous agents gives the best results in 
majority of cases.

within an A-Team influences the overall A-Team performance. This has been done 
through elimination of the worst performing optimization agents from the All A-Team 
and, at the same time, adding some good performers. In Fig. 3 the results of such an 
approach are shown for the case of the pr226 instance and the population (i.e. com-

5   Conclusions 
The presented research has confirmed that constructing an A-Team from heterogene-
ous optimizing agents might result in achieving a synergetic effect and thus increasing 
a quality of the computation results.  In case of the investigated Euclidean planar 
travelling salesman problem, where several A-Teams have been built using relatively 
low quality optimizing agents, a synergetic effect has, on average, appeared for all 
sizes of the common memory. For the larger problem instances such an effect to  
appear requires some computation-time lag. Small size instances can however be 
effectively solved using a number of homogenous local-search optimizing agents 
working together for a certain time, which would be shorter than the time required by 
a heterogeneous A-Tem to achieve a comparable quality. All these findings refer to 
the working strategy used in the experiment where escaping from the local optima has 
been based on inserting to the common memo ry during the computation process some 
random solutions from time to time.  
The experiment results do not allow to draw any general rules for construction of 
an A-Team from heterogeneous optimizing agents with a view to achieving a syner-
getic effect even for a specific problem type. Future research will focus on introduc-
ing different working strategy schemes and evaluating their effect on computation 
results and a synergetic effect, which might be helpful in identifying more general 
observations.

Besma Zeddini1 and Mahdi Zargayouna2
1 University of Le Havre, LMAH Laboratory

Abstract. Vehicle Routing problems are highly complex problems for
which diﬀerent Artiﬁcial Intelligence techniques have been used. In this
paper, we propose two agent-oriented self-organization models for the
dynamic version of the problem with time windows. The ﬁrst model
relies on a spatial representation, and the second is based on a space-time
representation of the agents’ action zones, which are able to maintain a
good distribution of the vehicles on the environment. This distribution
provides better results than traditional methods by allowing the agents
to take their decisions while anticipating future changes in the system’s
parameters.

Deﬁnition 1 (Spatial Action Zone)
Let G =( N,A ) be the graph representing the transportation network, with a set
of nodes N ={(ni)},i ={0, ... ,m} (node n0 is the depot) and a set of arcs
A ={(ni,n j)|ni ∈ N,n j ∈ N,n i ⁄= nj}. Let the costs matrix C ={(Cij)} of
size m×m (the arc (ni,n j) has a travel time ofCij). We deﬁne the spatial zone
ζ =( Nζ,Aζ) as a subgraph of G.

Abstract. Cooperative multi-agent systems are rapidly growing sub-
class of the multi-agent systems where autonomous components allow to
built and use several agent types acting in parallel while cooperatively
solving a task. Possible form of such cooperation may be based, for ex-
ample, on adaptive memory methods, where partial elements of good so-
lutions are stored and next combined to create new complete solutions.
Alternative possibility forms central memory approaches, where complete
elite solutions are exchanged among various heuristics. Moreover, cooper-
atively solving a task is often combined with learning mechanism, where
agents adapt their behavior to the new conditions of environment during
the process of solving the problem. The goal of the paper is to propose a
dedicated cooperative multi-agent system for solving the Vehicle Rout-
ing Problem with a reinforcement learning mechanism implemented in it.
Keywords: multi-agent systems, multi-agent learning, cooperative
problem solving, heuristics, vehicle routing problem.

Abstract. Reinforcement Learning is an optimal adaptive optimiza-
tion method for stationary environments. For non-stationary environ-
ments where the transition function and reward structure change over
time, the traditional algorithms seems to be ineﬀective in order to fol-
low the environmental changes. In this paper we propose the Anomaly
Detection Q-learning algorithm which increase learning abilities of stan-
dard Q-learning algorithm by applying Chauvenet’s criterion to detects
anomalies.

Abstract. In this paper we propose two ensemble classiﬁers using ex-
pression trees as weak classiﬁers. The ﬁrst ensemble uses the AdaBoost
approach and the second makes use of Dempster’ˆa˘A´Zs rule of combina-
tion and applies triplet mass functions to combine classiﬁers. The per-
formance of both ensemble classiﬁers is evaluated experimentally. The
experiment involved 9 well known datasets from the UCI Irvine Machine
Learning Repository. Experiment results show that using GEP-induced
expression trees allows to construct high quality ensemble classiﬁers.
Keywords: gene expression programming, AdaBoost, evidentional
reasoning.

The reported research allowst o draw the followingc onclusions:
– Genee xpression programming isau s e f ul andp r a c tical tool toi nduce ex-

Experimental Evaluation of the A-Team Solving
Instances of the RCPSP/max Problem
EwaR a t ajczak-Ropel
Department of Information Systems
Gdynia Maritime University, Poland
ewra@am.gdynia.pl
Abstract. The paper proposes an agent-based approach to solving in-
stances of the RCPSP/max problem. Since the problem is known to be
NP-hard, the proposed solution takes advantage of the parallel and dis-
tributed computations abilities of the E-JABAT which is a middleware
supporting the construction of the dedicated A-Team architectures based
on the population-based approach. In this paper the E-JABAT-based
A-Team architecture dedicated for solving the RCPSP/max problem in-
stances is proposed and experimentally validated. Computational exper-
iment involves evaluation of the inﬂuence of the time used to solve the
problem on the results obtained. The paper contains the RCPSP/max
problem formulation, overview of the E-JABAT environment, descrip-
tion of the E-JABAT architecture for solving the RCPSP/max problem
instances and a discussion of the computational experiment results.
1 Introduction
The paper pr oposes an agent-based approach to solving instances oft h er e-
source constrained project schedulingp roblem with minimal andm aximal time
lags (time windows) known in the literature as the RCPSP/max. RCPSP/max
has attracted a lot of attention andm any exact andh e u ristica lgorithms have
been recently proposed fors olving it (see fore xample [5], [12], [15]). Since the
problem isk nown to be NP-hard the approaches proposed so far produce either
approximate solutions orc an be applied fors olving instances oft h elimited size.
Hence, searchingf orm ore eﬀectivea lgorithms ands olutionst o the RCPSP/max
problem iss till a lively ﬁeld of research. One of the promisingd irections ofs u c h
research ist o take advantage of the parallel andd istributed computation abili-
ties,w hich are the feature oft h econtemporary multiple-agents ystems.
The multiple-agents ystems are ani mportanta nd intensively expandinga r e a
of research andd evelopment.T here isa number ofm ultiple-agent approaches
proposed to solved iﬀerentt ypes of optimization problems. One oft h e mist h e

2 Problem Formulation
In the RCPSP/max problem a set of n + 2a c tivities V ={0, 1, ... ,n ,n +1} is
considered. Each activity has to be processed without interruption to complete
the project.T he dummy activities 0 and n +1 representt h eb e ginninga ndt h e
end of the project.T he duration ofa n activity j, j =0 , ... ,n +1i sd enoted by
dj where d0 = dn+1 =0 .T here are r renewabler e source types.T he availability
ofe a c hr e source type k in each time per iod is rk units, k =1 , ... ,r . Each
activity j requires rj,k units ofr e source k duringe a c hp e riod of its duration,
where r0,k = rn+1,k =0 , k =1 , ...,r . Each activity j∈ V has a start t ime sj
which isad e cision variable.T here are generalized precedence relations (temporal
constraints)o ft h es t a r t-to-start type sj− si≥ δij, δij ∈ Z, deﬁned between the
activities.
The structure ofap r oject can be represented by an activity-on-node net-
work G =( V,A ), where V ist h es e tofa c tivities and A ist h es e tof precedence
relationships.T he objective ist o ﬁnd a schedu le ofa c tivities start ingt imes
S =[ s0, ... ,s n+1], where s0 =0( project alwaysb e ginsa tt ime zero) andr e-
source constraints are satisﬁed, such that the schedule duration T(S)= sn+1 is
minimized.T he detailed description of the problem can be found in [11].
The RCPSP/max, as an extension oft h eR CPSP, belongs to the class of
NP-hard optimization problems ([1], [4]). The objective ist o ﬁndam a k e s p an
minimal schedule that meets the constraints imposed by the precedence relations
andt h elimited resource availabilities.

6 Conclusions

Presented results are better then the best solutionsk nown fromt h eliterature.
Itc an be alson oticed that they are obtained in as horter time.T ime comparisons
are however diﬃcults ince the discussed implementation haveb e en usingd iﬀer-

the signiﬁcantp a r toft h etime isu s e dfor agentc ommunication which has an
inﬂuence on both - computation time andq u alityo fr e s ults.
Investigatingt h er e s ults itc an be noticed that the size oft h epopulation in
the common memory shouldb es e lected in accordance with the t ime allowed
forc omputations.I n case oft h etime periods of 15 and 30 seconds the results
obtained with 50 individualsh aveb e enw orse theni n case of2 5i ndividuals.F or
the computation lasting 60 seconds the results obtained by5 0i ndividualsh ave
been better then these produced by 25. Interesting isa lso the fact of obtaining
the same results for 10 activities (j10) fora ll cases.I t indicates that algorithms
shouldb e improved ort h enumber of iteration shouldb e increased.
It is worth noticingt h a tin this implementation the main disadvantage oft h e
approach presented in [10],that ist h epossible lack ofs olutions in some cases, has
been eliminated.I n all cases the 100% off e a sibles olutionsh aveb e eno btained.
The main advantage ofb oth approaches isq uite simple implementation oft h e
optimization algorithms.
Future research will concentrate on ﬁnding, testinga nda d dingt o E-JABAT
more diﬀerent optimization agents and improvingt h eexisting ones.M ore ex-
periments are needed to establish rules on ﬁndinga no ptimal conﬁguration:

Early Warning of Cardiac Problems in a Crowd
Przemys/suppresslaw Gawro´nski, Khalid Saeed, and Krzysztof Ku/suppresslakowski
Faculty of Physics and Applied Computer Science,
AGH University of Science and Technology,

gawron@newton.ftj.agh.edu.pl, saeed@agh.edu.pl,

Abstract. We propose a new system of early warning of the presence
of persons with heart problems in a crowd. Such a person is detected
by a signal from her/his personal intelligent device, which continuously
measures the cardiac activity. Once the signal is abnormal, the warning
is transmitted to devices of neighboring persons, who can react. The sim-
ulation of crowd dynamics is based on the Helbing model.
Keywords: crowd dynamics, biometrics, simulation.

Symmetry Approach to Evacuation Scenarios
Wieslawa Sikora and Janusz Malinowski
Faculty of Physics and Applied Computer Science, AGH - University of Science
and Technology, Al. Mickiewicza 30, 30-059 Krakow, Poland
Abstract. The symmetry analysis method based on the theory of group
representations is used for description of complex systems and their be-
havior in this work. The ﬁrst trial of using the symmetry analysis in
modeling of behavior of complex social system is presented. The evacua-
tion of large building scenarios are discussed as transition from chaotic to
ordered states, described as movements of individuals according to ﬁelds
of displacements, calculated correspondingly to given scenario. The sym-
metry of the evacuation space is taken into account in calculation of dis-
placements ﬁeld - the displacements related to every point of this space
are presented in the coordinate frame in the best way adapted to given
symmetry space group, which is the set of basic vectors of irreducible rep-
resentation of given symmetry group.. The results obtained with using the
symmetry consideration are compared with corresponding results calcu-
lated under assumption of shortest way to exits (Voronoi assumption).
Keywords: social systems, evacuation scenario, symmetry analysis
method.

Development of a Cognitive-Emotional Model  
for Driver Behavior 
Christian Maag, Christian Mark, and Hans-Peter Krüger 
Universität Würzburg, Psychologisches Institut III, Röntgenring 11,  
97070 Würzburg, Germany 
{maag,mark,krueger}@psychologie.uni-wuerzburg.de 
http://www.izvw.de 
Abstract. Aggressive driving has become a very common phenomenon. It 
highlights the importance of emotional states as an influencing factor for driv-
ing style and behavior. Advanced driver assistance systems are implemented in 
the car with the objective to enhance road safety and to assist the driver. In  
order to develop these systems according to the users’ needs and to assess the 
potential effects, the driving behavior of drivers (with and without these new 
technologies) must be known. This modeling of drivers’ behavior has to take 
into account cognitive and emotional mechanisms, in order to be as realistic as 
possible. The paper presents a cognitive-emotional driver model focusing on 
anger and reports evidence for its valid ity. This driver model can be imple-
mented in microscopic, agent-based traffic models and expands the output and 
scope of traffic modeling and analysis on cognitive and emotional variables. 
Keywords: driving behavior, driving simulation, aggressive driving, driver 
state, driver emotion. 
1   Introduction 
Conflicts and aggressive episodes between drivers in road traffic are very common [1] 
and receive increasing awareness by road users and the general public. In the view of 
most people the traffic climate has become more stressful and more aggressive within 
the last years.  
The phenomenon of aggressive driving is also reflected by scientific articles relat-
ing to that topic. Studies on aggressive driving show that the state of drivers changes 
the way how people drive and interact with other road users [2] [3] [4]. Moreover, it 
changes driving conditions on the system level (traffic climate). Therefore, in traffic 
psychology emotional driver state is known as an important factor influencing driving 
behavior (individual level), interactions on the road (dyadic level), and resulting traf-
fic characteristics (system level). 
The analysis of complexity issues in road traffic is part of the FP7 funded project 
SOCIONICAL that develops complexity science modeling methods and tools for 
socio-technical systems. In this context, SOCIONICAL aims at analyzing effects of 
Ambient Intelligence (AmI) devices (in terms of traffic psychology advanced driver

Development of a Cognitive-Emotional Model for Driver Behavior 243 
assistance systems – ADAS). Therefore, an interesting research question in  
SOCIONICAL is the modeling of driver behavior including cognitive-emotional 
mechanisms of drivers and the analysis of potential effects of future AmI devices. 
In the following, some background information is given concerning agent-based 
modeling of driving behavior, AmI, ADAS, and C2X (car to infrastructure (C2I) 
communication with giving traffic information and recommendations to drivers, and 
car to car (C2C) communication with one car influencing others and vice versa) tech-
nology in road traffic, and influence of emotional state on driving behavior (chapter 
2). After that, the overall modeling approach is presented and the cognitive-emotional 
driver model explained by focusing on anger while driving. Furthermore, the parame-
ter specification and validation issues concerning the developed model are described 
(chapter 3). A summary and outlook concludes the paper (chapter 4). 
2   Background 
2.1   Agent-Based Modeling of Driving Behavior 
In the last years, agent-based modeling has become more and more popular in the 
social sciences and has created an own research approach within computational social 
sciences. Agent-based modeling is an approach to study effects of individual behavior 
on a system level by simulating the actions and interactions of autonomous individu-
als (agents). Different agents interacting with each other (multi-agent system) allow to 
observe emerging phenomena going beyond the properties of single agents.  
The modeling of driver behavior has become more and more important in the last 
years. Reasons for that are new technologies like ADAS and mobile ICT in the car 
that offer new ways for improving the overall performance and safety of road traffic. 
But in order to develop these systems according to users’ needs and to assess potential 
effects, the behavior of drivers (with and without new technologies) must be known. 
In reality, drivers are autonomous, dynami cally adapt their driving behavior to the 
dynamics of the surrounding environment, in teract with other drivers/vehicles, and 
want to achieve a specific goal. Moreover, dr ivers are characterized by a limited view 
of the whole system, incomplete information or capabilities to solve a problem,  
asynchronous acting, and a missing central control system [5]. Therefore, micro-
scopic, agent-based modeling is the appropriate method for modeling traffic. This 
approach has to take into consideration the limited capabilities of human drivers and 
their driving attitudes [6]. 
In general, two kinds of agents are distinguished: reactive agents and cognitive 
agents. Whereas a reactive agent links perceptions to responses and is e.g. used for 
describing general mechanisms of car following behavior, a cognitive agent is also 
able to perform knowledge based tasks and reasoning (e.g. including experience or 
memory). The differentiation between reactive and cognitive-emotional aspects of 
driving suggests a multi-layer architecture for describing the road user. Wahle et al. 
[5] choose a two-layer architecture and distinguish a tactical layer responsible for the 
task of driving, i.e. acceleration, braking, lane changing, and a strategic layer respon-
sible for information assimilation and decision making.

244 C. Maag, C. Mark, and H.-P. Krüger 
2.2   AmI, ADAS, and C2X Technology in Road Traffic 
The science of ambient intelligence explores technical possibilities to improve the 
way how environments could help people and how technology could help society [7]. 
Cook et al. [7] describe the “basic idea behind Ambient Intelligence (AmI) is that by 
enriching an environment with technology  (e.g. sensors and devices interconnected 
through a network), a system can be built such that acts as an ‘electronic butler’, 
which senses features of the users and their environment, then reasons about the  
accumulated data, and finally selects actions to take that will benefit the users in the 
environment.” (p. 278). Taking that idea into account, Cook et al. (2009) define ambi-
ent intelligence as “a digital environment that proactively, but sensibly, supports peo-
ple in their daily lives” (p. 279). 
In the last years, a variety of different systems assisting the driver were introduced 
in the market [8]. From safety systems that support the driver in safety-critical situa-
tions and stabilize the car (e.g. antilock brake system), over comfort systems that 
reduce the workload of the driver (e.g. crui se control), to information systems that 
carry out secondary tasks and give the driver important information (e.g. navigation 
system). Another banding of these systems is based on the level of intervention from 
information over recommendation and assistan ce to control [9]. Besides the intended 
safety and comfort issues [10], such systems are discussed because of their effects on 
traffic flow and environment [11]. 
Up to now, most of these technical systems are related to a single vehicle, e.g. 
automatic cruise control or lane departure warning. Such assistance functions carry 
out to some extend the same tasks as the driver. Therefore, the role of the driver  
begins to change from controlling to monitoring – the driver observes system per-
formance and intervenes only, if something is suboptimal. This could lead to new 
problems, e.g. reduced vigilance and situation awareness [12] [13].  
Currently, more and more ADAS are developed (e.g. hazard warning, automatic 
emergency call, intersection assistance) that are based on the C2X communication. 
Nevertheless, the actual consequences of such AmI systems for driving safety must be 
analyzed very carefully before they are brought to the market. 
2.3   Emotional State and Driving Behavior 
Driver state is an important factor influencing the individual evaluation of driving 
situations, the driving behavior, and the overall system characteristics of traffic. 
Driver state is a multidimensional construct. Exemplary dimensions are attentiveness 
(e.g. sleepy, reduced vigilance, awake), fitness to drive (e.g. no substances, driving 
under the influence of alcohol), and emotional state (e.g. anger, aggression). 
In the scientific literature, different reasons for aggressive driving are discussed. 
Some authors make the overall setting of driving (especially motorway driving) re-
sponsible for aggressive conflicts. The ability of the drivers to communicate with each 
other is very limited. Only by giving signals like blinker or high beam (that are often 
understood as aggressive) and by driving style (e.g. short headway, fast approaching 
of leading vehicle) drivers can communicate with others (Bösser, 1987). As direct 
communication is crucial in order to avoid misunderstandings, conflicts between 
drivers are very likely [14].

Development of a Cognitive-Emotional Model for Driver Behavior 245 
Frustrating situations (e.g. a traffic jam or a leading vehicle on the left lane that is 
not changing to the right) are a starting point for driver aggression [15] [16] [17]. 
Such a situation could lead to anger and a tendency to behave aggressive. Mostly, 
aggressive driving could be understood as an expression of instrumental aggression, 
because drivers tailgate in order to reach a specific objective – e.g. being in due time 
at their destination. 
The mentioned situational factors that contribute to aggressive driving interact with 
personal factors. The personality of a driver (e.g. frustration tolerance, anger, sensa-
tion seeking) influences the coping behavior while confronted with a frustrating situa-
tion [16] [17] [18]. An additional phenomenon linked to aggressive driving lies in the 
emotional value of cars and driving. Therefor e, drivers feel personally insulted, if 
another person hinders their journey and frustrates them [19]. 
3   Development of a Cognitive-Emotional Model of Driver 
3.1   Modeling Approach 
The objective of developing a cognitive-emotional driver model is to clarify the inter-
actions between driving behavior and emotional states during driving. Later on, this 
model can be implemented in agent-based modeling approaches of traffic and is used 
to study phenomena in road traffic that are based on cognitive-emotional mechanisms 
of drivers.  
The basic steps for driver modeling are: 
• Definition of prototypic traffic situations for later implementation in the driv-
ing simulator (example: tailgating driver on a motorway).  
Prototypic situations are demonstrated in the virtual environment of a driving 
simulator, in order to study the characteristics, triggering situations, phenome-
nology, and local consequences of emotional driving. 
• Description of driver behavior in these situations and parameter specification 
by performing driving simulator studies (example: behavior and emotional  
response of the driver who is tailgated). 
The parameter specification is based on behavior functions. A behavior func-
tion links characteristics of the traffic situation to driver emotions and  
behavior. 
• Modeling of driver behavior in these situations (example: emotional response 
as a function of following distance).  
A behavior model including cognitive-emotional processes is developed and 
validated (see chapter 3.2 and 3.3). 
After that, the developed cognitive-emotional driver model can be used. Exemplary 
application areas are the implementation of the driver model in the ambient traffic 
model of a driving simulation and in microscopic, agent-based traffic modeling.  
3.2   Cognitive-Emotional Driver Model 
The visualization of the cognitive-emotional driver model (Fig. 1) is based on the 
notation of the systems theory by Bischof [20] and is divided in a traffic layer and a

246 C. Maag, C. Mark, and H.-P. Krüger 
cognitive-emotional layer. The arrows stand for input or output variables. These vari-
ables are processed in units that are identifi ed by boxes or circles. The boxes in the 
traffic layer process objective and observable data (e.g. position of vehicles). The 
circles in the cognitive-emotional layer handle cognitive and/or emotional inputs that 
are not directly measurable or observable. The rounded boxes work on both types of 
input variables.  
The traffic layer covers the objective surrounding of the driver and contains a “tra-
ditional” driving model [21] [22]. That means the traffic layer specifies the longitudi-
nal and lateral behavior of a driver/vehicle unit and the changing of lanes depending 
on road characteristics, traffic situation, weather, etc. The cognitive-emotional layer 
models the driver who is able to change his driving behavior due to emotional  
responses and anticipation of future events. It contains internal processes of the driver 
(e.g. anger) and their interdependency with driving style and traffic situation.  
The model proposes the following key processes: (a) Detection of interactions be-
tween road users, (b) Calculation of final emotional response, (c) Influencing driving 
style, (d) Changing of driver’s maneuvers. 
• Detection of interactions between road users (box 5 and box 6): The positions 
and dynamics (speed, acceleration) of the surrounding vehicles (“POS and 
DYN of Vehicles”; output of box 6) in relation to the position and dynamics of 
the ego driver (“POS and DYN of EgoVehicle”; output of box 8) are used to 
detect dyadic (ego driver interacts with one surrounding vehicle) interactions 
of the surrounding traffic with the driver (this detection is done in box 5). 
These interactions are compared with the intentions of the driver (box 1) and 
influence driver state (box 2).  
• Calculation of the final emotional response (box 2 together with box 1, box 5): 
The emotional reaction of a driver is based on the following input: 
(a) Dyadic interactions with other drivers/vehicles (box 5 to box 2): The  
dyadic interactions with other driver s/vehicles are characterized by an 
emotional surplus. Emotional surplus means that dynamic interactions  
between vehicles have not just physical parameters (e.g. braking and fol-
lowing distance) but also emotional effects (e.g. anger). This emotional 
surplus is directly perceived by the driver and changes his driver state. 
(b) Evaluation of current traffic situation relating to driver intentions (box 1 to 
box 2): The driver evaluates the current traffic situation by relating it to 
his intentions. If e.g. other drivers constrain the driver in reaching his  
target speed, the driver feels reactive anger. 
(c) Inter-individual differences (“Person” to box 2): Depending on these dif-
ferences (e.g. trait of driving anger) and how the driver copes with the 
situation the final emotional response varies for different drivers. 
(d) Emotional memory (“Memory” to box 2): The final emotional response 
(output of box 2) is composed of the emotional reaction concerning  
the current traffic situation and the emotional short-term memory where 
the experience of former situations is stored.

Development of a Cognitive-Emotional Model for Driver Behavior 247 
 
Fig. 1. Cognitive-emotional driver model 
• Influencing driving style (box 4 together with box2, box 3): The final emo-
tional response is an important input parameter for the driving style of a driver. 
The driving style can be operationalized by driving parameters like e.g. time 
headway (THW), time to collision (TTC), accepted longitudinal/lateral accel-
eration, and reaction time. The following factors influence driving style: 
(a) Driver state (final emotional response; box 2 to box 4): Driver state is well 
known as an influencing factor of driving style. E.g.: Angry drivers that 
are in conflict with other drivers hinder ing them to drive as fast as they 
want show different approaching and following behavior.  
(b) Anticipation (box 3 to box 4): Anticipation also influences driving style. If 
other drivers seem to drive abnormal (e.g. driving from the left side of the 
lane to the right side of the lane), the arousal and safety system of the 
driver recognizes this behavior pattern as potential dangerous and causes a 
more cautious driving style. 
(c) Contagion (box 6 to box 4): Contagion means a direct connection between 
traffic environment and driving style. The maneuvers of all surrounding 
vehicles influence the individual driving style. The driver is neither aware 
of this influence nor does contagion change the emotional state of a driver. 
• Changing of driver’s maneuvers (box 7, box 8): The driving style selects and 
shapes the driving maneuvers (output of box 7). An aggressive driver will 
show other driving maneuvers (or at least another likelihood for specific

248 C. Maag, C. Mark, and H.-P. Krüger 
driving maneuvers) than a cooperative one. This change of driving behavior is 
modeled by changing the parameters of a “traditional” driving model [21] [22]. 
Another input to box 7 (besides driving style) are the positions and dynamics 
of the surrounding vehicles. 
The model displayed will be further elaborated and validated by future driving simu-
lator studies. Some of the already existing evidence for the validity of the model is 
presented in the following chapter. 
3.3   Parameter Specification and Preliminary Validation of Model 
An important part of every modeling of human behavior is validation. Therefore, the 
behavior functions that specify the cognitive-emotional driver model have to be veri-
fied by empirical tests, e.g. in the driving simulator. In the following, some exemplary 
validation evidence is reported. 
The driving simulator used for the empirical studies is a pc-based simulator with 
motion system. The visual system of the simulator provides a horizontal field of view 
of 180 degrees and a vertical view of 47 degrees generated by LCD projectors and 
presented on a spherical projection screen with a diameter of 6m. The mockup con-
sists of a real BMW 520i that is cut off behind the B-pillar. Three mirrors (left, right 
and rear mirror) are realized via TFT displays that replace the real mirrors. For  
presenting a driving scenario 14 computers are connected via 100MBit Ethernet  
connection. The update frequency of the visual system is guaranteed to be 60Hz at 
minimum. The software of the simulator is called SILAB and was developed by the 
company WIVW GmbH. SILAB is a high-end driving simulation software that cre-
ates a realistic impression of driving which includes a complex simulation of vehicle 
dynamics, an image generation for urban, highway and rural scenarios, day and night 
simulation, and an eight channel sound simulation. SILAB supports Windows as well 
as Linux as operating systems. 
For the simulator studies subjects are chosen from a panel of drivers already 
trained in simulator driving. This training is important, in order to make the test driv-
ers familiar with the handling of the simulator and to reduce the problem of simulator 
sickness. 
Fig. 2 presents the first experiment. Eight subjects drive on the left lane of a mo-
torway (160 km/h) and approach a preceding vehicle (110 km/h). On the right lane 
further vehicles drive with 80 km/h. The distance of the vehicles on the right lane is 
70, 90, 110, or 130 meters. The subjects evaluate the situation and the driving behav-
ior of the vehicle in front of them. As the preceding vehicle never pulls into the gaps 
on the right lane, the subjects also report their feeling of anger. 
Fig. 3 shows the results of an analysis (ANOVA for repeated measurements) of the 
subjects’ answers. Both variables, the evaluation of the situation as well as the feeling 
of anger highly correspond with the gap size on the right lane. The greater the gap the 
more explicit is the request that the precedi ng vehicle should change to the right lane, 
F(3,21) = 24.53, p = .001, and the higher is the feeling of anger if this lane change is 
not performed, F(3,21) = 18.10, p = .001.

4   Summary and Outlook 
Aggressive driving is a significant problem in  modern road traffic. Scientific research 
has yielded different explanations why drivers become angry and aggressive. That 
implies that (agent-based) modeling of driver behavior has to take into account emo-
tional and also cognitive processes of the driver, in order to be able to realistically 
explain the behavior of drivers. This article has presented a cognitive-emotional 
model of a driver. During the project SOCIONICAL this driver model will be elabo-
rated and validated in more detail and will be used to study the influence of individual 
driver actions on the overall characteristics of the traffic system.  
This driver model can be implemented in microscopic, agent-based traffic models 
and expands the output values of traffic modeling and analysis on cognitive and emo-
tional variables. An important research question will be the effect of innovative 
ADAS on driving behavior and driver state and emerging phenomena in traffic.

Modelling Dynamic Forgetting in Distributed
Information Systems
Nicolas Höning 1 and Martijn C. Schut2
1 Centrum Wiskunde en Informatica (CWI), Amsterdam, Netherlands
2 VU University, Department of Computer Science, Amsterdam, Netherlands
Abstract. We describe and model a new aspect in the design of distributed in-
formation systems. We build upon a previously described problem on the micro-
level, which asks how quickly agents should discount (forget) their experience:
If they cherish their memories, they can build their reports on larger data sets;
if they discount quickly, they can respond well to change in their environment.
Here, we argue that on the macro-level, where agents disseminate information,
the coordination of these micro-level strategies of discounting can have signif-
icant consequences on the system performance if the environment is uncertain.
In our proposed model, a referral network disseminates information about a dis-
ruptive environment (a service provider) to a risk-averse client agent, who uses
this information to maximise his proﬁt and then gives feedback into the refer-
ral system. We model two simple strategies to dynamically ﬁnd better discount-
ing factors, through central and decentral control. We show that with dynamic
discounting rates, the system can become more reactive. We discuss interdepen-
dence of the system components in the light of differing discounting scenarios.
In this work, we build on a certainty-based trust representation and operators for
it in referral systems, developed by Josang [7] and Hang, Wang and Singh [13,2].
1 Introduction
In dynamic environments, information beco mes less accurate over time – this is why
forgetting exists, as a reﬂection of uncertainty in a changing world. In many distributed
information systems that are modelled, the forgetting rate (in the literature, this is
mostly referred to as the discounting factor ) is set for all agents and never changes.
But by deﬁnition, autonomous agents can forget (discount) old information at a rate
of their choosing. Here, we propose a model to study this design aspect. We believe
it is necessary to investigate the problem that the nature of these micro-level decisions
can have signiﬁcant consequences on the macro-level, affecting the ability of the sys-
tem to accurately model the environment. This is certainly the case in sophisticated
information systems, where information is not merely passed on and accumulated, but
agents evaluate information before and after they pass it on. To our best knowledge, this
problem has not been investigated so far.
In particular, we investigate the interactions between agents in so-calledreferral net-
works, in which trust forms the basis of cooperation and information sharing between
agents. If such networks are employed in dynamic environments, then the agents in
the networks have to react to changing info rmation. This raises the question how each
P. J ˛edrzejowicz et al. (Eds.): KES-AMSTA 2010, Part II, LNAI 6071, pp. 252–261, 2010.
c© Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2010

Modelling Dynamic Forgetting in Distributed Information Systems 253
agent must decide for itself what part of the information that it has received so far re-
ﬂects the current situation best. We model these dynamics by a referral network which
disseminates information about a disruptive environment (a service provider who some-
times changes his quality level from good to bad or vice versa) to a risk-averse client
agent, who uses this information to maximise his proﬁt and then gives feedback into the
referral system.
Again more focused, for such referral networks, we look at the (distributed)discount-
ing of information, i.e., agents in a referral network discount old information to correctly
reﬂect the current situation, while trying to keep their evidence base (their "certainty")
as large as possible (this constitutes a trade-off as both old and new information have
their own value to the agent). For such discounting, one often employs a discounting
factor with which to deprecate information ( comparable to an interest rate on a loan).
This discounting factor affects the information directly, but indirectly it is also likely
to affect other information in the system. For instance, the information is evaluated in the
light of the trust of the recipient in the referrer before being passed on. The trust in the
referrer itself should be subject to discounting (to become independent from malicious
or badly informed referrers) and, in turn, is via feedback mechanisms evaluated on how
accurate the referred information was. Here, we provide a starting point to model this
seemingly complex design problem and investigatethebehaviour of twosimplestrategies.
The contributions of this paper are twofold: ﬁrstly, we model a service provision
setup in which distributed discounting in r eferral networks can be studied (here we
extend existing work by Singh and colleagues [2,11,12,14] on certainty-based trust
models for multi-agent systems). Secondl y, we perform a number of computer simu-
lation experiments, observing effects of distributed discounting strategies in different
disruptiveness-scenarios.
This paper is structured as follows. In the following section, we discuss relevant lit-
erature and position our work in the areas of certainty-based trust, referral networks
and inter-temporal value of information (i.e., balancing the factors of recency and cer-
tainty in order to make good decisions). In Section 3 we present our model, including
the referral network and the embedding of this networking between disruptive service
provider and risk-averse client. In Section 4 we describe simulation experiments we
performed on the system and analyse the outcomes of these experiments. We close in
Section 5 with conclusions and pointers for future work.
2 Literature
In this section, we discuss related literature concerning certainty-based trust (including
a complex representation of trust with an explicit notion of certainty), referral networks
(especially the work of Singh and colleagues on the issue of how to propagate trust
in such networks), and inter-temporal value of information (about how to effectively
balance the recency and certainty of information).
2.1 Certainty-Based Trust
Trust is based on experience (e.g., with other agents or with an uncertain environment in
general). The more experience a trustor collects about the trustee, the more accurate his

needs to be accompanied with an update func tion, so that new experience somehow
alters the existing opinion. A trust report can then be seen as a compressed history of
experience. When agents translate their experience history into their trust reports, they
compress it and thereby need to give up some of the inherent information.

[6,7,8]. While trust can be represented as a simple scalar (e.g.∈ [0, 1],i tm a yb em o r e

r and s are collected, we compute a three-fold belief space, where the third fold takes

decreases in the belief space and certainty (which consists of belief plus disbelief) starts
to get its share. This helps to distinguish on how much experience a trust report is ac-
tually based. By calculating over evidence space, the certainty c∈ [0, 1] can be derived
from the integral of a probability density function (see Figure 1(b)), which we do ac-
