certainty is divided into belief and disbelief.
2.2 Referral Networks
When agents make use of the trust reports provided by other agents, they form a referral
network. A referral network is an information dissemination system consisting of au-
tonomous and possibly self-interested agents. A referral is provided by agent B to agent
A by giving A a report about his (B’s) trust in C. The path from A to B to C is called a
referral path (and could in principle also extend over several other agents). Agents who
have no direct experience can only refer to other agents and are called referrers, while
agents who can provide their direct experience are called witnesses.
Referral networks have been studied widely (e.g. [11,1]) and are a state-of-the-art
technique to model information dissemination in multi-agent systems. Hereby, direct

Modelling Dynamic Forgetting in Distributed Information Systems 255
experience becomes indirect knowledge to its recipients. As such, trust (direct experi-
ence) becomes reputation (indirect knowledge).
For the precise formalisation of operators used in referral networks employing a
certainty-based trust representation, see [9] for the path operators aggregation and con-
catenation (which was reconsidered in [14]) and [2] for the update operator (which was
reconsidered by us in [4]). The update operator updates an agents trust in a referrer by
considering two other trust reports: the referred opinion and the agents actual (ex post)
opinion.
2.3 Discounting
The most basic approach to incorporate recency in one’s memory is that old experience
should be accounted for less, since circumstances might change over time. Discounting
mostly happens with a discounting factor. For instance, here is the formula used by [6]
for a simple scalar trust representation:
gd(tv, ev)= d∗ tv +( 1− d)∗ ev
where gd is the update function which updates the trust value tv∈ [−1, 1] in light of a
new experience ev∈ [−1, 1], using a discount factor d∈ [0, 1]. The existing tv is also
discounted by d to normalise the result of gd in the range [−1, 1].
For the addition of experience in eviden ce space, we use a similar update function
(following [2]), for r and s. Here is the update of existing r with new experience r′:
r = r′+( 1− β)∗ r
Note that the choice of the discounting factor β is crucial and should depend on the
situation at hand. Hang [2] experimented with varying static values for β in different
situations, but we have not come across any research in which agents use dynamic
values for β or choose their values themselves.
2.4 Recency and Certainty
Agents generally strive for more information in order to learn about their environment.
When they are more certain in their actions, they can take higher risks and maximise
their proﬁts. The trust model described in section 2.1 enables agents to build up certainty
over time, as agents interact. However, when stored experience gets forgotten, the cer-
tainty also decreases. Meanwhile, agents will have more accurate opinions if they base
their reports on more recent information. As agents in a trust syst em try to maximise
both of these values, a trade-off situation occurs: How much should old experience be
discounted in order to to beneﬁt from both certainty and recency?
Several researchers have noticed this issue (while none that we know of have focused
their analysis on it). For instance, [10] note the recency/certainty trade-off when agents
produce less failures with smaller history windows, but become more vulnerable to ma-
licious behaviour which exploits small history windows. Also, in [5] a simple reputation
system is modelled, in which two ﬁrms and many customers are present. Customers dis-
count their memories of direct experience and ﬁrms choose how to invest in their next

256 N. Höning and M.C. Schut
intended quality level, based on their current reputation. They show that discounting is
a necessary condition for equilibrium points to be reached but that uncertainty makes it
unlikely that the system reaches any equilibrium point.
To accumulate certainty is generally rewarding, unless the environment becomes too
uncertain for accumulated mem ory to yield any valuable predictions. In that case, a
focus on certainty can even be harmful as t he agent(s) will be too slow to react to a
disruption. In general, we do not need to speak of recency versus certainty: to some
degree, a system should manage to have both.
3M o d e l
We model a referral network - a system in which a client needs to learn about a service
provider and relies on referral agents for this. This network involveswitnesses who have
direct experience with the service provider and referrers who only deal with indirect
experience. The client knows all referrers and can access them to ask for information
and give them feedback. Each referrer has access to some other referrers, while only
some have access to a witness. We strictly separate referral agents from witness agents
for simplicity (such that an agent can only have one role).
A service provider provides a service, the quality of which can change between being
good or bad. The client asks several (randomly selected) referrers he knows for informa-
tion about the service quality. On each of those referral paths, he gets referred to another
referrer until he ﬁnds a witness. Then, information travels from the service provider as
ﬁrst-hand experience to witnesses. It then becomes reputation when the client makes
use of it. Note that he does not use the witnesses opinion as-is, but he incorporates the
referrers opinions about the agent (referrer or witness) they referred to. Thus, the client
needs to concatenate the trust values along the paths. Then, he aggregates the results
from all paths into one ﬁnal trust report, which represents the networks opinion. See
Figure 2 for a broad overview over information ﬂow. Note that also the client has direct
experience. In this system, this is solely used to evaluate the reputation information he
receives in order to give feedback.

dotted arrows indicate referrals, and dashed arrows indicate feedback. The four types of agents
are explained in the text.

Fig. 3. Functional overview of the service provision system
We use the notion of service provision to evaluate the effectiveness of information
dissemination. In particular, a client on one end of the referral network is about to use a
service on the other end of the referral network and uses the referred trust information
to calculate the risk he is prepared to take.
We view the service quality as an external input to the system and the clients utility as
an output. Furthermore, the client might provide evaluations and feedback as input into
the system. Figure 3 shows a functional system overview, modelling the referral sys-
tem (referrers and witnesses) as the system under consideration, with input and output
connected to the client and the service provider.
The general setting we want to investigate with this system is an uncertain, poten-
tially disruptive and non-deterministic environment, in which agents have ademand for
recency. For this, the disruptiveness of the service needs to be a controlled variable,
alike [3]. We implement a service provid er who initially provides good service. The
disruptiveness denotes the probability of service level disruptions between rounds (a
change from good to bad quality or vice versa).
On the other end of the system, the client implementation should model that there
is a demand for certainty . The assumption that certainty is useful has to be set into
practice. Therefore, we propose that the c lient can accumulate a payoff, representing
the usefulness of the system (to provide accu rate information). The client takes a risk
each round. He puts a stake into the interaction with the service provider. If the service
is good, his return is twice the stake he put in, otherwise he gets nothing back.
In our model, the stake is the belief of the referral network in a good service, minus
the disbelief. Thus, the stakes upper bound is the belief (if there is no disbelief) and the
lower bound is zero (if disbelief is higher than belief). Note that stakes would rise with
certainty, assuming the relation between belief and disbelief stays constant.
Finally, we make the agents act adaptively. This means that they control their own
views of the world (the trust in their neighbours and – in one scenario – their own
discounting behaviour). To inform the adaptation process, they need to receive feedback
from the client for each of their referrals. With this, they can use the update operator
(see Section 2.2) to update the trust in their neighbours and various mechanisms (to be
explained in Section 4.1) to update the discounting factor β.
4 Experiment
We have observed in preliminary experiments that the disruptiveness of the environment
signiﬁcantly affects the effectiveness of static discounting strategies (e.g. low values for

258 N. Höning and M.C. Schut
β (the discounting parameter, explained in section 2.3) are hurtful in highly disruptive
scenarios) and that this system is stable in the light of malicious witnesses and referrers
[4]. We turn now to an experiment in which values forβ are dynamically determined in
various ways1.
4.1 Setup
As dependent variables
, we measure the client payoff, the certainty reported by the
referral network, the clients stake and the values of β in referrers and witnesses. The
experiment ran for 1000 iterations and was conducted 30 times, with a population of 18
agents (10 referrers, 8 witnesses). We show the averages along with the sample standard
deviations.
In each run, the network structure was newly conﬁgured - agents were randomly
connected such that the client knew four of the referrers, each referrer knew three other
referrers and each witness was known by one re ferrer. The client asks all referrers for
opinions (and then concatenates and aggregates their reports to make a decision), while
referrers only ask one witness if they know one, or one random referrer otherwise. Each
round, the client updates his feedback in the ref errers and the referrers get the clients
feedback, so they can update their trust in the agent they referred to.
As independent variables
, we control the probability of service disruptions (we use
0.05 and 0.33) and the agents adaptation of their discounting factor β in response to
the accuracy of their referrals. We always let all agents begin with a value for β drawn
randomly from [0.1, 0.9].I nt h estatic scenario, all β values will stay ﬁxed during the
runs. We design two dynamic scenarios:
1. The centrally controlled scenario, in which the client deﬁnes the new β for all
agents, according to how accurately the network described his experience.
2. The decentrally controlled scenario, in which each referrer and witness uses the
feedback from the client to adjust his β himself. In order to do this, they keep
a trust in their own history of accuracy to, according to which they adjust their
discounting: β =1 − to.α (α denotes the probability of a good outcome, see
Section 2.1). When they learn through f eedback that their recent referrals were
accurate/misleading, they will thus lower/raise their β. In this experiment, we set
the β of to to 0.1.
4.2 Results and Discussion
In Figures 4(a) and 4(b), we see that payoff-wise, the dynamic scenarios fare much
better than the static scenario. As coul d be expected, it is beneﬁcial to adjust β values
according to the situation at hand. When the service quality changes, agents raise β in
order to discount old information that has just become less accurate. This way, stakes
rise faster in times of good service and drop faster in times of bad service, so big losses
are avoided. Note also that for a disruptiveness of 0.33, much less payoff can be made
than with 0.05, since much less certainty can build up in the trust reports.

network is belief + disbelief , so if the stakes are (roughly) equally high with lower
certainty, this most likely means that in the decentralised scenario, agents refer stronger
opinions (a higher value of belief− disbelief , which normally happens with higher
values for β).

5 Conclusions
In this paper, we approach a trade-off between certainty and recency which each infor-
mation system faces when its environment is uncertain. We develop previous research
in certainty-based trust in referral netwo rks into a model where this trade-off can be
studied. Then we run initial experiments in w hich the agents dynamically ﬁnd better
discounting factors.
In our model, a referral network disseminates information from a disruptive envi-
ronment (a service provider agent) to a risk-averse client agent, who uses this informa-
tion to maximise his proﬁt and then gives feedback into the referral system. We model
two simple strategies to dynamically ﬁnd better discounting factors (β)i nad i s t r i b u t e d
multi-agent context. In the ﬁrst scen ario, the client agent chooses one β centrally. In
the second scenario, all agents in the referral network choose their next β themselves,
based on the clients feedback about their last referral. Both strategies are signiﬁcantly
better in maximising the clients pay-off than static values for β, though they seem to
differ much in their behaviour.
In future work, the behaviours of these two strategies will be investigated closer in
order to discover interaction effects on referral paths, and surely there can be new ideas
on how to dynamically and decentrally compute discounting factors. Furthermore, one
could make the agents more complex in various ways, for instance by letting them
reason about future dynamics of the world. Another direction could be to investigate
how incentives to agents to behave self-inter ested affects the recency/certainty trade-
off. To model this, the client agent could be r equired to share parts of its generated
utility as payments for referrals.

Integrated Modeling of Cognitive Agents in  
Socio-technical Systems 
Alexei Sharpanskykh 
Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Department of Artificial Intelligence,  
De Boelelaan 1081a, 1081 HV Amsterdam, The Netherlands 
sharp@few.vu.nl 
Abstract. Modern socio-technical systems are characterized by high structural 
and behavioral complexities, which impede understanding and modeling of 
such systems. In particular, reciprocal relations between diverse local system 
processes that determine global system dynamics are not well understood. In 
this paper we focus on the problem of establishing relations between cognitive 
processes that determine social dynamics of an actor in a socio-technical  
system. To address this problem, a formal, integrated, agent-based modeling 
approach is proposed. The approach de fines relations between such cognitive 
processes as belief revision, trust dynamics, generation and development of 
feelings and emotions, and decision making. Furthermore, it is described how 
the behavior of an agent is related to its cognitive dynamics. Preliminary  
experimental results for the approach are discussed in the paper. 
1   Introduction 
Modern socio-technical systems are characterized by high structural and behavioral 
complexities. These systems include hardware and software components with a vary-
ing degree of autonomy and complexity that interact with and enable interaction be-
tween humans. Among highly autonomous technical components are ambient devices, 
dedicated to assist humans in the achievement of their objectives (e.g., to maintain 
well-being, to complete a task in time). Modeling and analysis of modern socio-
technical systems is a challenging task. Models of such systems should account for 
complexity of human behavior, heterogeneity and autonomous behavior of technical 
systems, and interaction among all system actors. Both quantitative and qualitative 
system properties are required to be modeled. Furthermore, relations between diverse 
processes and states of different aggregation levels of a system should be defined  
explicitly. Whereas the last modeling requirement has been addressed in Systems Biol-
ogy and Physics of Complex Systems with some success, it constitutes a serious issue 
for modeling complex socio-technical systems. In this paper we focus on the problem 
of establishing reciprocal relations between cognitive processes that determine decision 
making and social behavior of an intelligent, autonomous actor in a socio-technical 
system. According to the literature [3, 4] among these cognitive processes are percep-
tion, belief revision, learning, trust dynamics, generation and development of feelings 
and emotions. The author is not aware of any existing formal cognitive model that 
incorporates all these processes and defines relations between them. To address this

Integrated Modeling of Cognitive Agents in Socio-technical Systems 263 
gap, a formal approach for integrated modeling of cognitive agents in complex socio-
technical systems is proposed in this paper. The proposed agent model is generic and 
can be used for modeling both human and artificial actors. In contrast to other existing 
agent models (cf [6]), cognitive states of agents (e.g., beliefs) used in decision-making 
are assumed to be emotionally loaded, which agrees with many research findings, e.g., 
[2, 3]. Furthermore, many modeling principles from Neuroscience were used in the 
proposed model, similar to the ones described in [2, 8]. 
The paper is organized as follows. A formal logic-based modeling language is in-
troduced in Section 2. In Section 3 modeling externally observable behavior of an 
agent is described. Integrated modeling of cognitive dynamics of an agent is consid-
ered in Section 4. Some preliminary experi mental results are provided in Section 5. 
Section 6 concludes the paper. 
2   Modeling Language 
To specify dynamic properties of a system, the order-sorted predicate logic-based 
language called LEADSTO is used [1]. Dynamics in LEADSTO is represented as 
evolution of states over time. A state is characterized by a set of properties that do or 
do not hold at a certain point in time. To specify state properties for system compo-
nents, ontologies are used which are defined by a number of sorts, sorted constants, 
variables, functions and predicates (i.e., a signature). For every system component A a 
number of ontologies can be distinguished: the ontologies IntOnt(A), InOnt(A),   
OutOnt(A), and ExtOnt(A) are used to express respectively internal, input, output and 
external state properties of the component A. Input ontologies contain elements for 
describing perceptions of an agent from the external world, whereas output ontologies 
describe actions and communications of agents. For a given ontology Ont, the proposi-
tional language signature consisting of all state ground atoms based on Ont is denoted 
by APROP(Ont). State properties are specified based on such ontology  by propositions 
that can be made (using conjunction, negation, disjunction, implication) from the 
ground atoms. Then, a state S is an indication of which atomic state properties are 
true and which are false: S: APROP(Ont) → {true, false}.  
LEADSTO enables modeling of direct temporal dependencies between two state 
properties in successive states, also called dynamic properties . A specification of 
dynamic properties in LEADSTO is executable and can be depicted graphically. The 
format is defined as follows. Let α and β be state properties of the form ‘conjunction 
of atoms or negations of atoms’, and e, f, g, h  non-negative real numbers. In the 
LEADSTO language the notation α →→e, f, g, h  β means: if state property α holds for a 
certain time interval with duration g, then after some delay (between e and f) state 
property β will hold for a certain time interval of length h. When e = f = 0 and g = h = 1, 
called standard time parameters, we shall write α→→ β. To indicate the type of a state 
property in a LEADSTO property we shall use prefixes  input(c), internal(c) and output(c), 
where c is the name of a component. Consider an example dynamic property:  
input(A)|observation_result(fire) →→ output(A)| performed(runs_away_from_fire) 
Informally, this example expresses that if agent A observes fire during some time unit, 
then after that A will run away from the fire during the following time unit.

264 A. Sharpanskykh 
In addition, LEADSTO allows expressing mathematical operations, e.g. 
has_value(x, v) →→ e, f, g, h  has_value(x, v*0.25).  
3   Modeling Externally Observable Behavior of an Agent 
From the external perspective the behavior of an agent is specified by dynamic rela-
tions between agent's input and output states, corresponding to interaction with other 
agents and with the environment. An agent perceives information by observation and 
communication and generates output in the form of communication or actions. Com-
munications are formalized as speech acts (e.g., inform, request, order) using the 
function  
communicated_from_to(ag1:AGENT, ag2:AGENT, s_act:SPEECH_ACT, message:STATPROP),  
here agent ag1 communicates speech act s_act to agent ag2 with the content message. 
Agents may communicate information about the environment (e.g., accessibility of 
locations), about other agents (e.g., their location, physical and mental condition), 
about plans to act (in form of informative messages, recommendations and orders to 
follow). A value from the interval [0, 1]  is associated with each speech act of type 
inform, indicating the agent's confidence in the communicated message. For this the 
function has_confidence(message:STATPROP, v:VALUE)  is used. For example, the  
communication of agent a1 to agent a2 about the accessibility of a location l1 from 
location l2 with confidence 0.9 is formalized as communicated_from_to(a1, a2, inform, 
has_confidence(is_accessible_from(l1, l2), 0.9)). Note that information about the dynamics 
of events and processes (e.g., about the rate of change) may be also communicated by 
agents. For example, the communication about the rate of change of smoke concentra-
tion with confidence 0.7 is formalized as communicated_from_to(a1, a2, inform, 
has_confidence(has_rate_of_change(smoke_concentration, 0.0001), 0.7)).  
Now observations of agents are considered. Passive and active observations are 
distinguished. In contrast to a passive observation, an active observation is always 
concerned with the agent's initiative. An active observation of a state property  p by an 
agent in the environment is formalized using the function to_be_observed(p: 
STATE_PROPERTY). Observation results are provided  to the agent's input using the 
function observation_result(p: STATE_PROPERTY) , which indicates whether p holds in 
the environment or for another agent. Similarly to an informative communication, a 
degree of confidence is associated with an observation, as some observations may not 
be completely reliable (e.g., due to smoke).  
Actions of an agent generated at its output are specified by performed(act:ACTION). 
4   Modeling Cognitive Dynamics of an Agent 
From the internal perspective the behavior of an agent is characterized by causal rela-
tions between internal states of the agent, based on which externally observable be-
havioral patterns are generated. The externally observable behavior of an agent is 
determined largely by the agent's decision making. The process of decision making of 
an agent in a highly dynamic environment (e.g., during an evacuation) is influenced 
by information provided to the agent by diverse information sources. The higher the

Integrated Modeling of Cognitive Agents in Socio-technical Systems 265 
agent's trust in an information source the more the agent is apt to accept information 
from this source and to adapt its beliefs using this information. It is often claimed that 
most beliefs of a human agent are emotionally loaded [2, 3]; also trust of an agent to a 
source and decision making are influenced by feelings and emotions. In the following 
the agent's internal states and cognitive processes, and relations between them are 
described in detail.  
4.1   Feelings and Emotions 
It is often claimed that cognitive states of a human, such as sensory or other represen-
tations induce emotions felt within the human [2, 3]. According to Damasio [2], emo-
tion generation proceeds via a body loop in the following causal chain: 
cognitive state  →  preparation for the induced bodily response → induced bodily response → 
sensing the bodily response → sensory representation of the bodily response → induced feeling 
As a variation, an as if body loop  uses a direct causal relation as a shortcut in the 
causal chain: preparation for the induced bodily response → sensory representation of the 
induced bodily response. The body loop (or ‘as if body loop’) is extended to a recursive 
body loop (or recursive ‘as if body loop’) by assuming that the preparation of the 
bodily response is also affected by the state of feeling the emotion as an additional 
causal relation: feeling → preparation for the bodily response . Thus, agent emotions are 
modeled based on reciprocal causation relations between emotion felt and body states, 
as shown in Fig 1. Within a model of agent's emotions both the bodily response and 
the feeling are assigned a level or gradation, expressed by a number, which is as-
sumed dynamic. The causal cycle is modeled as a positive feedback loop, triggered by 
a cognitive state and converging to a certain level of feeling and body state. Here in 
each round of the cycle the next body state has a level that is affected by both the 
cognitive state and the level of the feeling state, and the next level of the feeling is 
based on the level of the body state. Formally causation relations are modeled by 
LEADSTO properties. 
For example, consider a property for generation of a sensory state and for the 
preparation state update: 
output(environment)|world_state(s, v) →→ input(agent)|sensory_state(s, v) 
internal(agent)|(feeling(b, v1) & preparation_state(b, v2)) →→ internal(agent)|preparation_state(b, 
func(v1, v2)) 
Belief, trust, and other cognitive states considered in the agent model induce body 
loops similar to the one from Fig.1. In the following section, belief and trust states, 
and relations between them are considered in more detail.  
4.2   Beliefs and Trust  
Beliefs of an agent are time-labeled internal representations created based on commu-
nication and observation results received by the agent. Beliefs are specified using the 
function belief(p:STATPROP, v:VALUE, t:TIME) , here p is the content of the belief, v is  
the degree of confidence of the agent from the interval [0, 1]  that the belief is true at 
the time point t. After obtaining a communication from an information source, the 
agent creates the belief about the communication of the source. Furthermore,  
the agent revises its own belief(s) taking into account the communication content.

266 A. Sharpanskykh 
Belief revision is considered further in this section. As beliefs are modeled as emo-
tionally loaded, the confidence value for a belief state is updated continuously in an 
‘as if body loop’ described in section 4.1. From a neurological perspective the  
existence of a connection from feeling to be lief may be also considered plausible, as 
neurons involved in the belief and in the associated feeling will often be activated 
simultaneously. Therefore, such a connection from feeling to belief may be developed 
based on a general Hebbian learning mechanism [5] that strengthens connections 
between neurons that are activated simultaneously. A formal model based on such a 
mechanism is described in [8]. Taking this model as a starting point, we extend it  
by relating beliefs to trust and by a belief update mechanism as described in the  
following.

The amount of trust to a source is represented by a feeling value - a number from the 
range [0, 1] -  which accumulates all experience with the source. The influence of in-
formation communicated by an information source s concerning a world state w on 
the agent ag’s belief is specified by the following property (all variables are univer-

From this property follows that the less the agent’s trust towards an information 
source (i.e., feeling for accepting information from the source), the less the effect of 
communication from this source on the agent’s beliefs. Agent beliefs are updated

based on the agent’s own observations in a similar manner. In this case the trust value 
is interpreted as the agent’s estimation of the reliability of its own observation. 
The trust to a source builds up over time based on the agent's experience with the 
source. In particular, when the agent has a positive (negative) experience with the 
source, the agent's trust to the source incr eases (decreases). Currently experiences are 
restricted to information experiences only. An information experience with a source is 
evaluated by comparing the information provided by the source with the agent's be-
liefs about the content of the information provided. The experience is evaluated as 
positive (negative), when the information provided by the source is confirmed by 
(disagree with) the agent's beliefs. The emotional content of trust is modeled by an as 
if body loop. The experience with an information source is accumulated in the feeling 
state for accepting information from the source. The preparation state in the ‘as if 
body loop’, which determines the value for the feeling state is defined as follows:

As beliefs of an agent change over time, so changes evaluation of experiences and, 
consequently, the trust to sources. Every time when a trust relation with a source 
changes, the confidence values of the beliefs influenced by communication from this 
source are re-evaluated. The belief re-evaluation is done using beliefs about commu-
nications and observation received in the past. Note that a communication about a 
dynamic event is evaluated taking into account the agent’s belief(s) about the form of 
the dynamics of the event (e.g., expressed by a temporal formula). Furthermore, the 
more the distance between the communication time point and the evaluation time 
point, the less the effect of the communicatio n on the current trust value to the source. 
For example, an agent may receive information about a low concentration of smoke at 
some location. If the agent knows that the smoke concentration at that location in-
creases over time, then it would expect a higher smoke concentration at the location in 
the future (according to the communicated information) and evaluate this communica-
tion accordingly. The developed re-evaluatio n procedure is rather elaborated; it is 
provided in Appendix A with a detailed model description [9]. 
4.3   Decision Making  
Agents act according to adopted plans. A plan is a (partially) ordered set of actions, 
required to be done to satisfy agent's desires. Plans are represented as beliefs and can 
be communicated between agents. For example, a part of plan P1 that specifies for an 
agent the sequence of locations to walk through {l1, l2, l3}  is formalized as be-
lief(follows_after_in(go_to_location_from(l3, l2), go_to_location_from(l2, l1), P1), 1).

268 A. Sharpanskykh 
Plan descriptions vary in the degree of specificity. Abstract (or partial) plans  
contain high level actions that can be further refined into more specific actions.  
Furthermore, alternative ways of refinement of high level actions can be specified. In 
an evacuation scenario an agent may have several plans how to reach possible exits. 
These plans may be partial and contain movement actions between significant loca-
tions only (such as junction points, locations with elevators, stairs). There could be 
different paths between two significant positions.  
In the model an agent evaluates each plan option using the following criteria: 
(1) Desirability of an option: to which extent the option brings to the satisfaction of 
the current desire(s). 
(2) Possibility to realize : indicates the agent's confidence that the plan option can 
be realized. 
(3) The amount of effort: how much effort needs to be invested to realize the option 
(depends on the skills, knowledge, physical and other agent characteristics).  
For each evaluation criterion a constraint(s) may be defined (e.g., in terms of thresh-
olds). If in the evaluation of an action from a plan a violation of a constraint is identi-
fied, then the evaluation of the whole option can be ceased and the option is considered 
as inapplicable. 
An agent evaluates options using its beliefs. Furthermore, a change of agent's be-
liefs about the environment may result into a change of agent's plan options.  
The literature [4, 7] confirms that feelings influence the process of evaluation of 
options. To account for this in our model, an aggregated value based on the evaluated 
criteria (e.g., a weighted average) for an optio n is provided as input for an ‘as if body 
loop’ as shown in Fig.2. 
After all available plan options have been evaluated the agent chooses and commits 
to the one with the highest feeling value:

After the agent has committed to a plan, it evaluates all possible refinements of the 
first action of the plan along the same evaluation criteria as for plans and chooses the

Integrated Modeling of Cognitive Agents in Socio-technical Systems 269 
one with the highest feeling. In the literature [4] it is recognized that when a human 
has high stress close to panic, it uses diverse shortcuts in the evaluation of options. 
We elaborated a number of such shortcuts, which will be discussed elsewhere. 
5   Experiments 
The proposed agent model has been applied in a number of variants of a subway 
evacuation scenario, which is a simplified version of a real incident. In the scenario an 
explosion occurred in a trai n situated in an underground tunnel between two stations. 
The explosion was followed by fire and smoke, which were spreading throughout the 
tunnel. Because of the blast some doors were  damaged, so people were able to escape 
outside of the train through the formed openings. Most of the people did not have a 
clear idea what was going on and how to es cape. The train driver guided people to 
exits of the tunnel. Many evacuees had a high trust towards the driver. People propa-
gated available information about paths to exits, accessibility of locations, and danger 
(smoke, fire) to others. All electronic communication channels with the outside world 
were broken. Variants of the scenario were considered in which some people pos-
sessed ambient devices, which communicated available information to other devices 
in their range. People were trying to find their way to an exit. In the following we 
consider how different aspects of this scenario were modeled. 
Modeling the environment 
The layout of the environment is modeled as a graph-like structure defined by a set of 
locations (nodes) that agents and passive objects may occupy and a set of edges be-
tween pairs of locations. With each edge a measure of distance is associated. Agents 
and other objects (e.g., smoke, fire) move around, over different locations. Objects in 
the environment may have certain state attributes. These attributes may change over 
time, for example, a person may become injured or unconscious or a location may 
become inaccessible. The dynamics of environmental processes is described by 
LEADSTO properties.  
Modeling agents 
Agents communicate and maintain beliefs about: possible paths to exits; accessibility 
of locations on these paths; the degree of  danger of each location on these paths  
determined by the amount of smoke and fire; the dynamics of the smoke and fire 
propagation; the dynamics of accessibility of locations. The creation and update of the 
beliefs of agents is performed as described in Section 4.2. The correctness and com-
pleteness of information about the environment possessed by agents vary depending 
on their previous knowledge and information acquired during the evacuation. An 
agent communicates its beliefs to all other agents at its location only when it has a 
high confidence that this information is correct ( ≥ 0.75). Agents do not repeat informa-
tion already communicated. Information is  communicated in turns. Agents are  
socially unrelated and have neutral trust to each other ( 0.5 initially). The only excep-
tion is the train driver agent, who is highly trusted (0.9 initially). 
When an agent comes to a location, it updates all its plans (i.e., possible paths to 
exits) with respect to its current location. In the following it is discussed how plans in 
the evacuation scenario are evaluated along the criteria proposed in Section 4.3:

In the developed simulation model 15 unrelated heterogeneous agents were speci-
fied. The parameters of the agent models were drawn for the uniform distribution on 
the unit interval. Below some results for three variations of the scenario are given. 
Variation 1 (Fig.3a): The driver agent provides information about paths to exits. A 
part of this information is incorrect. The simulation showed that some agents followed 
the driver’s directions even after the driver’s mistake was revealed. Other agents were 
losing trust to the driver quickly after finding the mistake, and preferred not to use the 
information regarding paths to exit provided by the driver after that.  
Variation 2  (Fig.3b): An agent unknown to other agents possesses complete and 
correct information about paths to the exits. The agent communicates this information 
to other agents which it meets. In the simulation a small number of agents used this 
information and found the way to an exit quickly. Many other agents did not trust the 
received information and continued searching for an exit themselves.

Variation 3  (Fig.3c): 7 agents use ambient devices able to communicate to other

agents. A device also exchanges information with its agent-owner. 2 devices

Integrated Modeling of Cognitive Agents in Socio-technical Systems 271 
misguided because of the spread of wrong information. However, the sources of 
wrong information were rapidly identified by the agents and trust to them decreased 
rapidly. Then, as can be seen from the graph, using the correct information agents 
were able to find their way to an exit very quickly. 
6   Conclusion  
In this paper a first step is made towards an integrated approach for modeling and 
analysis of complex socio-technical systems. Specifically, a formal generic agent 
model has been proposed with explicitly defined relations between cognitive proc-
esses that influence the agent’s decision making and behavior. Such relations remain 
implicit in other existing agent-based models. Similarly to [8], cognitive states in the 
model are assumed to be emotionally loaded. The model has a high complexity. To 
address this issue, in the future model abstraction mechanisms will be developed. 
Furthermore, techniques for establishing relations between local dynamics of agents 
and global system properties will be developed in the future. The model will be vali-
dated in a large-scale case study in the frames of the SOCIONICAL project.

Aggregated Information Representation for Technical 
Analysis on Stock Market with Csiszár Divergence 
Ryszard Szupiluk1,2, Piotr Wojewnik1,2, and Tomasz Ząbkowski1,3 
1 Polska Telefonia Cyfrowa Ltd, Al. Jerozolimskie 181, 02-222 Warsaw, Poland 
2 Warsaw School of Economics, Al. Niepodleglosci 162, 02-554 Warsaw, Poland  
3 Warsaw University of Life Sciences, Nowoursynowska 159, 02-787 Warsaw, Poland 
{rszupiluk,pwojewnik,tzabkowski}@era.pl 
Abstract. The paper presents a new method for multidimensional representa-
tion of financial information in the context of technical analysis. Typically, 
technical analysis of given financial instrument does not take into account 
a broader view on the market. We want to analyze the information about the 
environment of the primary instrument. Hence, there is the problem of the re-
sults synthesis in a coherent and a transparent way. In this paper we propose 
aggregation of the information from different sources into a single aggregate 
graph which enables a technical analysis. The complete information is obtained 
with the p-norms approach. To assess the impact of particular information on 
the primary instrument we applied divergence measures such as Csiszár diver-
gence and Beta divergence. Practical experiment on the stock exchange data 
confirmed the validity of proposed approach.  
Keywords: information representation, data transformation, technical analysis. 
1   Introduction 
Technical analysis is one of the standard methods of analysis on financial markets. 
Regardless of the controversy concerning technical analysis, both on scientific and 
philosophical aspects, the fact is that it is widely used [7,15,18]. Moreover, the litera-
ture gives plenty examples of successful investment strategies based on technical 
analysis [21,22,23].  
In this study we treat technical analysis as a special issue of searching for patterns 
where the main elements of a graphical analysis are the price and the volume of the 
securities [11,15]. In this approach the most problematic issue is the synthesis of in-
formation from the other relevant instruments such as the price of the securities, the 
industry branch of the company and the market index assigned. The article will pre-
sent a method of multidimensional transformation for information representation that 
is adequate for the standard technical analysis. 
The main advantage of analyzing the aggregated data in a single chart is the sim-
plicity of the decision making process. It is convenient to synthesize the information 
at the data preparation step  rather than drawing the conclusion based on separate 
analysis of given financial instruments (often giving inconsistent signals).

Aggregated Information Representation for Technical Analysis on Stock Market 273 
This concept seems to be particularly important in modeling behavior of financial 
markets as well as in formulating the investment systems. In particular, it can be  
applied to the automated trading systems which are based on artificial intelligence, 
neural networks, agent and multi-agent systems, and basically everywhere where the 
information representation plays an important role [8,9,12,13].  
2   Problem Formulation 
Technical analysis is a technique for forecasting the future direction of stock prices 
through the study of historical data. Typical input data for technical analysis are the 
price and the volume of the securities. The most popular approaches to technical 
analysis are: the analysis of indicators and average values, graphical inspections of the 
formations and trends, Elliott’s waves analysis or Fibonacci numbers approach 
[15,17,19]. By default, these methods are addressed to a single stock and are based on 
the assumption that the current stock price is the result of having comprehensive  
information about the market.  
The practice of stock exchange investments, however, shows that it is appropriate 
to take into account the broader market context [16]. Under the assumption that there 
are no unusual circumstances, the stock prices rarely behave separately from the in-
dustry to which it belongs to, or the market considered (eg. small, medium or large 
companies indexes). Hence, the present studies stress the need of the cross market 
analysis taking into account the different markets and major indices. The problem 
here is to synthesize the information from the different instruments. Having distin-
guished given formations on the certain markets it is difficult to aggregate them in a 
coherent and a transparent way.  
Input data averaging for the stock prices and volumes does not seem to be a good 
approach. It is rather simplistic approach and it narrows the cognition process.  
Assuming that stock prices are presented in a multidimensional space where the axis 
represents the prices of given shares, the simple average assigns a Manhattan metric 
to each point. It is relatively easy to compute, however, it is hard to justify its superi-
ority over the most popular and natural, in human perception, Euclidean metric. 
Another issue is the relationship between analyzed instruments and the implica-
tions of this analysis on aggregate information. Standard analysis of dependencies 
between the data accustoms a kind of symmet ry that results in adopting symmetrical 
mathematical characteristics, such as p-norm s, or correlations. Such a perception is 
highly established by the analysis and cognition process of physical and technical 
phenomena. Still, it is an open question whether such an approach is always correct in 
the context of social and economic problems.  For example, if a statement that CEZ's 
share price (on Polish market) followed the global market as represented by the 
S&P500 is true, then the finding that the S&P500 follows the company CEZ is mean-
ingless. However, the standard dependency measures based on correlation and norms 
do not distinguish the point of view. Taking into account the asymmetry of percep-
tion, instead of symmetric distance measures , it enables application of the approach 
based on divergence functions. In the context of these considerations, we separate the 
primary instrument from those additional. Basic instrument is treated as a reference 
point in the measures of divergence.

274 R. Szupiluk, P. Wojewnik, and T. Z ąbkowski 
Given the above considerations, our goal is to aggregate the stock price and vol-
ume information at various multi-dimensional metric spaces and to estimate the  
impact of additional instruments on the primary instrument.

The aggregation of the data related to financial instruments values is performed with 
transformation in the phase space. In this space each point represents values of the all 
the instruments analyzed. The main aggr egation process and instruments inter-
influence can be treated as information ex ploration from the relations between points 
and coordinate system.  We can also note the important fact that we only process the 
price and the volume of given share or index – what means that we have only non-
negative data.

background [10], will not be considered. We try to find more objective and measurable

With the assumption that the values of the weights are the result of dependency 
analysis among the instruments, we will focus here on the possible methods to apply. 
3.1   Correlation Analysis 
In the most general sense the correlation measures the dependency between two vari-
ables. Because the variable values are colle cted in the vector form we can say the 
variables are interdependent, if these vectors have common direction. Thus, the angle 
between the centered vectors might be used to analyze the variables interdependency. 
The formula for the Euclidean space is empl oyed directly in the Pearson correlation 
coefficient. So the algebraic formula is used for probabilistic entities. Although the 
calculation of the correlation coefficient is quite simple it is not obvious how to  
analyze the effect in probabilistic sense. In practice, the resulting value might be unin-
terpretable. In fact, we can find three obstacles in proper interpretation of the value 
obtained from Pearson formula. These barriers include: delays, nonlinearities and 
nonstationarity [3,20,24]. 
More or less consciously we expect the correlation to present the interdependencies 
in every possible dimension. Whereas, there are domains, where the Pearson coeffi-
cient does not reveal the real relation. One of them is time. If the relation is shifted in 
Y

276 R. Szupiluk, P. Wojewnik, and T. Z ąbkowski 
time, the simple correlation analysis is not enough, because it might present lack of 
dependency. It has to be extended to cross-correlation, where the set of correlations is 
calculated successively as one of the vectors is delayed in comparison to the second 
vector. The cross-correlation function would expose the dynamic structure of the 
dependency. 
The second problem of measuring the inte rdependency with the correlation coeffi-
cient considers the interdependence form. If the variables are inter-reliant but the form 
is non-linear, the Pearson correlation close to zero says nothing about it. We have to 
linearize the dependency and then we could employ the correlation. The approach has 
two drawbacks. We have to know in advance what is the dependency form (and actu-
ally know the solution) or we have to find it (e.g. graphically), what is impossible in 
four and more-dimensional space.  
The third problem is related to definition of the Pearson coefficient. It is said to 
measure the dependency between random variables. This fact makes impossible to 
compare most time series where we can observe the stochastic trends. Stochastic trend 
informs on nonstationarity that means the values are generated from a set of random 
variables and not from the one variable. Moreover, the set is not generic and in some 
other run it could give quite opposite trends and conclusions. 
The presented features of the correlation show that it is not universal tool of inter-
dependency analysis. Therefore, with respect to its popularity we do not recommend 
the correlation for the interdependency analysis in the sense presented in this paper.

cal norms. Given two instruments, x1=[x1(t)] and x2=[x1(t)], Nt ,...,1= , we can meas-
ure the distance with the p-norm:

3.3   Divergence Analysis

to be reasonable and comfortable if we consider them in terms of their similarities 
rather than distance. This also seems to be more related to human perception process. 
Comparing the share prices on the chart we generally perceive them in terms  
of (dis)similarity and not the remoteness of them. Looking for the mathematical de-
scription of this perception we assign some weights to the instruments before the 
aggregation what leads to divergence analysis.

or similarity distances between two nonnegative sequences or patterns can be

4   Practical Experiment 
To present the capabilities of proposed approach we make simple technical analysis 
for JWConstruction (JWC) – real estate developer at Warsaw Stock Exchange.

generated by trend analyses as well as such indicators as MACD, RSI or system based 
on moving averages.

the effect of aggregation with Pearson distance.

5   Conclusions 
The uniform representation of the multivariate information that comes from different 
market instruments enables to perform the one coherent financial analysis. To obtain 
final results we should answer the two questions: how to calculate the mutual depend-
ences between different financial instruments and how to aggregate them. In our  
approach we use the distance derived from p-norm to calculate dependencies and  
the divergence concept for aggregation. In our opinion it is important to distinguish 
the operation that aggregates the information from the operation of mutual dependen-
cies and similarities recognition. The practical experiment with stock technical analy-
sis confirms validity of our methodology. Due to the limitations which are the size  
of the article and the methodological nature of the paper the experiment has the form 
of simple example and it aims to present the methodology of the multivariate informa-
tion representation.  
There are many open questions for further work. One of the most important is the 
problem of the optimal divergence form selection. For the moment we shall test dif-
ferent formulas from the divergence list presented in the paper.

Implementation of Network Oriented  
Manufacturing Structures 
Marek Dudek1 and Paweł Pawlewski2 
1 AGH University of Science and Technology, ul. A. Mickiewicza 30,  
 30-059 Krakow, Poland 
mdudek@zarz.agh.edu.pl 
2 Poznan University Of Technology, ul.Strzeleckar. 11,  
60965 Poznan, Poland 
pawel.pawlewski@put.poznan.pl 
Abstract. The paper presents the results of the authors’ studies which consisted 
in implementation of network oriented manufacturing structures. New paradigm 
of modern (flexible/agile) production is sketched. The manufacturing systems 
and models are described. The manufacturing systems and their structures 
should be made from components (modules) occurring in various organizations, 
which are nodes of a cooperation network. Creating the structure for the  
specific conditions and parameters of flow is only possible if the best organiza-
tion of flow can be selected. This can be determined with use of simulation 
modeling. Such modern structural systems supported by appropriate software 
are often called e-manufacturing. The results of researches performed in 15  
enterprises are presented in paper. Basic components and additional key tools 
for the proper functioning of e-manufacturing are identified. Finally the conclu-
sions and proposition of integration organized in the form of e-manufacturing is 
presented. 
Keywords: network manufacturing structures, flow simulations, e-manufacturing. 
1   Introduction 
Manufacturing environment has come under more pressure. Customer demand shorter 
lead times and a higher product variety. Transforming the structures of manufacturing 
systems comes out of the need for conformity to the present and foreseen market 
conditions. There are many factors which affect the necessity for change: 
- turbulent environment, 
- process variety, 
- technologically oriented basic strategies, 
- life-cycle thinking, 
- time compressing, 
- event-impulse management approach, 
- subdivide large, complex structures into smaller, 
- combination of different production techniques during production, etc.

Implementation of Network Oriented Manufacturing Structures 283 
The basic production paradigm is still changing. One basic manufacturing model is 
replaced by another. According to their intensity, changes can be distinguished into 
constant-evolutionary changes or abrupt-revolutionary changes. The evolutionary 
change is a modification of the present syst em into a continuous adaptation process. 
Revolutionary changes are radical changes of the current system (they are often in-
duced by the existence of drastic problem situations). It is possible to sketch a new 
paradigm of modern (flexible / agile) production with the following points [1]: 
- improvement of three broad cross-functional factors (quality, cost, time), 
- satisfaction of customers by increasing customer-perceived value of products and 
controlling process to produce quality at the source: customer responsiveness, 
- continuous improvement between bolder innovation phases, 
- workers at the operations level are empowered through working in various types of 
teams, including self-organizing and self-directed work groups, 
- suppliers are chosen carefully, with a view to fostering long-term relations with the 
company, 
- the organizations appears as an open system in search of harmonious relations with 
its environment, 
- technological choices are linked to the co rporate strategy and are closely coordi-
nated with organizational changes to allow the workforce to adopt to the fluctuations 
of production and other processes, 
- performance evaluation at spurring and sustaining both innovation and continuous 
improvement. 
The aim of the paper is to present the results of the authors’ researches which con-
sisted in implementation of network oriented manufacturing structures. The article 
consists of four sections, the second of which presents the literature overview of net-
work oriented manufacturing structures. The third one describes E-manufacturing, its 
definition and components. The main contribution of this paper which consisted on 
presentation results performed in 15 enterprises is enclosed in section four. This  
section is formed by definition stages of implementation, simulation modeling of 
manufacturing structures and principles orf integrating the network by means of  
e-manufacturing. The fifth section depicts conclusions and proposition of integration 
organized in the form of e-manufacturing. 
2   Network Oriented Manufacturing Structures 
The structure of a manufacturing system should allow its flexibility. Elasticity of mod-
ern manufacturing systems should give the possibility for activities reflecting an  
individual customer’s demand. It can be achieved by the possibility of creating 
changeable configurations of a manufacturing system. Manufacturing systems with 
such a configuration can adapt to changes in the environment (new products, new 
processes, new technologies new structures, etc.). They are open to changes, as well as 
flexible in reactions to adaptation to these changes. The possibility for adaptation to 
new conditions increases by creating new external cooperation between components 
from different production systems. Adaptation skills can be secured by a modular 
structure which gives flexibility by changes of cooperation structure. Manufacturing 
systems which have the texture of a modular structure can be called adaptation

284 M. Dudek and P. Pawlewski 
systems. Adaptation manufacturing systems are process structures with elastic produc-
tion teams which adapt to a given situation. These are logic dynamic production struc-
tures. These are collections of components carrying out following phases of the process 
and connected by a network of cooperation. The cooperation defines where a given 
fragment of a production process is to be placed, in what time and amount. 
Contemporary manufacturing systems should adapt better to changeable demands 
because they will tend to operate in changeable environment. Their structures must be 
able to change dynamically so as to ad apt the production capacity to given needs. 
Organizing the production for defined circumstances and parameters of flow will be 
possible when, in each situation, it will be possible to choose the best way of flow. 
Such a way of flow can be chosen when branched off structures of internal and exter-
nal cooperation are organized. Designing and organizing the manufacturing system 
will resolve into creating a network of connections, where modules (components) of 
the manufacturing system will be joints of network. The network is understood as a 
structure of modules cooperation, for cooperation relations which are in manufactur-
ing processes create an integrated network of connections. The network configuration 
must connect the components (modules) originating from different structures and 
parameters (operations, production techniques, production capacity). Network struc-
tures facilitate many forms of flows depending on the adopted kind of cooperation. 
Table 1 presents various organizational approaches which apply new organization 
forms in order to enhance the structure flexibility.

Some of the above manufacturing systems and production models have been 
maturely applied to practical manufacturing areas, some are still undergoing investi-
gation or conceptualization [2] . 
The presented concepts and models of organizing manufacturing systems are the 
foundation of creating manufacturing systems, which ought to provide operational

Implementation of Network Oriented Manufacturing Structures 285 
and structural flexibility. Each of these concepts is characterized by a network struc-
ture of cooperating units, modules. The selection of a specific organization variant 
depends upon numerous factors, such as: 
- goal of a system operation and its strategy 
- resources availability 
- mobility, friendliness, calibration ability of a system 
- organizational knowledge as for the organization, implementation, evaluation of 
probable structural systems 
- technical capacity for adaptation changes  
- complexity of production techniques necessary to execute an order 
- potential of prospective cooperating parties 
Therefore, one cannot explicitly say which of  the presented concepts is the best.  
The new forms of organizing manufacturing structures, such as segmented, fractal, 
holonic, bionic, modular factory, make it possible for an enterprise to be changeable, 
productive and increase the level of adaptability. It is possible through decentraliza-
tion and increasing the independence of basic manufacturing elements. Even though 
these approaches have certain similarities, each of them seeks to increase organiza-
tional autonomy. A common idea of all the a pproaches is to esta blish decentralized 
units on the factory level, called segments, fractals, holons, agents, etc., in order to be 
able to subdivide a complex system into smaller organizational units.  
The organization of flows in network structures has to be distinguished from the 
organization of conventional flows. The differences have to be precisely defined in 
order to avoid ambiguous misunderstandings and result from the form of the structure. 
Conventional organizational units, such as manufacturing cells and manufacturing 
groups are basically the result of a production planning activity. Organizational units 
are created to subdivide large, complex struct ures into smaller, manageable units with 
the purpose of an increased autonomy, transparency and efficiency. Contemporary 
organizational units (based on network struct ures) are designed to assign processes to 
a physically separated formation without aff ecting other units. Strategic aims of net-
work structures are to increase the overall company value, minimize waste, reduce 
organizational complexity and meet customer expectations (needs). Network oriented 
thinking allows designing optimal structures for present requirements. 
3   E-Manufacturing – The Form of Networks Organizing 
The network organization of flows makes it possible to apply solutions based on e-
manufacturing. E-manufacturing is a combination of separate components of systems, 
following the determined production path in order to execute assigned tasks as fast 
and cheaply as possible [3]. The implementation of e-manufacturing principles means 
the necessity to exhibit the company’s own internal systems (resources, knowledge, 
technologies, etc.) and to make them available to cooperating parties. Such actions 
induce obligatory release of auxiliary and major activities, which in practice means 
making the organizational knowledge public. Therefore, e-manufacturing is the kind 
of organizing which, with use of appropriate tools, will integrate the internal and 
external components of various organizations into one manufacturing system. One

286 M. Dudek and P. Pawlewski 
should remember that it is not the availability of components which is an organiza-
tional problem (they are available in the environment), but identifying them and unit-
ing into one efficiently working system. 
E-manufacturing, which includes all the aspects of manufacturing, i.e. sale, market-
ing, customer service, creating new products, supply, logistics and manufacturing 
itself, should integrate actions of a single system with other parts of a chain  
(network). This may bring numerous profits [4], such as fast acquisition of feedback 
information, costs reduction, improved  communication, sharing knowledge and  
information, stock reduction in the delivery chain, improved efficiency and effective-
ness, harmonized and standardized procedures, improved customer service. 
E-manufacturing can also be defined as collaboration systems with numerous  
external links, using IT solutions in order to integrate with the environment [5]. The 
term can also be used for such a form of organizing the manufacturing system struc-
ture, which uses advanced IT solutions in order to make real-time decisions which are 
purposed to determine the mode of organization, the principles of module selection 
and configuration and the indispensable resources. E-manufacturing guarantees in-
formation exchange between all the cooperating parties. The information, experience, 
knowledge are exchanged via appropriate module relations with use of the Internet. 
Therefore, these are the forms that play the role of integrators which lay out paths for 
cooperation, which can possibly be implemented (internal and external ones). Artifi-
cial Intelligence (AI) is the tool for inferring: AI will plan, coordinate and create the 
courses of implemented processes in the distributed systems. AI will be able to make 
real-time decisions as for the distribution and implementation of tasks. As a result, the 
decision-making nodes will be transformed into automatic-information-processing 
nodes, which means that e.g. interpersonal relation will be replaced by network links 
between computerised modules. All the system functions will be solely performed by 
electronic equipment (with no human intervention).  
4   Research of Implementation of Network Oriented Structures 
Organizing modern structures of manufacturing systems (components and their recip-
rocal relations), one should take into c onsideration both time and space links of  
particular components because it is possible to shape a given structure of system only 
when all partial processes undergoing within the system will be considered as a whole 
in integrated manufacturing process. Also, the structure of system needs to be seen as 
a process of flow in time and space,  i.e.  [5] streams of flows and their volume, ways 
of flow and their structure, phases of activity and their time dependence. The above-
mentioned components of flow determine the structure of a production system i.e. a 
number of components and their space location. Foreseeing different flows of proc-
esses in the production system allows to define the most flexible structure. The inves-
tigation of changeability of tasks in time allows also to calculate the number of the 
system components and their distribution. While organizing the structure, one should 
take into consideration both the course an d structure of the integrated manufacturing 
process, as well as mutual dependences of processes in the network, often and often 
going beyond the area of manufacturing system (lack of visible system boundaries, 
where changeability of tasks results in the fact that environment becomes a system).

Implementation of Network Oriented Manufacturing Structures 287 
Investigations aiming at verifying the suggested methodology of structure modelling 
were conducted with use of manufacturing system model. The model was created and 
verified on the basis of investigations and analyses carried out in fifteen electrical en-
gineering industry enterprises in the south of Poland. Electrical engineering industry is 
one of the best developed branches of Polish industry. The courses of manufacturing 
processes in this industry are characterized by the greatest technical diversity and can 
be representative of other branches of industry products. That is why, selecting electri-
cal engineering industry as a subject of the research appears to be correct. Moreover, 
products made by this branch of industry are marked by great structural complexity, 
multistage production process, variety of flows, diversity of the type and scale of  
production with a changeable product line.  
4.1   Stages of Implementation  
The concept of putting manufacturing structures into economic practice can be pre-
sented regardless of the choice of organization form, which will be the basis of con-
structing these structures. The concept includes eight stages, shown in Figure 1. 
 
Fig. 1. Stages of implementing network structures 
At the first stage, the analysis of the current structural solution is made in order to 
identify the strengths and weaknesses of the existing solution and to map all the flows 
occurring in the system. The second stage is the stage of identifying market require-
ments as for the introduction of a new structural system. At the third stage, the  
requirements to be met by the new solution are confronted with the present structure 
potential. At this stage, there is a question whether the target solution will be achieved 
with use of a company’s own resources (if yes, what they will be) or what external 
sources should be used. The fourth stage is  the stage of confronting the selected  
solution with the well-known and used-in-the-market concepts. In case when similar 
solutions occur in the market, the available knowledge can be copied. Yet, creating a

288 M. Dudek and P. Pawlewski 
solution which will be innovative in the market seems to be a better idea. At the fifth 
stage, the necessary resources are chosen and complemented so as to create the se-
lected system and determine principles of cooperation between units (modules). At 
the sixth stage, the potential organizational variants are simulated. At the seventh 
stage, the potential systems are selected with use of appropriate criteria and the most 
effective solution, considering the given conditions, is chosen. The eighth stage is 
especially noteworthy since at this stage a number of actions are taken, which lead to 
the implementation of e-manufacturing[6]. 
4.2   Simulation Modeling of Manufacturing Structures  
The sixth stage is critical for implementing the most effective structural solution. It is 
impossible to take into account all the potential process combinations without using 
appropriate tools, such as, e.g. simulation modelling. The usefulness of simulation 
modelling to solving similar problems is often described in literature, e.g. [7]. The 
modern approach to modelling the structure of system should be based upon deter-
mining the principles of flow and components cooperation. The principles may be as 
follows: deadline for executing the whole task, deadlines for intermediate stages, 
intensity of flows (parallelism, multiflux), scheduling of tasks. Therefore, modelling 
modern structures consists of [8]:  
- searching for cooperating parties 
- determining potential networks, cooperative relations 
- selecting the most efficient courses 
The conducted research made it possible to determine the basic characteristics of an 
average investigated manufacturing system (Figures 2 and 3): 
- an average volume of production in the investigated period and an average number 
of operations per product, 
- average time and cost of manufacturing one product

Fig. 3. Average time and cost of manufacturing one product 
The main principle of modelling the manufacturing structure in a given situation 
was the deadline for implementing the tasks imposed by a customer. The analysis 
showed that it is possible to create alternative manufacturing paths, that use resources 
of various organizations under investigation (e-manufacturing). At first, the plan was 
implemented on the basis of one organization’s resources and the basic characteristics 
of the manufacturing process were determined (time, cost, productivity etc.). In the 
course of subsequent experiments, the most time- and cost-consuming operations 
were assigned for implementation to the investigated organization. On the foundation 
of knowledge base, fifty hypothetical configurations of manufacturing structures were 
created so as to execute the appointed production plan; the calculations were  
made with use of Witness software. The simulation allows to determine the basic 
parameters of the processes that form the structure of the manufacturing system. The 
investigated parameters were time and cost. The experiments lead to the preliminary 
conclusions; as the number of operations assigned to cooperating parties grows 
- the time and cost of implementing the set production increase 
- in case the time and cost of transport are not taken into consideration, the total time 
and cost of production decrease 
- amount of time devoted to control increases 
- there is a shift in the occurrence of bottlenecks 
- the structural elasticity increases.  
Moreover, in spite of times losses caused by the external transport, contracting critical 
operations to cooperating parties in many cases led to the prompt execution of tasks.  
4.3   Integrating the Network by Means of E-Manufacturing  
According to studies on e-manufacturing, its basic components are [9] Manufacturing 
Execution System, Equipment Engineering System, Supply Chain Management and 
Engineering Chain Management. As a result of research made by the authors in 15 
enterprises, additional key tools were identified; they are indispensible for the proper 
functioning of e-manufacturing. Hence, it also necessary to:

290 M. Dudek and P. Pawlewski 
- construct knowledge base, i.e. a tool for continuous acquisition of information on 
suppliers and their offer, possible cooperating parties and their potential as well as 
production capacity, possibilities and terms of cooperation, 
- develop tools for identification and current analysis of resources, which makes it 
possible to verify production resources in real time, and to determine the most effi-
cient manufacturing paths (simulation), 
- develop mechanisms of relationship management in the network, 
- develop negotiation tools in the network, 
- develop tools for evaluating confidence in cooperating parties, 
- develop tools for integration in the network, in the form of universal applications 
able to reduce the operating costs of the infrastructure, and ready to cooperate with IT 
systems of other networks.  
Implementing solutions based on e-manufacturing structures [10] will result in a sig-
nificant increase in efficiency and effectiveness of manufacturing. It will also expand 
the data accessibility so as to support making a decision, and it will identify knowl-
edge in the system, which can later be the foundation of the knowledge base.  
Moreover, it will generate and facilitate tools and applications used in the decision-
making process, expand the control over resources and equipment, thoroughly secure 
communication channels, create standards of communication and terminology,  
synchronize data in real time and integrate various links of manufacturing process.  
5   Conclusions 
The conducted experiments lead to the following conclusions: 
- cheaper and shorter paths of executing tasks can be found in a network. 
- at the stage of constructing alternative paths of manufacturing, Artificial Intelligence 
can be substituted with simulation modelling, which is a cheaper solution. 
- model investigations make it possible to select the most effective way of implement-
ing a process (process map) for the given conditions. 
- the accessible knowledge base allows to analyse a huge number of potential cooper-
ating systems. 
- it is possible to implement the network forms of manufacturing structure, which are 
integrated by means of e-manufacturing. 
The analysis of the organization of production indicates that numerous enterprises, 
although provided with CAx computer assistance tools, are still separated from  
external business environment. The implementation of ERP or MES class systems 
guarantees only the internal integration of the system, and communication with the 
environment is developed with use of additional modules (e.g. CRM, SCM, LCM, 
EDI), which support manufacturing processes. E-manufacturing allows external ac-
cess by using appropriate software purposed for servicing manufacturing process. Due 
to the contemporary manufacturing conditions:  
- enterprises deal with global competitiveness (consignees demand competitive prod-
ucts, which reduce their manufacturing costs); 
- systems cannot elastically respond to customers’ demands, since their owns  
resources are limited;

Implementation of Network Oriented Manufacturing Structures 291 
- automation and outsourcing processes are much too slow in regard to market  
requirements; 
- not enough resources are allocated for increasing communicativeness between the 
system and environment.  
Therefore, it seems advisable to closely integrate the links of a supply chain. Such 
integration can be achieved with use of network manufacturing structures organized 
in the form of e-manufacturing.
