The practical purposes for ontology development are [5]: 
─ to share common understanding of the structure of information among people or 
software agents, 
─ to enable reuse of domain knowledge, 
─ to make domain assumptions explicit, 
─ to separate domain knowledge from operational knowledge, 
─ to analyze domain knowledge. 
The most prominent application of ontologies—as seen today—is a component of the 
semantic web architecture [2]. The role of the ontology in the Semantic Web ‘layer 
cake’ is to provide vocabularies and shared meanings to the web content. 
More on the ontology languages, tools and applications can be found in [3]. 
4.2   Role of Ontology in the EA Development 
As it was stated earlier in this paper, authors would like to propose a creation of an 
ontology-based TOGAF (and, perhaps, IT project management method that would 
support it) model. It would be a generic ontology, applicable to any organization  
interested in formal Enterprise Architecture development that refers to TOGAF guide-
lines. A knowledge engineer’s task is easier since the release of TOGAF Version 9. It 
introduces a content metamodel for architecture framework (see: [9]). It is a collection 
of verbal descriptions, tables, figures and UML class diagrams that present terms and 
their relationships in the ADM domain. An efficient use of such document in order to 
capture the structure of EA and TOGAF itself can be questioned. However, this me-
tamodel serves as a convenient starting point to develop an ontology. 
Such TOGAF ontology has been developed by the Working Group [11]. It  
addresses version 8 of the framework, which was not equipped with a content meta-
model. Figure 2 presents the graphical representation of main classes taxonomy 
(class-subclass relation). The root of all the terms (classes) is owl:THING—it is al-
ways a parent class in the OWL ontology. 
TOGAF generic ontology should be designed as a template that can be applied to 
any EA developing organization. As the ontology would be fed with knowledge on 
a given enterprise (especially these regarding four main domains: business, data, ap-
plication and technology), there would be a transition process from the generic to the 
(enterprise-)specific ontology. In fact, it is a natural process when ADM cycle is in 
progress (Fig. 1). 
On figure 3 one can see main terms of the TOGAF ontology presented as contain-
ers. The Enterprise class has been highlighted with an included instance of the same 
name. It depicts—as it was proposed in the preceding paragraph—that the ontology 
has a capability of being adjusted to the specific organization. The same figure shows 
other semantic relations than class-subclass in the TOGAF ontology (as arrows). 
Their intensity (multiplicity) is denoted by the thickness of the lines.

It is clear that the generic ontology development is only a first step towards ex-

Ontology would only be one of the layers of the system, as it proposed in the Seman-

5   Ontology Support for Development/Manufacturing Standards 
The goal of presenting TOGAF and ontology model of this framework was to initiate 
a research on usefulness of a developing semantic knowledge structures of technology 
and management standards. 
The next phase of the research would be focused on the attempts to apply the on-
tology metamodels to a wider range of the development/manufacturing processes. 
And if this goal is successful, in the next phase one would try to capture the whole 
enterprise (there was a TOVE project [12] trying to achieve it, but seems to be discon-
tinued for the time being). 
6   Summary 
Some claim that the great thing about standards is there are so many to choose from. 
But when the selection phase is over, there is another challenge awaiting: how to 
successfully execute implementation of the standard within organization? This  
requires a whole project team to understand and apply to the standard’s ‘letter and 
spirit’. In case of the such complex process guidelines as these found in the IT project 
management area one should consider developing and then using ontology as 
a metamodel of the given standard or guidelines. Such metamodel should have the 
adaptability and reusability for sake of all the organizations that wish to have their 
processes in conformance with the ontologically described standard. 
This paper is a result of the research on applying the intelligent methods for the IT 
evaluation founded by the Ministry of Science and Higher Education.

Methods of Incomplete and Uncertain Knowledge 
Acquisition in the Knowledge Processing Environment 
Cezary Orłowski, Tomasz Sitek, and Rafał Rybacki 
Gdańsk University of Technology, Department of Management and Economics,  
ul. Narutowicza 11/12, Gdansk, Poland 
{cezary.orlowski,tomasz.sitek}@zie.pg.gda.pl,  
rafal.rybacki@gmail.pl 
Abstract. The authors in this paper present a concept of the environment to  
acquire and process knowledge about information technology. This solution is 
part of a project of which the objective is to build a system for the evaluation of 
IT tools and methodologies. Knowledge within this domain is always either  
uncertain or incomplete. Therefore, the authors focused on designing a dedi-
cated algorithm for its acquisition and processing. One of the main factors de-
termining success in such conditions is effective collaboration with experts. An 
important part of the research on this problem was done based on an application 
built for this purpose. The application was used for several experiments which 
were expected to verify theoretical assumptions. This paper is the documenta-
tion of one such experiment. The authors’ priority was to identify real and  
potential problems through collaboration with invited domain experts. 
Keywords: knowledge base, uncertain knowledge, reasoning, expert system, 
information technology. 
1   Introduction 
The development of information technology nowadays creates opportunities for every 
organization or company. It gives the chance to select the appropriate solutions for  
the maturity level of business processes and their state of computerization. It is no 
longer possible to act in an effective way using a certain number of separate, non-
cooperative applications. Business structures expect the IT environment to provide 
safe and instant flow of all information resources for the support of organization man-
agement. The selection of these systems is usually preceded by a preliminary analysis 
of the existing infrastructure and available market offer. All products which are taken 
into consideration should be evaluated [1]. To perform such an assessment it is  
necessary to apply a model dedicated to the domain of information technology.  
As the IT domain is very wide, the authors’ research focused only on technologies 
dedicated to supporting project management. It was assumed [2] that the selection of 
the most adequate tool or method depends on three aspects: maturity of own organiza-
tion, customer characteristics and entropy of  the project. Each of these is treated by 
the authors as a variable in the algorithm.  The algorithm describes possible actions of

Methods of Incomplete and Uncertain Knowledge Acquisition 341 
project leaders in the process of the selec tion of the most adequate method/tool for a 
certain project. It is the base for the multi-layered model of the selection of IT meth-
ods and tools, which makes use of the mentioned variables for rule-based knowledge 
representation with the use of fuzzy modeling. 
For the purpose of the developed model it is necessary to gain knowledge about the 
project and its environment. However, knowledge may be either distributed or uncer-
tain and incomplete. Such characteristics of knowledge are the result of the large 
entropy of the project environment. IT projects very often become a sequence of  
disordered events which are difficult to manage [3].  
Therefore, the next sections present the mechanisms for acquiring such knowledge 
for the model and the system for information technology evaluation. The authors 
focused in the paper on processes of cooperation between experts and knowledge 
engineers.  
2   Research Area and Objectives 
The primary research (as well as utilitarian) objective of the authors’ team is the 
building of a system for information technology management. 
It is assumed that such a solution will be dedicated to the selection of methods and 
tools for IT project management support. This will be a knowledge-base solution. 
Therefore, its built-in mechanisms for facts/rules acquisition and processing must be a 
key component [4]. 
As it was mentioned in the introduction, knowledge of this domain is usually char-
acterized by some kind of imperfection. Therefore, we may have to deal with [5]: 
 
• incomplete knowledge, 
• uncertain knowledge, 
• imprecise knowledge. 
 
However, in most cases knowledge engineers must face more than one of these prob-
lems (for example, an expert may not have complete knowledge, while he also cannot 
be completely sure of his knowledge). It is important to take this aspect of knowledge 
into account already at the stage of selecting or designing an appropriate tool to build 
the mentioned system. It must be able to deal with knowledge imperfection because it is 
expected to support either the process of rules/facts acquisition or chaining procedures. 
It turns out that incompleteness of knowledge may be the result of either gaps on 
the specialists’ side or the low efficiency of applied knowledge engineering methods 
(e.g. too long sessions make experts tired and impatient). In such conditions, the main 
priority is to design such a logic of dialogue with an expert that knowledge-acquiring 
sessions are optimal due to the efficiency criteria. Efficiency is defined as the number 
of rules/facts added to the base in a given unit of time. What is important is that inter-
action ‘the system-person who enters the knowledge’ must be maintenance-free. It is 
assumed that there will be many experts involved in the project. Therefore,  
co-operation with them must be organized in the way that no personal support of 
knowledge engineers is needed. In the context of these requirements the goal of the 
authors is to build an environment which will have:

342 C. Orłowski, T. Sitek, and R. Rybacki 
• optimal logic of the knowledge acquisition process - due to the criterion of time 
and other hard-to-measure or not-measurable criteria such as easiness of entering 
knowledge to the base, 
• an ergonomic and fault-tolerant user interface; an expert should be supported by 
the system at every step. 
 
For the purpose of the verification of the developed concept, a dedicated application 
was built. The authors expected such a tool to be helpful in analyzing and controlling 
every step of the information acquisition process. The application is described in the 
next section. Then the authors present details of an experiment which was carried out 
at Gdansk University of Technology. A group of knowledge engineers, domain  
experts and specialists in methods of reasoning were invited and involved. 
3   The System for Acquiring and Processing Knowledge 
This section concerns the concept of a designed knowledge-base system. The  
mentioned application is an expert system, which aims to support decision-making 
processes on the basis of acquired knowledge, knowledge processing algorithms and 
procedures for determining the response. 
3.1   Knowledge-Base Structure 
The most basic functional unit of knowledge is a case. Every case contains informa-
tion about a real or simulated situation. Each case is described by two sets of facts: 
facts that describe the situation and facts that point to a suggested solution to the con-
sidered problem. 
Each case is described by a vector of input variables. The corresponding solution is 
determined by a vector of output variables. So, the unit of knowledge – the case – is 
therefore an relation between two vectors of values. Additionally, input variables can 
be described using attribute weights, which express the level of significance of each 
variable in the decision-making process. An example case has been shown in Table 1. 
Table 1. The case structure 
Input variables Output variables 
A (1) B (1) C (2) X Y 
a1 b 1 c 1 x 1 y 1 
 
where: A (1) stands for the variable A with the weight amounting to 1. 
The case described in Table 1 may be interpreted as a rule in the form of a logical 
implication, which means: 
IF (A = a1) AND (B = b1) AND (C = c1) THEN (X = x1) AND (Y = y1)       (1)

Methods of Incomplete and Uncertain Knowledge Acquisition 343 
The second functional unit of knowledge  in the considered  concept is the adapta-
tion rule. These rules may support the process of introducing the knowledge as well 
as boosting the accuracy of reasoning when seeking a solution. The purpose of adap-
tation rules is to fit the knowledge stored in a set of cases to the query. These rules are 
introduced in order to capture the relations hip between the changes in the states of 
input and output variables. An example of the implementation of adaptation rules is 
presented in Table 2. 
Table 2. An example of adaptation rules 
Input variables Output variables 
A B C X Y 
a1 →  a2   x1 → x1  
 
The interpretation of such an adaptation rule should be: 
Assuming the constant character of other variables, if the value of A changes from 
a 1 to a 2, then the value of output variable X changes from x 1 to x 1.. 
3.2   Knowledge-Base Content 
A decision supporting functionality cannot be executed unless the knowledge is intro-
duced to the knowledge-base. When a state of complete information is provided, the 
contents of the knowledge base may have the nature of: 
 
• incomplete knowledge, 
• uncertain knowledge. 
 
The incompleteness of the knowledge is expressed by the number of cases, which is 
less than the maximum number of variable combinations. 
The system also allows for the introduction of knowledge in the form of cases with 
limited degrees of belief which describe both the entire rule and every specific fact. 
The proposed implementation of uncertain knowledge assigns a value of confidence 
for every input variable. This has been shown in table 3. 
Table 3. Structure of a case with uncertain knowledge 
Input variables Output variables Degree 
of belief  
A P(A) B P(B) C P(C) X P(X) Y P(Y) 
90% a 1 100% b 1 90% c 1 75% x 1 100% y 1 60% 
 
where P(X) – the function determining the confidence level of variable X .

344 C. Orłowski, T. Sitek, and R. Rybacki 
3.3   The Procedure for Reasoning  
The system achieves its purpose – the support of the decision-making process – 
through analyzing the query and suggesting the best possible solution. The query sent 
to the system is determined by the vector of input variables. 
The process of reasoning consists of two steps. In the first step, the best-matching 
case is searched. This is achieved by comp aring the query with every case stored in 
the knowledge-base and extracting the Euclidean distance of every pair on the basis of 
normalized values of input variables of each of the input vectors. The best match is 
determined by the lowest value of such a calculated distance. This is the realization of 
the nearest neighbor algorithm. 
If the confidence levels are being in use, system is treating them as modifiers that 
decrease the general solution confidence level. 
The idea of the second step is to modify the found best-matching case in order to 
make it fit better to the query. This is done by analyzing all adaptation rules stored in 
the knowledge-base and trying to apply them to the case found in the first step. Then, 
the Euclidean distance between such modified cases and the query are calculated. 
Provided that the value of the distance is lower than the distance found in the first 
step, the best set of adaptation rules is a pplied to the selected case and such a modi-
fied case is thought to be the final solution. If the Euclidean distance between the 
selected case and the query is zero, it means that the system has found a case which is 
identical to the query and the solution of this case will be suggested as the final reso-
lution for the query. The adaptation rules are being applied in the order of entering to 
base. Therefore all of them are always taken into consideration during reasoning.  
3.4   Implementation of the System 
The concept of an expert system presented in this section has been introduced as the 
application called EXPERT2. The application has been implemented in Software-as-a-
Service technology, so that it enables a multiple number of users to work with the 
application and cooperate simultaneously. The functionalities of the created software 
include such capabilities as: 
 
• knowledge-base structure modification, 
• adding cases with a degree of confidence, 
• adding adaptation rules with a degree of confidence, 
• automatic building of adaptation rules based on inserted cases, 
• performing queries in order to get problem solution support. 
 
There are also additional features that ease management and ensure the proper func-
tioning of adaptation rules. When the option is selected, all duplicate and conflicting 
adaptation rules will be removed from the analysis. The use of adaptation rules can be 
switched off so that the second step of reasoning is not being performed. The ability 
to control these options can be made through the tab with the main preview of the 
knowledge base. It is shown in figure 1. 
The following figures present the tabs that allow the cases to be defined and the

problem concerned in the survey had alread y been pre-identified and resolved, so the 
correctness of every response was able to be assessed. The study was performed on a 
sample of 100.000 queries, with varying degrees of completeness of the knowledge 
base. Two concepts were tested: 
 
• NN – reasoning on the basis of cases only, 
• NNA – reasoning on the basis of cases and automatically-built adaptation rules.

4   Verification of the Developed Approach for the Reasoning and 
Acquisition of Knowledge in the IT Domain 
The idea of the application presented in th e previous section was determined by the 
need to verify the authors’ (theoretical, so  far) concept. As their research focused on 
mechanisms for obtaining and processing knowledge, it was therefore decided to 
organize and perform a special experiment. 
4.1   Assumptions for the Experiment 
Such an experiment was arranged as several working sessions with the participation 
of experts. It was intended to verify the approach and guide the way for further work. 
The experiment was planned as part of an ongoing scientific research project  
conducted with the IT department (called the IT Support Organization) of a large 
international financial company. The project aims to build a tool which allows the 
identification of prognostic factors which influence the evolution of IT support or-
ganizations. Success in obtaining the desired results depends largely on the quantity 
and quality of available knowledge about occurred and probable changes in organiza-
tion structures. In particular, there are some  collected rules which describe the impact 
of the organization’s initial state and the possible processes of transition on its final 
state (measured on a scale of maturity levels, as well as in CMMI methodology). 
Because of the high complexity of the project (calculated by the number of possi-
ble parameters to be analyzed), it was agreed that the domain should be confined for 
the first experiment. Based on that assumption the authors focused on the preprocess-
ing of one variable - the level of maturity of the organization. The general form of 
rules was accepted as follows: 
 
IF <initial level> AND < transition processes> THEN <end level>            (2) 
 
where all variables are expressed on a scale of 1-5, which corresponds to the level of 
organization maturity.  
All these agreements were implemented in the tool presented in previous sections. 
4.2   The Experiment – Participants and Schedule 
The experiment was carried out in the Laboratory for Research on Information Tech-
nologies at Gdansk University of Technology. Representatives of three organizations 
agreed to take part in it: 
 
• Knowledge engineers from the Department of Information Technology Manage-
ment (including the authors), 
• Specialists in algorithms of imperfect knowledge processing,

348 C. Orłowski, T. Sitek, and R. Rybacki 
• Domain experts from the IT support organization, with knowledge about the proc-
esses determining changes in levels of maturity in such entities. 
 
The schedule of the meeting was divided into three main parts: 
 
• introducing participants to topics of research, presentations of established assump-
tions, 
• adjusting the system, correction of the initial structure of the knowledge base,  
selection of limit values, 
• four sessions (consultations) with experts, during each one additional features 
available to the expert were introduced; the authors aim was to verify the validity 
of each of the four approaches to knowledge acquisition. 
 
Session #1 was carried out in order to gain only certain knowledge from the invited 
specialists. They were provided with an interface for entering only case-type rules and 
were instructed to input only knowledge without any doubts. All uncertain cases were 
rejected. It was also assumed that the experts were starting with an empty knowledge 
base and beginning to fill it at their own rate. During this process, reasoning was 
launched several times in order to verify expected outcomes. It also gave some over-
view of how the system works with different levels of base completeness. An impor-
tant conclusion was that the experts decided to finish this session after entering quite a 
low number of rules (compared to the goal - a full knowledge base, which should be 
the consequence of all combinations of input variables). The experts considered only 
a small part of their knowledge as fully certain and ready for implementation.  
Session #2 entered the concept of adaptation rules. It had to answer the following 
question: is it easier for an expert to enter many cases or to focus on an alternative 
way of expressing knowledge – entering a few rules that describe general principles 
regarding transition between states of variables? This new functionality determined a 
need to correct the existing knowledge (previously added in session #1). Some cases 
were replaced by adequate adaptation rules. The experts did the modifications in sev-
eral iterations and analyzed different answers received from the system. Again, only 
certain knowledge was taken into consideration. The conclusion after this part of the 
experiment was quite unexpected. The experts found adaptation knowledge too diffi-
cult to express. Therefore, the proce ss of knowledge acquisition becomes too  burden-
some. It is much easier to generate many rules describing experiences than to think 
out more general principles. 
During session #3 certainty factors were introduced (called also degrees of belief). 
The application is prepared to record every rule with additional information regarding 
the level of certainty. The experts have four levels at their disposal: low, moderate, 
high, absolute.  Each of these levels names an exact numeric value (e.g. absolute = 
100% certainty that a given statement is true). This session was started with an analy-
sis of knowledge acquired so far. Despite having new opportunities, the experts  
decided not to adjust the existing rules. They asked for the knowledge base to be 
cleaned and entered a set of rules again. For every rule or single variable, they took

Methods of Incomplete and Uncertain Knowledge Acquisition 349 
into consideration certainty factors. After adding the possibility of expressing the 
degree of certainty, the experts considered the tool more useful. They found it more 
flexible as well.  
Session #4 was planned as an attempt to archive a complete set of rules in the base. 
The higher the level of knowledge completeness (quantity of rules), the more precise 
are the answers generated by the system. Unlike sessions 1-3, when the experts had to 
fill an empty base with new rules, during session #4 a new approach was suggested. 
The specialists received an automatically generated complete knowledge base (all 
combinations of input variables). However, each rule had not been assigned a hy-
pothesis. The experts were expected to analyze such a knowledge base and add all the 
hypotheses for each case. Although from a knowledge engineering point of view, the 
objective seemed to be well founded, the ex perts rejected it. They considered such a 
method of knowledge acquisition as an impediment. This approach has proved to be 
too difficult to implement, especially if the complete database consists of too many 
(according to the subjective evaluation of each of the experts) rules to analyze. 
5   Summary 
In this paper, the authors described an experiment which adds new value to their  
research. It also gives experience within their work on knowledge acquisition and 
processing. 
The authors prepared special conditions for gathering knowledge with different 
types of imperfection. At the same time, they made many observations of experts’ 
behavior during key moments in the process (e.g. making final decisions when the 
opinions of different experts are contradictory to each other). All parties involved 
proved the usefulness of the meeting. 
The most interesting result of the experiment was completely unexpected. Knowl-
edge engineers together with experts came to  the conclusion that there is a significant 
difference between their particular goals. The primary scientific goal was set by the 
team from the Department of Information Technology Management. The authors 
(designers of the algorithm), being aware of the key aspects of processing incomplete 
and uncertain knowledge, decided to eliminate them. Introducing additional function-
alities during every new session was supposed to help the experts to express their 
knowledge in the most complete way. However, the experts defined their goals from a 
business perspective. They did not consider incomplete knowledge as an obstacle for 
using such a system in a live environment. According to their assumptions, there is no 
need to generate all case rules. There is no need to think of hypothetical situations that 
may never happen. Both sides agreed that only constant monitoring of the knowledge 
acquisition process can guarantee success in building a fully functional application 
and using it in an effective way. This can be archived by the great number of consul-
tations with experts.  
The presented project was the first such session with experts organized by the  
Department of Information Technology Management. It was agreed that it constitutes 
an important step in building an applicatio n to acquire and process knowledge for the 
evaluation of information technology.

An Approach to Agent-Based Supporting  
System for IT Projects 
Cezary Orłowski and Artur Ziółkowski 
Gdansk University of Technology, Department of IT Management,  
80-233 Gdańsk, Narutowicza 11/12 
{cor,aziolko}@zie.pg.gda.pl 
Abstract. The natural development of information technology area stimulates 
intense growth of various technologies which support basic organization proc-
esses. The range of technologies implies appropriate management thereof, as 
well as accurate correspondence with conducted activities. Abandonment of ac-
tivities within individual branches in fav our of project approach to performed 
assignments (especially those connected with software development) has re-
cently become a popular subject of management. This approach involves a vari-
ety of technologies which support project tasks. Yet the question arises, how to 
harmonize proper technologies with project management in an effective way. 
Agent system that is built by authors is a kind of solution to this problem. That 
system is a kind of tool which serves to help project managers with the choice 
of a proper method and technology of project management. One of most impor-
tant decision taken before project start is method and tools selection. When 
method is not fitted to project team it can provide to project’s failure. Also 
many times client’s knowledge about IT project area can be important for  
getting success. 
Keywords: IT project, agent system, decision supporting. 
1   Introduction (Context of Research) 
The natural development of information technology fields stimulates intense growth 
in various technologies which support basic organization processes. The range of 
technologies implies appropriate management thereof, as well as accurate correspon-
dence with conducted activities. The abandonment of activities within individual 
branches in favour of a project approach to performed assignments (especially those 
connected with software development) has recently become a popular subject of man-
agement. This approach involves a variety of technologies which support project 
tasks. Yet the question arises of how to harmonize proper technologies with project 
management in an effective way. Agent system designed by authors is a tool for  
support some managers work, especially tied with choosing method and tools for their 
projects.  
The following agent system [2], supported by ontologies and an expert system, is a 
tool which serves to help project managers with the choice of a proper method and 
technology of project management. The above-mentioned system for information

352 C. Orłowski and A. Ziółkowski 
technology assessment is based on intelligent units designed for acquiring and proc-
essing knowledge [4]. The role of these units is performed by agents which are the 
basic components of multi-agent systems and at the same time are identified as inde-
pendent beings able to take action and perform tasks for the user. The idea of using 
agents for information technology assessment results directly from their immanent 
features, in addition to the broad spectrum of possibilities (particularly considering a 
Semantic Web, where the function of intelligent agents seems to be essential) [1]. 
The function of agents is to acquire and process information. Therefore, their sig-
nificance for the assessment system might be seen in two ways. The first task is to 
acquire information from the environment (supplying the system at the same time); 
the second task is to generate an assessment and upload it to the user (or customer). In 
order to avoid subjective assessment, the assessment should be generated by inde-
pendent agents. The assessment is based on the attached fact database, free from any 
preconceptions held by user, expert or any other individual. 
2   Stages of Model Evolution 
The following model of an agent system for IT project management support is the 
effect of a few iterations. The model has been developed and tailored during research 
at Gdansk University of Technology. Succes sive iterations have been applied to the 
final version of the model of the agent system that is presented in this article.  
In the first stage, the main elements have been defined. The authors decided that 
the main components of the system should be (in addition to the agent system): 
 
• An expert system (based on facts and rules that are necessary for inference of 
fuzzy rules) 
• Ontologies (that are responsible for the formal correctness of information) 
• Other intelligent objects (like neural networks, genetic algorithms), which can 
support the main process in the system  
 
This pointed to research which needed a definition of cooperation for all system com-
ponents. At the same time, independent research was undertaken for all elements such 
as agents, ontologies and the expert system. This was needed to ensure the correct 
model evolution. 
The next step of the research was focused on the definition of the main functional-
ity of the system. The authors had to check how the system can be useful from  
the point of view of information technology evaluation. This stage was finished by 
working out the functional prototype of the system for IT evaluation. The functional 
prototype included the definition of all agents and tasks for them. This enabled the 
definition of information flow inside the system. The main conclusion of this stage 
was the definition of the main functionality of the system. This was as follows: 
 
• Information acquisition from the system’s client (user) 
• Resources searching 
• Inference founded on resources 
• Management of agents in the system

An Approach to Agent-Based Supporting System for IT Projects 353 
3   Identification of the Main Variables 
3.1   Problems with Matching Management Methods to IT Projects 
The problem of selection methods for the management of IT projects is the increas-
ingly frequent managers’ "dilemma". It turns out that the wrong choice of method 
often contributes to the failure of the project (in the form of non-compliance with its 
limitations - the budget or schedule). It thus follows that support for decision-making 
methods and tools used for project planning is an essential task of the project man-
ager. Support should therefore focus on the function of planning in particular, because 
it was within this function that a decision is taken on how to continue the project. In 
other words, it appears that this function of management is crucial for the further 
course of the project. Mistakes in planning (both the team and work schedule) may 
have far-reaching consequences for the conduct of the project. It follows, therefore, 
that the most important decisions regarding the method of project management must 
be planned carefully. The planning project manager should identify the method in-
tended to carry out the project and select a tool that will assist its implementation. 
The issue of the choice of the correct way to implement the project may thus  
determine its success. If a manager chooses a little-known method or one poorly rec-
ognized by the team, it can result in stopping work in the course of the project. 
It appears that the question of the proper method of selection is very important 
from the perspective of the whole project. The appropriate selection method therefore 
seems crucial for the entire project. It seems more reasonable to support managers just 
at the stage of decision-making in planning a project with an independent IT system 
indicating which method will be optimal for the specific project. 
The issue of the selection method of project management is therefore an integral 
part of the basic functions of management-planning. It therefore seems reasonable to 
support project managers in the choice of implementing IT projects as well as the 
selection of appropriate tools to manage such projects. 
This also means that the hypothesis that managers should be systematically  
supported in terms of their choice of the implementation of projects appears to be 
confirmed by the above considerations. It is worth noting also that there is now a very 
large number of formal methods for project management (approximately 10 major 
methods, such as RUP, PRINCE, SCRUM, XP). In addition, managers can find many 
methods individually-created by software  manufacturers for their own needs (as in 
SAP). By contrast, there are even more information tools in support of these methods 
(the portal 4pm.pl reported that there were more than 100 free applications supporting 
the management of projects in 2008). A system solution allowing for the input 
method to specify the conditions for the implementation of projects as well as identify 
the appropriate IT tool to the project s eems to be very much needed, and connects 
with the main objective, that is, optimizing management processes performed by 
project managers. 
But to define these input variables, which may be relevant to the selection method 
of project management, it is necessary to analyze the key components occurring at the 
very beginning when planning IT projects. These components and their description 
will allow for the extraction of the basic parameters influencing managerial decisions 
regarding the selection of methods and tools.

354 C. Orłowski and A. Ziółkowski 
4   Identification of Key Variables Affecting the Choice of Method 
One of the main characteristics of project specific information is that it is unique, or that 
it is difficult to identify two identical or nearly identical implemented projects. It ap-
pears, however, that despite this uniqueness, a set of factors can be distinguished that 
will occur in every project and that the specificity of these factors depends on the subse-
quent decisions by managers which translate into success (or failure) of the project. 
These factors also appear to be relevant to the methods of selecting the project. These 
features certainly should include the maturity of the client and the maturity of the team 
implementing the project. A typical factor seems to be the complexity of work in the 
project, which can be called the entropy of the project (the degree of disorder). 
 
Client 
The customer is the primary subject of any ongoing project. It can be concluded that 
the presence of the client (usually present at the beginning of negotiations and discus-
sions on the scope of the project) provides a starting point because it is the client’s 
order which usually begins the planning of projects. This allows you to recognize that 
the implementation of computerized processe s are a kind of draw (pull), where the 
whole process starts with customer orders, followed by a "pull value", which is col-
lecting information about what is to be the subject of the execution of the project. The 
presence of a client in the process of impl ementing IT projects confirms the validity 
of the project. The presence of the customer can therefore be considered as a constant 
feature of all projects. 
However, the question remains of the customer’s impact on the course of the pro-
ject itself. A typical phenomenon is the changing of customer requirements during the 
implementation of projects. Something that seemed important to the customer at the 
beginning shall be replaced by other requirements in the course of the project. A typi-
cal phenomenon is also the client increasing the scope of the project, which often 
translates into changes in cost or schedule. The role of the manager in this case is to 
steer the work to meet those expectations or  adapt them to the constraints of the pro-
ject. It is said that customer satisfaction is a guarantee of future cooperation as well as 
building a strong market position for the company pursuing the project. American 
studies show that one unhappy customer contributes to a loss of from 7 to 12 potential 
customers, and therefore meeting the expectat ions of the customer seems to be a pri-
ority (indeed some formal project management methods such as RUP say this explic-
itly). This does not mean that the role of the customer is unlimited. There may in fact 
be situations in which certain customer ex pectations cannot be achieved, or are not 
relevant to the ongoing project and, according to manager, might be ignored. In this 
situation, the most recommended way for the negotiations is to lead to a common 
direction for both parties - the contractor and the client. 
A very common phenomenon is the lack of concrete expectations for the project by 
the client’s computer. This means a situation in which the customer does not fully 
know what is expected, needs "some" IT so lution, but is not able to determine the 
parameters of this solution. The client is not able to precisely define his needs, which 
makes it more difficult to translate the expectations of the system design. This situa-
tion is quite difficult especially for the project manager. Firstly, it is very difficult to 
determine the scope of the project (how much time it will take, what should be done). 
Secondly, during the implementation of the project, it may be that the client begins to

An Approach to Agent-Based Supporting System for IT Projects 355 
identify what is expected and these expectations are quite different from the goals at 
the beginning. This obviously results in the need to make changes in the project, in 
the worst case meaning that some work has been done in vain. 
The opposite situation may happen, however, when the client knows what he needs 
and he is able to further specify precision at every stage of the project. This may be 
due to his knowledge of the IT industry, or his awareness that his precise expectations 
are essential - to himself and the contractor of the project. 
So how can one understand the role of the customer IT enterprise? Certainly, the key 
to all of the work. Customer requirements may change; the customer may modify a set 
of desired functionality. They may also require changes to the project and conclude that 
the work carried out does not coincide with their own vision of the IT solution. 
In addition, it should be noted that the team becomes a necessity and yet the project 
cannot predict customer behavior. Unfortunately, any unpredicted customer behavior 
can affect the course of work, causing changes in the schedule or scope. This means, 
therefore, that the project manager should co nsider binding a client to plan. This also 
means that the client behavior must be taken into account when matching the imple-
mentation method of the project. It may be that for certain types of customer behav-
iors, it is better to use an agile method; for others a classical one. 
The presented characterization of the client should be called maturity. Maturity 
means how the client is able to imply changes in the realized project. In other words, 
the maturity of the client is this combination of traits and behaviors that affect the 
course of the project and the chosen method for this project. 
Customer maturity may be presented as a model matrix, which serves to precisely 
define the customer profile, where the maturity of the client is represented by two 
features: matching (fitting) and suitability. The combination of these features there-
fore allows us to build the following matrix:

Thus shown, a combination of key parameters are a starting point for the client to

4.1   Team and Organization 
Prior to the implementation of IT projects, the role of the manager is to plan properly 
and obtain resources (including human), which should be used during the project’s 
lifetime. The primary resource is undoubtedly the team and the people creating it. 
Over roughly a decade, the role of the human factor in business activity has in-
creased substantially. Knowledge management in a highly dynamic market has led to 
a growing interest in intellectual capital, which largely consists of what people do. 
The definition of human capital is that it is understood as " inseparably integrated 
with the man (employee), his knowledge, experience, presence and capabilities of the 
enterprise." [7] This means, therefore, that the quality of that capital can have a large 
impact on the success of any conducted activities. 
There is therefore no doubt that in the case of the implementation of IT projects the 
team's role is particularly important. How effective and efficient the team will be, will 
determine the success of IT projects. The role of the manager is to steer the work in 
such a way that all members work in an optimal manner. 
The maturity of the project team should therefore be analyzed by the project man-
ager, so that the right team is selected for the method of the project. It very often turns 
out that less mature teams do not do well in projects with a high degree of variability 
(which is carried out using agile methods). Analogously, for such projects it is easier 
to organize the work of a very experienced team (which is consistent with agile meth-
ods) than to fit into a fairly rigid framework of classical methods. The validity of the 
level of maturity of the team to the selection method convinced the authors of this 
article in one of our projects. At the beginning of the proposed project, a small experi-
enced team composed of 18 members divided into smaller groups, which organized 
their work. Unfortunately, such a decision was not matched by significant progress. 
When a lack of top-down task clarifica tion was observed, it was decided to create a 
plan of action (i.e. reference is made to the assumptions of classical methods of pro-
ject management). Then this was presented to participants in areas of task forces (in 
accordance with RUP, where the tasks are defi ned in disciplines, reflecting the nature 
of tasks, such as testing, manufacture, management, etc.). This approach was met with 
great enthusiasm by the participants and constituted a breakthrough in the project, 
giving the chance to continue to work more effectively in the separate groups of tasks 
from the top down. It thus follows that the selection method is important from the 
standpoint of the implementation of a group of tasks. 
4.2   Project Entropy 
Entropy (dispersion) of the project is a new concept for the project and is a measure 
of the degree of disorder. It is assumed that the entropy is a measure of the uncertainty 
of project implementation and management of manufacturing processes.

An Approach to Agent-Based Supporting System for IT Projects 357 
4.3   Agent System Architecture 
In the course of the work on the model, the following components of the model have 
been accepted (Figure 1): 
 
 
Fig. 2. Architecture of an IT assessment agent system 
The User reports that he or she wants to ask a question on a specific domain (1). 
The request is handled by the Intermediary Agent 1 (with a GUI role). The Ontology 
Agent 1 is then used to provide the proper domain ontology (2, 3). The questionnaire 
form is presented to a User by an Intermediary Agent 1 (4). The User inputs a ques-
tion (5), which is further transferred to the Managing Agent (6). This Agent sends the 
User’s question to the Searching Agent (7). Depending on the question provided, 
different parts of the knowledge base may need to be utilized in this process. That is 
why dedicated searching agents can be run—for rule bases (8a) or fact bases (8bc). 
The searching process is in progress (9) an d the results are collected (10) and passed 
to the Searching Agent (11). The answer is transferred to the Managing Agent which 
sends it to the Intermediary Agent 2 (12). The answer must be provided to the User in 
a human-readable form. That is why the ontology is used to serve the appropriate 
notions and semantics (14, 15). After these post-processing activities, the answer is 
displayed to the User (16).[9]. 
Thus the task of agents and the issue of input into the system is set, allowing for 
the appointment of the next step, the presented concepts. Indeed, it seems reasonable 
to continue to carry out a detailed stage parameterization of input variables (customer 
maturity, maturity group, and the entropy of the project) by defining measurable val-
ues, so that it will be possible to complete their processing by the system agents. It is 
also reasonable to have a proxy agent equipped with such knowledge resources,

358 C. Orłowski and A. Ziółkowski 
which enables the agent to accurately determine the input parameters of the system.

parameterization can be the vector-matrix approach.

the user is suggested which method of IT project completion should be used for the 
purpose of enterprise architecture development. At the first stage of the system opera-
tion, the agent downloads information entered by the user in the query field. The 
information is uploaded to the management agent. Based on the information, the 
management agent makes a decision about using the system resources. Such task flow 
results from the established organization of the system, where agents are classified 
according to functions and hierarchy. With the help of the knowledge base, the man-
agement agent analyses the uploaded query. If a search is needed, the management 
agent activates the search agent and sends the message concerning a search of the 
knowledge base (fact base). When a calculation is needed, the management agent 
activates the calculation module (expert system, neuron network) and then orders the 
search agent to collect the results. Next, the results are sent to the management agent. 
The results collected from the calculation are uploaded to the customer through the 
mediator agent. 
At the same time, this structure indicates the need for the optimal choice of as-
sessment model. Currently, a system which could use fuzzy modeling appears to be 
the most efficient one. It has also been planned to extend the module responsible for 
statistical analysis as well as modeling using data correctness verification. The thus 
constructed whole is aimed at achieving high-quality results. 
5   Summary 
The dynamic development of the IT branch causes a great need for specialists in in-
formation project management. The development of computerization in Poland in-
volves the increased demand for employees to know not only information problems 
but management problems too. Information project management is a kind of sphere 
that joins both these aspects. To lead a project well, a manager should be knowledge-
able in information science topics, but should also be someone that can build a good 
team, define tasks for all project participants and can guarantee full-effective realiza-
tion of the project. Thus, when someone wishes to make their project successful, he 
should support all the processes during the realization of the project using information 
tools. It is very important to match these tools well. The agent system presented in 
this article should help project managers to match the right methods to the projects 
they are leading.

Abstract. Conference management that requires proper coordination
and international communication, is a complex task. There are many
Conference Management Systems (CMS), which can be used to carry
out the conference. A convenient to use, free and eﬀective module for au-
tomatic paper-reviewer assignment is still not available. Searching for the
best assignments relying only on common paper-reviewer topics not al-
ways will give good solutions. This paper proposes an approach, that uses
the reviewers responses information, to tune the solution up. Proposed
algorithm combines genetic algorithm (GA) and ant colony optimization
(ACO), to quickly ﬁnd good solutions. The experiment results conﬁrm
the superiority of proposed algorithm.

Updatable Multi-agent OSGi Architecture
for Smart Home System
Piotr Jaszczyk1 and Dariusz Kr´ol2
1 Faculty of Computer Science and Management,

Abstract. Smart home is an adaptive system that controls house to
make household members’ life easier. There are plenty of not yet re-
searched issues concerning this concept, such as the ability to update the
architecture during system runtime. This paper presents a solution how
to design such system on the JADE framework. To solve the problem
of on-the-ﬂy update, each agent needs to work in an OSGi environment.
The proposal of new architecture is evaluated by means of the use case
technique.

4 Conclusion and Future Research
In this research, an architecture which tries to solveaf e w problems that may
occur whiled eveloping Smart Home Systems has been developed.F irst problem
is“The Accidentally Smart Home”,see [5]. The vast majorityo fs m a r thomes are
notb uild in the ground-up approach.P eople will upgrade theire xistingh ouses
by buying new smart devices (architecture upgrade). The proposed architecture
allows new devices toi ntegrate andc ooperate with the existings ystem. Other
issue is the upgrade ofd evices’ agents (software upgrade). Software isc ontinu-
ously andr a pidly developing, thus the need ofs ome mechanism of upgrading.
Nextp roblem which proposed architecture tries to solve ist h ea r c hitecture self-
optimization. Since the arch itecture will be continuously changingt h e r em ay
occur neww ays of agents’ distribution. The result isa no pen, expandable agent
architecture implemented on the JADEa ndO SGi platforms.
However there are few more issues which shouldb ec onsidered in future work.
Probably the most important one is security. While installinga new device it
registers itself in the cDMA via wireless network.B ut what ifu s e r’s neighbour

An Approach to Evaluate the Impact
of Web Traﬃc in Web Positioning
Pawe/suppresslK o walski1 and Dariusz Kr´ol2

Abstract. Search engine algorithms are constantly changing. One of
the factors that can gain importance in these algorithms is measurable
web traﬃc. This fact can aﬀect the web positioning techniques. The aim
of this article is to evaluate the impact of users activity on the website
position in Google search result pages. The paper presents an approach
to generate a web traﬃc visible for search engines. However, click fraud
protection in search engines requires this traﬃc to be human-like in or-
der to avoid having been ﬁltered. A multi-agent system seems to be the
reasonable solution to this issue. It allows to generate distributed web
traﬃc. If appropriate algorithm to coordinate agents is used, the system
should imitate human activity more and, therefore, be more user-friendly.
Keywords: click fraud, PageRank, search engine optimization, web po-
sitioning, web traﬃc.

Agent System for Managing Distributed  
Mobile Interactive Documents  
Magdalena Godlewska 
Gdańsk University of Technology 
Faculty of Electronics, Telecommunications and Informatics 
ul. Narutowicza 11/12, 80-952 Gdańsk 
magdal@eti.pg.gda.pl 
Abstract. The MIND architecture of distributed mobile interactive document is 
a new processing model defined for facilitate informed decision-making in non-
algorithmic decision-making processes carried out by knowledge-based organi-
zations. The aim of this architecture is to  change the static document to mobile 
agents, which are designed to implement the structure of the organization 
through autonomous migration between knowledge workers in accordance with 
the built-in policy. An extensible functi onality of the agents also extends the 
static document to interface unit. The prototype of the agent system, based on 
the MIND architecture, shows the possibi lity of its implementation using avail-
able technology. The case studies provide the possibility of using architecture to 
solve specific decision problems with external knowledge of organization’s 
workers. 
Keywords: Agent system, collaborative computing, knowledge-based organi-
zations, policy-driven management, interactive documents. 
1   Introduction 
MIND architecture  of distributed mobile interactive document is a new processing 
model. Traditionally electronic documents have been treated as static objects 
downloaded from a server or sent by an e-mail. The MIND provides for exchange of 
static documents into a set of mobile agents, that can migrate between authors accord-
ing to a fixed migration policy. 
The MIND architecture makes possible a radical shift from data-centric distributed 
systems, with hard-coded functionality, to flexible document-centric ones, where only 
generic services are provided by local environments, while specialized functionality is 
embedded in migrating document components.  
In order to verify the assumptions of the MIND architecture and its possible  
implementation with the use of available technology, a set of prototype tools was 
implemented. This set of tools can be defined as an environment for designing and 
managing document migration. Among these tools is a document editor that supports 
the design of documents in accordance with the assumptions of the MIND architec-
ture and agent system that allows management components of documents.

Agent System for Managing Distributed Mobile Interactive Documents 391 
The aim of research on this architecture is to develop a new model of object proc-
essing based on a system consisting of migrant components. Each document compo-
nent is intelligent because of built-in functionality and mobile because of capabilities 
of migration in the system according to the inscribed policy. Workflow description 
language supported by the agent system will perform the workflow control-flow pat-
terns, which are used in decision-making processes involving documents. Intelligent 
and mobile components form the MIND architecture that supports decision-making 
by participants in collaborative computing of virtual knowledge-based organizations. 
In this paper the author presents the general assumptions of the MIND architecture, 
describes the elements of the agent system for managing distributed mobile docu-
ments and shows case studies that use the MIND architecture. 
2   Related Work 
The presented proposal combines existing technologies and new idea to extract some 
new functionality in the topics of distributed electronic document and collaborative 
environments. Unmarshalling and marshalling [1] allow XML documents [2] to be 
switched from static to dynamic form. Full distribution guarantees convenience of 
working in group and minimizes needs to connect with central server. Proposed solu-
tion differs from collaborative editing problem (algorithms solving that problem are 
introduced e.g. in [3]-[5]). Collaborative editing is the situation when users edit 
together the same document (the same part of document). This paper introduces 
problem when users work on different parts of one document. 
It is worth mentioning that the proposal is something different than shared work-
space (e.g. BSCW – Basic Support for Cooperative Work [6]) or repository (e.g. CVS 
- Concurrent Versions System [7]). Those concepts are based on server. Users are 
able to upload and download some objects (documents, sources etc.), to communicate 
with other users, to be informed about some restrictions like deadlines. But most op-
erations take place on the server. In the proposed concepts agent-objects have build-in 
functionality that has effect of shifting some services from server location to user 
location. That solution limits client-server communication. That feature distinguishes 
the proposal from client-server based applications like Collaboratus [8].  
Full distribution and minimizing client-s erver communication are needed in work-
flow. Components of document do not have common location. They are able to  
migrate between users according to some policy. When there are many users in  
collaborative group (e.g. in court trials), the problem of too many client-server com-
municates appears. More independence form server allows also for implementing 
assumption that system managing documents should be as transparent to user as it is 
possible.  
Workflow, based on the agent platform, is also implemented by WADE – Work-
flow and Agents Development Environment [9]  software platform. The proposed 
concept differs from that implemented in WADE, because WADE is a data-centric 
approach and MIND is a document-centric one. In MIND architecture, workflow (as a 
XPDL [10] file) is a part of the whole document. Workflow in the form of a document 
may be modified during the process execution. This allows the implementation of

392 M. Godlewska 
complex workflow patterns, i.e. Multiple Instances with a Priori Run-Time Knowl-
edge or Multiple Instances without a Priori Run-time Knowledge presented in [11]. 
3   MIND Architecture 
The main goal of the MIND architecture is to change the static document to mobile 
components, that meet their mission in the distributed agent system. This architecture 
has been proposed with a view of facilitating the collaboration of knowledge workers 
in virtual knowledge-based organizations. In such organizations, a set of particular 
decision taken by workers contributes to the final decision. There are some important 
elements in decision-making process: the structure of organization and knowledge of 
workers passed through the documents. In such a process the external data sources 
(knowledge of workers) appear, therefore the process can be defined as non-
algorithmic. The examples of such processes are court trials, integrative bargaining, 
medical consultations, or crash investigations. 
The MIND architecture involves the creation of a document that contains structure 
of the process and basic documents. The basic documents follow a defined structure 
(migration policy) to move between their authors in the form of mobile agents and 
then, as the interface unit, assist in extracting knowledge from authors . 
The main components of the architecture are:  HDDL (Hub Document Description 
Language) [12] document template, that is defined in XML Schema [2] and the agent 
system for document managing. The document template contains the following com-
ponents: 
− document.xml – basic information about the document in the form of a header and 
a specification of embedded services 
− authors.xml – data about the authors (knowledge workers) 
− templates.xml – a set of basic document templates  
− parts.xml – initial elements of the document 
− path.xml – a workflow definition 
In the architecture some additional services can be defined. They allow for adjust the 
architecture to the particular use case. From the user's perspective, these services can 
be local (installed on local computer), external (accessible from the outside) and em-
bedded (build-in in agent). 
Accurate discussion of the MIND architecture assumptions, as well as a model of 
non-algorithmic decision-making process carried out by knowledge-based organiza-
tions can be found in the earlier paper [13].  
4   Prototype System for Managing Distributed Documents 
The static MIND document is designed in such way that it can be transformed into the 
object form, and then into a set of mobile agents. The mobile agents migrate between 
user’s local workstations in accordance with a defined migration path. Based on the 
MIND architecture the prototype system for remote management of distributed com-
ponents of the document has been implemented.

Agent System for Managing Distributed Mobile Interactive Documents 393 
In the prototype system for managing distributed documents the following tech-
nologies are used. Static documents are implemented in XML language in accordance 
with the HDDL format designed for the MIND architecture. HDDL format has been 
specified in XML Schema. To design workflow process XPDL format [10] is used. 
Server application [14] has been written in Java and JADE platform [15] is used for 
the creation, migration and tracking of agents. XMLBeans [1] is a technology used for 
accessing XML by binding it to Java types, Java Mail platform [16] is used for trans-
ferring  agents via e-mail and Log4j [17] tool is used for creation of event logs.  
The reasons for choosing these technologies in prototype are described in detail in 
previous publication [18]. The MIND architecture is not dependent on the chosen 
technologies and for its implementation different ones may be chosen. To describe the 
structure of documents and workflow XML language was selected. The possibility of 
its transformation and processing with programming languages allows to use its also 
in the future. The advantage of easy archiving of XML documents is particularly 
important in the documents, which will remain valid for many years, such as e.g. 
property rights. 
In order to facilitate the preparation of the documents in HDDL format the follow-
ing tools have been implemented: HDDLEdit [12] for creating and editing  patterns of 
document and STMPEdit [12] for creating and editing of basic documents, that form 
the basic units in the prototype system. 
4.1   The Life Cycle of a Distributed Document in the Agent System 
The system for managing components of the document is designed to implement the 
concept of converting a static form of th e document to the autonomous agents that 
will meet their mission in the system, and then create a final document (cf. Fig.1.).

Fig. 1. The life cycle of a MIND document in the implemented system

394 M. Godlewska 
Agents have built-in migration functionality defined in the MIND policy file. Ac-
cording to the next stage of the document’s life cycle, the agents migrate between the 
authors computers with a basic document. The basic document’s content is processed 
by the respective authors. Organization of the agents population is involved in the 
agent system. The components of the system are run on the users computers. They 
create a platform that enables the functioning of the agents on each workstation, pro-
vides access to memory and enables the use of communication protocols. These pro-
tocols allow agents to exchange messages, and migrate independently on the network. 
If the author's computer is offline in terms of  the agent platform, the system sends the 
agent by e-mail. 
During the completion of the life cycle of the document, the agents reach different 
states, which, in the form of a diagram, is shown in Fig. 2.  
Active
Final
Archived
SentHibernate
Deleted
 
Fig. 2. Agent’s states diagram 
An active state is a state when the agent is run on the agent platform. The agent is 
in a hibernate state in a situation when the user of the current agent’s container 
chooses to stop work and turn off the application. The agent in this state is saved as a 
file (this operation called serialization) on user’s local computer. When the system is 
restarted, the agent can be rerun (transition from hibernate to active state). When the 
next agent’s author is offline in the agent platform, the agent is sent to him by e-mail. 
This additional functionality moves the agent to a sent state. Agent is in this state, as 
long as the agent is stored on the mail server. The agent is received from the e-mail 
server and brought back to the active state after restarting the application. When the 
agent arrives to final activity in the process, it moves to the final state. The agent in 
the final state may be deleted or archived (saved to a file). 
4.2   The Main Modules of the System 
The application server for remote management of distributed document components 
consists of the following modules: agent server module, e-mail module, policy mod-
ule, document module, mediator module and initial module 
Agent Server Module 
The basic element in the agent server module is a JADEServer class. The object of 
this class starts JADE platform. JADE platform provides a set of containers. One of 
them is called a main container. The container is JADE object that allows to run the 
agents. In the main container, three functio nal agents (AMS, DF, RMA) are run. They

Agent System for Managing Distributed Mobile Interactive Documents 395 
control the JADE platform and move the agents. Any other containers must liaise 
with the main container in order to join the JADE platform. 
The cooperation of the various computers in one agent system is possible when all 
containers are connected to the main container.  Users of containers must enter IP 
address of main container to connect to the platform. A successful connection to the 
main container determines that the local system will work online. If connection to the 
main container is not possible, the user must work offline. When the JADE platform 
is started, the agent server module is responsible for managing agents, i.e. for creat-
ing, awakening and deleting agents. 
The agent is built on the basis of the XML document conforming to the MIND archi-
tecture. The agent gets as input arguments the following information: a unique name, 
policy file and basic document ID. Awakening of the agent means running it from a file 
and changing it state from hibernate to active or from sent to active (cf. Fig. 2). 
Functionality of migration enables the agent to transfer in the JADE system. For 
this purpose, some parameters are determined: the name of the agent to be sent, the 
place of its destination after a jump and the basic document to be forwarded. 
E-mail Module 
E-mails are not saved directly in a recipient’s computer, but are stored on mail serv-
ers. Implementation of the e-mail module allows to transfer the serialized agent by  
e-mail when sending it to the JADE server is not possible. This allows the agent to 
reach to assigned recipient even if at the time of dispatch his container is not regis-
tered in the system (i.e. from the viewpoint of the system the recipient is offline). 
The e-mail module uses the Java Mail platform and it is equipped with a set of 
classes responsible for handling e-mail servers, sending and receiving e-mails with a 
specific name. This name allow to distinguish messages with agents from others. A 
main class of module ( MailServer class) implements the operations of sending and 
receiving the agents. Before sending, the agent is serialized to a file. To take advan-
tage of this mechanism, the authors specified on the migration path must have e-mail 
addresses. 
Policy Module and Document Module 
The policy module is separated from the module that manages the other parts of the 
document, because of the very important role in the agents migration. The XPDL file 
defines the process of moving the agents in the system. The policy module provides a 
binding XPDL file to Java objects. For this purpose, XML Beans tool was used to 
generate xpdl.jar file based on XML Schema template for  XPDL language. The 
xpdl.jar library allows for creation of the object representation of XPDL files within 
the system. 
The task of the policy module is mapping a static representation of the policy file 
(path.xml) to the Java reference mechanism. The module opens the policy file (or 
files), interprets its structure and then creates Java objects. 
Completion of work on a basic document in current node triggers the movement of 
this document to another node. In this case, the policy server searches possible transi-
tions. The module creates a collection of locations, which the agent must visit in the 
next step. In this case, the location means a container in the JADE system or e-mail 
address of the next user of the system.

396 M. Godlewska 
The document module allows to load and manage other components of the MIND 
document. In particular, its task is to choose the appropriate basic document in accor-
dance with an activity element from the policy file. 
This module also maps the static XML document to Java objects.  XML Beans tool 
was used to generate XMLHubDoc.jar library based on XML Schema template de-
fined for the MIND architecture. 
The document module is responsible for extracting the basic document from the 
agent and saving it on the local computer of the author assigned to the activity. Then 
the author can perform on that document some actions. After that, the document's 
current version is re-loaded by the agent and moved to another location. When the 
agent reaches the final location, the document is integrated. 
Mediator Module and Initial Module 
Unlike other modules, the mediator does not provide any operation. This service is 
implemented only to provide the communication between other modules and mediate 
in the running of methods. It also allows for easy implementation of subsequent mod-
ules in the evolution of the system. 
The initial module runs all subsystems (modules). The task of the module is to take 
data from the user during the login to the system and booting the system. 
4.3   Prototype Application’s Performance 
The system for managing of components is used to implement the life cycle of the 
MIND documents. The authors defined in the document should be the holders of the 
application, that creates the containers that forming a part of the JADE platform. After 
running the application, dialog box for authors authorization appears. During the login 
operation, the author gives the IP of the main container  (unless the main container is 
created) and the name of the local container. The author may choose to work offline, 
i.e. a work without connection to the main container. After the successful authentica-
tion, the particular modules are run. That l eads to join the container to the JADE plat-
form and runs the possibility of receiving, status changing and sending agents. 
Launching an application as a main container causes running an additional mecha-
nism to monitor the agents and containers on the JADE platform. For this purpose, 
JADE provides a tool in the form of a dialog box. 
In the next step after running, the application converts the MIND document to ob-
jects (this operation is called unmarshalling). The policy and document modules are 
responsible for that. A set of agents is created on the basis of start activities. A unique 
number (consistent with the activity ID) and ID number of the basic document are 
assigned to each agent. 
An agent interface is a simple dialog box with two possible actions: Done and Exit. 
The agent’s GUI may be expanded depending on the system use cases. When the 
author finishes work on a basic document, selects the Done action. The agent then 
reads from the policy file its next activity and moves to a new location. If the con-
tainer of the target activity is present on the platform, the agent is sent by the JADE , 
otherwise the agent is sent by e-mail. In this way, the agent transfers the basic docu-
ment according to the defined workflow. Once the agent reaches a final location, 
Done action deletes the agent or transfers it to the archiving location. In both cases, 
the basic document is saved on the local computer.

Agent System for Managing Distributed Mobile Interactive Documents 397 
If the author chooses the Exit action, it means that he has not finished to work on 
the basic document yet. Then the agent is saved on his local computer as a file and the 
basic document is also saved as a static XML document. When the system is rerun, 
the agent is awaked and the basic documen t is upgraded in accordance with the new 
version from the local computer.  
5   Case Studies of the MIND Architecture 
The MIND architecture was created with a vi ew to facilitating a decision-making in 
complex decision-making processes, in which the electronic circulation of documents 
and extracting knowledge from them is crucial. In order to demonstrate this possibil-
ity of the MIND architecture, two case studies have been implemented. The first of 
these concerns the large-scale problem of ju dicial proceedings. Document in the form 
of complete files can reach an enormous size. The prototype system is not yet ready to 
carry out experiments in this target environment. The experiment took place to verify 
the adequacy of the used notation and the scope of the required functionality. 
In a court trial, there are many documents that are often small and have specified 
structure. The workflow of the files is defined by organizational structure of the 
courts. In this case, there is a possibility to use the agent system for managing the 
electronic files.  
The second case study involved the issue of evaluation of students in a typical  
university environment. This problem allows to test the mechanisms of the MIND 
architecture. In a teaching management system, a person, who receives a document 
template, is a student, and an evaluation card of one subject is a single MIND docu-
ment. In the authors file, there are teachers that leads one subject for a group of  
students. The basic document is transmitted from one teacher to another, according to 
the policy file. The teacher responsible for the subject and the student receive the final 
version of the evaluation card. In the first case the agent is archived, and in the  
second, the agent is removed.

system. AUT000 is the student’s ID. The student is the author placed in the start ac-

person responsible for the part of subject is the author of the second final activity. The

agent is archived on his computer. This allows to trace the migration path of the 
document by the responsible author. 
The teaching management system in its current form is meeting its objectives, but 
it is not completely user-friendly. To edit the basic documents on the system nodes 
the STMPEdit editor may be used as a local  service. However, it is rather cumber-
some solution. Hence, the are plans to implement tools to improve the system from 
the user perspective. There are possibilities to implement new functionalities in the 
MIND architecture through a mechanism of embedded, local and remote services. 
6   Conclusions 
The prototype server for managing components in the current stage does not imple-
ment all the principles of the MIND architecture. In the next version of the prototype 
new functionality will be added, such as: adding new components, granting of various 
rights of access and views of the basic documents, adding new authors and modifying 
the policy files. A persistent addressing will be implemented to identify author’s lo-
calization by name instead of computer’s IP. This functionality allows the author to 
work on different computers. A control of the agent migration and edition of the 
document will be extended by adding conditions of transitions and checking the time 
of execution of the various tasks. 
The next stage of development of the MIND architecture is to ensure the reliability 
of processing and security of document. Reliability of the process refers to the  
possibility of self-diagnosis of distributed document in a situation where some of its 
component are lost or where some components are changed by unauthorized persons. 
Security of document concerns encryption of its the content and digital signatures.

Abstract. Internet and demand for bandwidth is growing rapidly. New
services are being constantly introduced. Static contracts do not reﬂect
the dynamics of customer’s needs. On the other hand, there is some
amount of valuation coming from safety and bandwidth price guarantee.
In order to satisfy both of those factors, two level allocation process is
introduced. This dual auctioning process allows to make long and short
term bandwidth contracts depending on speciﬁc agent preferences. By
exploiting iterative Vickrey auction mechanism at both allocation levels,
eﬃciency of the process is maintained.
